prompts.title: Email Welcoming a New Buyer Lead
prompts.useWhen: A new buyer inquiry comes in (website form, sign call, referral) and you need a first email that sounds personal, not like a form letter.
prompts.prompt: You are a friendly, professional real estate agent named [YOUR NAME] at [BROKERAGE] in [CITY]. Write a short welcome email to a new buyer lead named [LEAD FIRST NAME] who asked about [PROPERTY OR AREA]. Thank them, share one helpful fact about [NEIGHBORHOOD OR MARKET], and ask 2 simple questions about their timeline and price range. End by offering a 15-minute call on [DAYS/TIMES]. Keep it under 150 words, warm and confident, with a clear subject line. Give me 2 subject line options.
prompts.proTip: Paste in what the lead actually wrote so the AI can mirror their words and make the email feel one-to-one.

prompts.title: Email Welcome Packet for a New Listing Client
prompts.useWhen: A seller just signed the listing agreement and you want to set expectations (welcome letter, "what happens next" message).
prompts.prompt: Act as a top-producing listing agent. Write a welcome email to my new seller client [SELLER FIRST NAME] for their home at [PROPERTY ADDRESS]. Explain in plain language what happens over the next 14 days: photos, prep, launch, showings, and feedback. Include a short bullet list of 5 things I need from them, such as [ITEM 1], [ITEM 2], and [ITEM 3]. Mention how often I will update them ([UPDATE FREQUENCY]) and how they can reach me. Keep the tone reassuring and organized. Use short paragraphs.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to turn the same email into a one-page PDF-style checklist you can attach.

prompts.title: Text Message Showing Confirmation and Reminder
prompts.useWhen: You need quick texts to confirm, remind, or reschedule a showing (appointment reminder, "running late" note).
prompts.prompt: Write 4 short text messages I can send to a buyer client named [CLIENT FIRST NAME] about a showing at [PROPERTY ADDRESS] on [DATE AND TIME]. Message 1: confirm the appointment. Message 2: a same-day reminder with parking tip: [PARKING NOTE]. Message 3: a friendly "running [NUMBER] minutes late" note. Message 4: a polite reschedule request with 2 new time options. Each text must be under 300 characters, friendly, and sign off with my name, [YOUR NAME]. No emojis.
prompts.proTip: Save the results in your phone's text shortcuts so you can send them in two taps.

prompts.title: Email Weekly Update to a Seller
prompts.useWhen: You need a listing activity report (seller update, feedback recap) that keeps a nervous seller calm and informed.
prompts.prompt: You are a listing agent writing a weekly update to seller [SELLER FIRST NAME] about [PROPERTY ADDRESS]. Use these numbers: [NUMBER] showings, [NUMBER] online views, [NUMBER] inquiries, and this buyer feedback: [PASTE FEEDBACK]. Write a clear email with a 2-sentence summary, a bullet list of the numbers, a section called "What we heard," and a section called "What I recommend next." Be honest and calm. If activity is low, suggest 2 practical options without blaming the seller. Under 250 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version that is shorter for sellers who only read the first three lines.

prompts.title: Email Explaining the Home Buying Process to First-Time Buyers
prompts.useWhen: First-time homebuyers feel overwhelmed and ask "what are the steps to buy a home?" (buyer roadmap, step-by-step guide).
prompts.prompt: Write a friendly email for first-time buyers named [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] that explains the home buying process in 8 simple steps, from getting pre-approved to closing day. Use a 6th-grade reading level and no jargon, or explain any term in one short sentence. For each step, add one line on what they need to do and one line on what I ([YOUR NAME]) will handle. Mention that timelines in [STATE OR CITY] can vary. End with an invitation to ask questions. Add a note that lender and legal questions should go to the proper professionals.
prompts.proTip: Follow up with "Turn this into a one-page checklist with checkboxes" for a handout.

prompts.title: Email Recap After a Client Consultation
prompts.useWhen: You just finished a buyer or seller meeting and want a written summary (meeting notes, next steps email) so nothing gets lost.
prompts.prompt: Turn my rough notes into a professional follow-up email to [CLIENT FIRST NAME]. Notes: [PASTE YOUR MEETING NOTES]. Structure the email with: a thank-you line, "What we discussed" in 3 to 5 bullets, "What you will do next" with dates, and "What I will do next" with dates. Confirm our next meeting on [DATE]. Keep the tone warm, clear, and organized, and keep it under 200 words. Do not add any facts that are not in my notes.
prompts.proTip: Say "Do not add facts" every time. It stops the AI from inventing details.

prompts.title: Email Congratulating Clients on an Accepted Offer
prompts.useWhen: The offer was accepted (under contract, "we got the house") and clients want to know what happens next.
prompts.prompt: Write an exciting but professional email to my buyer clients [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] congratulating them on their accepted offer for [PROPERTY ADDRESS] at [PRICE]. Include a dated timeline of the next steps: earnest money due [DATE], inspection [DATE], appraisal [DATE], loan approval [DATE], and closing [DATE]. Add a short "Please do not do these things" list about their finances, such as opening new credit or making big purchases, and tell them to check with their lender. Keep the tone celebratory and clear.
prompts.proTip: Double-check every date against your contract before you send.

prompts.title: Checklist Email for Closing Day
prompts.useWhen: Closing is near and clients ask "what do I need to bring to closing?" (closing day reminder, settlement checklist).
prompts.prompt: Write a closing day email for my client [CLIENT FIRST NAME] who is [BUYING OR SELLING] at [PROPERTY ADDRESS]. Closing is on [DATE] at [TIME] at [LOCATION]. Include a checklist of what to bring (photo ID, payment method as instructed by the title company, [OTHER ITEMS]), what to expect at the table, and how long it usually takes. For buyers, add a final walkthrough reminder. For sellers, add a reminder about keys, garage remotes, and utilities. Tell them to confirm all money details directly with [TITLE COMPANY].
prompts.proTip: Never let the AI guess wire or payment instructions. Always send clients to the title company by phone.

prompts.title: Text and Email Check-In 30 Days After Closing
prompts.useWhen: You want to stay in touch after the sale (post-closing follow-up, client care) and ask for a review or referral naturally.
prompts.prompt: Write two messages for a past client named [CLIENT FIRST NAME] who closed on [DATE] at [PROPERTY ADDRESS]: a short text and a longer email. Both should ask how the move is going and offer help with [HELPFUL RESOURCE, such as trusted movers or handyman list]. In the email only, softly ask for a review at [REVIEW LINK] and mention that I love helping their friends and family. Keep the tone genuine, not salesy. Text under 200 characters. Email under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Send this on day 30, not day 3. Clients are settled in and more likely to leave a review.
fields: HELPFUL RESOURCE, such as trusted movers or handyman list

prompts.title: Email Home Anniversary Note to Past Clients
prompts.useWhen: You want a yearly touch to stay top of mind (past client outreach, client appreciation, sphere follow-up).
prompts.prompt: Write a warm home anniversary email to [CLIENT FIRST NAME] to mark [NUMBER] year(s) since they bought their home at [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Include one sentence about the local market ([MARKET FACT]), one useful home tip for this season ([SEASON]), and an offer for a free, no-pressure home value check. Keep it short, personal, and under 120 words. Do not predict prices or promise anything about future value. Give me 2 subject lines.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a matching handwritten card message of 25 words so you can send both.

prompts.title: Listing Description for a Single-Family Home (MLS)
prompts.useWhen: You need MLS remarks or a property write-up for a house (listing copy, home description) and want it to sell without breaking fair housing rules.
prompts.prompt: You are an expert real estate copywriter. Write an MLS listing description for a single-family home at [ADDRESS OR NEIGHBORHOOD]. Facts: [BEDS] beds, [BATHS] baths, [SQFT] sq ft, [LOT SIZE], built [YEAR], updates: [UPDATES], features: [KEY FEATURES]. Price: [PRICE]. Write 3 versions: 500 characters, 900 characters, and a longer 200-word version for my website. Describe the property only, never the type of buyer. Use fair housing safe language, avoid clichés like "must see," and only use facts I gave you.
prompts.proTip: Put your best feature in the first sentence, since many sites only show the first two lines.

prompts.title: Listing Description for a Condo or Townhome
prompts.useWhen: You are marketing a condo, townhouse, or apartment-style unit (HOA property, low-maintenance home) and need to explain the lifestyle features clearly.
prompts.prompt: Write a listing description for a [CONDO OR TOWNHOME] at [BUILDING OR COMMUNITY NAME]. Facts: [BEDS] beds, [BATHS] baths, [SQFT] sq ft, floor [FLOOR], HOA fee [HOA FEE] covering [HOA INCLUDES], amenities: [AMENITIES], parking: [PARKING]. Write 2 versions: a 600-character MLS version and a 150-word website version. Highlight the low-maintenance features and location perks such as [NEARBY PLACES] using only facts. Do not describe who should live here. Fair housing safe language only.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a separate "HOA and fees explained" paragraph. It answers the questions buyers always ask.

prompts.title: Listing Description for a Fixer-Upper or Investor Special
prompts.useWhen: The home needs work (as-is sale, handyman special, investment property, rehab) and you want honest, positive copy.
prompts.prompt: Write a truthful, upbeat listing description for a fixer-upper at [ADDRESS OR AREA]. Facts: [BEDS] beds, [BATHS] baths, [SQFT] sq ft, built [YEAR], sold as-is. Known needs: [REPAIRS NEEDED]. Strong points: [STRENGTHS, like lot size, location, layout]. Price: [PRICE]. Use words like "opportunity" and "potential" without making promises about profit or value. Mention any cash-only or financing notes: [FINANCING NOTES]. Keep it under 180 words. Include a one-line disclosure that buyers should do their own inspections.
prompts.proTip: Never hide known problems. Honest copy attracts serious buyers and protects you from complaints.
fields: STRENGTHS, like lot size, location, layout

prompts.title: Listing Description for a Luxury Home
prompts.useWhen: You have a high-end property (luxury listing, estate, premium home) and need elegant, specific copy instead of generic words.
prompts.prompt: You are a luxury real estate copywriter. Write a refined listing description for a [PRICE] home at [ADDRESS OR COMMUNITY]. Facts: [BEDS] beds, [BATHS] baths, [SQFT] sq ft, [ACRES] acres, design details: [ARCHITECT OR STYLE], premium features: [FEATURES]. Write a 120-word version for print and a 60-word version for social media. Use specific, sensory details instead of vague words like "stunning" or "luxurious." Describe the home, not the buyer. Keep the tone confident and calm.
prompts.proTip: Give the AI real materials and brands (marble type, window maker). Specifics signal luxury more than adjectives do.

prompts.title: Checklist Fair Housing Review of Your Listing Copy
prompts.useWhen: You want to check an ad, post, or description for fair housing problems (discriminatory wording, steering, compliance check) before you publish.
prompts.prompt: Act as a careful fair housing reviewer for real estate marketing in [STATE]. Read the text below and flag any words or phrases that could suggest a preference or limit based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, or other protected classes in [STATE OR LOCAL AREA]. Show results in a table with columns: Phrase, Why it may be a problem, Safer replacement. Then rewrite the full text. Text to review: [PASTE YOUR LISTING OR POST]. Remind me this is a helpful check, not legal advice.
prompts.proTip: Run every new listing and social post through this before you publish, and confirm gray areas with your broker.

prompts.title: Post Property Feature Sheet Bullet List
prompts.useWhen: You need a quick flyer, brochure, or feature sheet (highlights list, property flyer text) from raw listing facts.
prompts.prompt: Turn these raw facts into a clean one-page feature sheet for [PROPERTY ADDRESS]: [PASTE YOUR NOTES OR MLS DATA]. Create these sections: Headline (under 10 words), Quick Facts (table), Top 8 Features (bullets), Recent Updates (with years), Location Highlights, and Call to Action with my name [YOUR NAME] and phone [YOUR PHONE]. Keep each bullet under 12 words. Use only the facts provided. Use fair housing safe language and do not describe the type of person who would like the home.
prompts.proTip: Paste the result into Canva or Word and you have a flyer in five minutes.
fields: PASTE YOUR NOTES OR MLS DATA

prompts.title: Script Video Walkthrough for a Listing Tour
prompts.useWhen: You are filming a video home tour (listing video, walkthrough, property tour script) and do not know what to say.
prompts.prompt: Write a 90-second video walkthrough script for a listing at [ADDRESS]. Rooms in order: [ROOM ORDER, such as entry, kitchen, living room, primary suite, backyard]. Key features to mention: [FEATURES]. Format as a twocolumn table: "What I say" and "What the camera shows." Start with a strong hook in the first 5 seconds. End with a call to action to call [YOUR NAME] at [YOUR PHONE]. Keep the language natural and spoken, in short sentences. Describe only the property.
prompts.proTip: Read the script out loud once. If any line feels awkward to say, ask the AI to simplify it.

prompts.title: Email Just Listed Announcement
prompts.useWhen: A new listing goes live and you want to tell your database (new listing email, "coming soon" blast, neighbor announcement).
prompts.prompt: Write a "Just Listed" email to my past clients and sphere about a new listing at [ADDRESS] priced at [PRICE]. Include: a subject line under 50 characters, a 2-sentence opening, 4 bullet highlights ([HIGHLIGHT 1], [HIGHLIGHT 2], [HIGHLIGHT 3], [HIGHLIGHT 4]), open house details ([OPEN HOUSE DATE AND TIME]), and a line asking readers to share with anyone who might be looking in [AREA]. Sign as [YOUR NAME]. Keep it under 130 words. Give me 3 subject lines.
prompts.proTip: Send it to neighbors too. People near a listing often know someone who wants to live close by.

prompts.title: Email Just Sold Announcement
prompts.useWhen: A home closes and you want to build your brand (sold announcement, market proof, "we did it" email).
prompts.prompt: Write a "Just Sold" announcement for [ADDRESS OR STREET] that closed in [NUMBER] days. Facts I can share: [SALE FACTS, such as price only if public, days on market, marketing steps]. Explain in 3 bullets what worked, like [WHAT WORKED]. Thank the sellers by first name only if they gave permission: [SELLER FIRST NAME]. End with a soft offer for a free home value estimate for neighbors in [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Keep it truthful, no guarantees, under 140 words. Give me 2 subject lines.
prompts.proTip: Always get the sellers' permission before you name them or share the price.

prompts.title: Checklist Room-by-Room Staging and Home Prep for Sellers
prompts.useWhen: A seller asks "how do I get my house ready to sell?" (staging tips, declutter list, pre-listing prep).
prompts.prompt: Create a room-by-room checklist for sellers preparing to list a home at [PRICE RANGE] in [CITY]. Rooms: entry, living room, kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms, garage, and curb appeal. For each room list 5 low-cost actions, and mark each one as "Do this week," "Do before photos," or "Skip if short on time." Include a budget note of about [BUDGET] for the whole house. Use plain words and a friendly tone. Add a final section, "What not to spend money on." Present it as a table.
prompts.proTip: Send the checklist before the listing appointment so sellers arrive already motivated.

prompts.title: Post Instagram Caption for a New Listing
prompts.useWhen: You are posting a new listing on Instagram or Facebook (social caption, listing post) and need copy that gets clicks.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 Instagram captions for a new listing at [NEIGHBORHOOD OR CITY], priced at [PRICE]. Top features: [FEATURE 1], [FEATURE 2], [FEATURE 3]. Each caption needs a hook in the first line, 2 to 3 short lines about the home, and a call to action such as "DM me for details" or "Link in bio." Add 8 relevant hashtags using [CITY] and neighborhood tags. Tone: [TONE, like friendly or polished]. Describe the home only, not who should buy it. No fair housing risks.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version with a question in the first line. Questions boost comments.

prompts.title: Plan 30-Day Social Media Content Calendar
prompts.useWhen: You keep running out of things to post (content calendar, posting schedule, what to post on social).
prompts.prompt: Create a 30-day social media calendar for a real estate agent in [CITY] who focuses on [BUYERS, SELLERS, OR BOTH]. I can post [NUMBER] times per week on [PLATFORMS]. Present it as a table with columns: Day, Post idea, Format (photo, video, carousel, story), and Caption starter. Mix in these themes: local spots, home tips, market updates, client wins, and behind-the-scenes. Include 4 posts that ask for engagement. Keep the ideas simple enough to shoot on a phone.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to write the full captions for the first week, then repeat for weeks two through four.

prompts.title: Script Short Video (Reel or TikTok) Home Tour
prompts.useWhen: You want a fast vertical video (Reel, TikTok, YouTube Short) that shows off a property in under 45 seconds.
prompts.prompt: Write a 30 to 40 second Reel script for a home at [PRICE] in [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Include these features in order: [FEATURE 1], [FEATURE 2], [FEATURE 3]. Format as a table with 3 columns: Time, What I say, On-screen text. Start with a 3-second hook, such as a surprising fact or a question. End with a call to action for [OPEN HOUSE OR DM]. Use short, punchy spoken lines. Keep it truthful and describe only the property.
prompts.proTip: Film the last shot first (the call to action) while your energy is highest.

prompts.title: Post Neighborhood Spotlight
prompts.useWhen: You want to show local expertise (area guide, community highlight, "life in [town]" content) without making risky claims.
prompts.prompt: Write a neighborhood spotlight post about [NEIGHBORHOOD] in [CITY]. Use these facts only: [LIST OF PARKS, RESTAURANTS, SCHOOLS BY NAME ONLY, COMMUTE TIMES, EVENTS]. Create a 120-word caption plus a 5-slide carousel outline with a headline for each slide. Describe places and things to do, not the people who live there. Do not rate or compare schools or say a neighborhood is "safe" or "family friendly." End with a question asking followers for their favorite local spot.
prompts.proTip: Tag the local businesses you mention. They often reshare, which grows your reach for free.

prompts.title: Post Just Sold Story for Facebook
prompts.useWhen: A deal closes and you want a story-style success post (sold post, closing celebration, client win) that builds trust.
prompts.prompt: Write a Facebook post celebrating a closing at [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Include a short story in 3 parts: the challenge ([CHALLENGE, like tight timeline or multiple offers]), what I did ([WHAT I DID]), and the result ([RESULT WITHOUT PRIVATE FINANCIAL DETAILS]). Thank my clients [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] only if they agreed. End with a soft invitation for anyone thinking of buying or selling in [AREA] to message me. Keep it under 150 words, human, and free of bragging.
prompts.proTip: Lead with the client's problem, not your win. Stories about problems get read.
fields: CHALLENGE, like tight timeline or multiple offers

prompts.title: Post LinkedIn Market Update
prompts.useWhen: You want to look like the local market expert (market report post, real estate stats update, monthly market snapshot).
prompts.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post about the [MONTH] housing market in [CITY OR COUNTY]. Use only these numbers: median price [NUMBER], days on market [NUMBER], active listings [NUMBER], and change from last year [NUMBER]. Explain in plain English what it means for buyers and for sellers in separate short sections. Do not predict the future or give financial advice. Add a closing question to start a conversation. Keep it under 200 words with short lines. Include the source of the data: [SOURCE].
prompts.proTip: Always name your data source and date. It builds trust and keeps you accurate.

prompts.title: Email Monthly Newsletter for Past Clients
prompts.useWhen: You want a simple monthly email for your database (client newsletter, sphere of influence email) that people actually open.
prompts.prompt: Write a monthly newsletter for my past clients and sphere in [CITY] for [MONTH]. Sections: (1) a friendly opening note from [YOUR NAME], (2) one market stat in plain English: [MARKET STAT], (3) one home maintenance tip for [SEASON], (4) a local event or spot: [LOCAL EVENT], and (5) a soft call to action for referrals. Keep it under 250 words, skimmable, and warm. Give me 3 subject lines and a short preview text.
prompts.proTip: Keep the format the same every month. Readers open faster when they know what to expect.

prompts.title: Post Carousel of First-Time Buyer Tips
prompts.useWhen: You want educational content (buyer tips, how-to posts, home buying myths) that people save and share.
prompts.prompt: Create a 7-slide Instagram carousel for first-time buyers on the topic "[TOPIC, like getting pre-approved or what closing costs include]". Write the headline for each slide (under 8 words) and 1 to 2 short lines of text below it. Slide 1 is a hook, slide 7 is a call to action to follow [YOUR HANDLE] or book a call at [LINK]. Also write the caption with 5 hashtags. Keep everything at a 6th-grade level, and remind readers to check with their lender or attorney for their situation.
prompts.proTip: Educational posts get saved. Ask viewers to "save this for later" in the last slide.

prompts.title: Post Open House Promotion
prompts.useWhen: An open house is coming up and you need promo posts (open house invite, event announcement, "come see it") for social and email.
prompts.prompt: Write an open house promotion for [ADDRESS] on [DATE] from [START TIME] to [END TIME]. Give me: 1 Instagram caption, 1 Facebook event description, 1 short email, and 1 text for my contacts. Highlight [FEATURE 1] and [FEATURE 2]. Mention that I will be there to answer questions and that refreshments are [REFRESHMENTS]. Include a call to action to RSVP or just stop by. Keep each piece short. Describe the home only, and welcome everyone.
prompts.proTip: Post the reminder 2 hours before start time. Last-minute posts drive drop-in traffic.

prompts.title: Response to Social Media Comments and DMs About Price
prompts.useWhen: Someone comments "How much?" or "Is it still available?" (DM reply, social media inquiry, comment response) and you want a friendly reply that starts a conversation.
prompts.prompt: Write 6 short replies I can use when people comment or DM on my listing posts. Situations: (1) "How much?" (2) "Is it still available?" (3) "Can I see it this weekend?" (4) "What is the HOA?" (5) "Do you have similar homes?" (6) "What is my home worth?" Use these facts: price [PRICE], status [STATUS], HOA [HOA], my number [YOUR PHONE]. Each reply must be under 50 words, friendly, and move the person toward a call or showing. Do not give legal or lending advice.
prompts.proTip: Reply within one hour. Quick replies turn comments into showings.

prompts.title: Script Cold Call to a For Sale By Owner (FSBO)
prompts.useWhen: You want to call homeowners selling on their own (FSBO call, "for sale by owner" outreach) without sounding pushy.
prompts.prompt: Write a 60-second phone script for calling a for sale by owner seller. My name is [YOUR NAME] from [BROKERAGE] in [CITY]. Open with a friendly, respectful greeting, mention I saw their home at [ADDRESS] listed, and ask permission to speak. Include 3 helpful questions about their timeline and goals, and one offer of value, such as [VALUE OFFER, like a free buyer pool report]. Add responses for 3 common replies: "I am not interested," "I do not want to pay commission," and "Call me later." Respect do-not-call rules.
prompts.proTip: Scrub your list against the National Do Not Call Registry before you dial.
fields: VALUE OFFER, like a free buyer pool report

prompts.title: Email Follow-Up Sequence for FSBO Sellers
prompts.useWhen: A FSBO seller did not say yes on the call (owner-listed follow-up, drip emails) and you want to stay helpful over time.
prompts.prompt: Write a 4-email sequence for a for sale by owner seller in [CITY]. Email 1 (day 1): a friendly intro and a free resource, [FREE RESOURCE]. Email 2 (day 4): a tip on pricing and paperwork risks. Email 3 (day 10): a short example of how I market homes, [MARKETING EXAMPLE]. Email 4 (day 21): a polite check-in. Each email is under 120 words, with a subject line and a soft call to action. Never criticize their choice. Sign as [YOUR NAME], [BROKERAGE].
prompts.proTip: Give value first. A helpful checklist beats a "list with me" pitch.

prompts.title: Script Expired Listing Call
prompts.useWhen: A listing just expired or was withdrawn (expired listing outreach, "your home did not sell" call) and you need a sensitive opening.
prompts.prompt: Write a 60-second call script to a homeowner whose listing at [ADDRESS] expired without selling. I am [YOUR NAME] at [BROKERAGE]. Be empathetic and never bash the previous agent. Ask 3 questions about what they think happened, such as pricing, photos, and showings. Offer a free review of their marketing and price, without commitment. Include responses for "I am done with agents" and "I am going to wait." Keep the tone calm, curious, and respectful. Follow do-not-call rules.
prompts.proTip: Listen for the "why." Most expired sellers are frustrated about communication, not just price.

prompts.title: Email Letter to an Expired Listing Homeowner
prompts.useWhen: You want a written follow-up or mailer (expired listing letter, direct mail) that stands out from other agents.
prompts.prompt: Write a short, respectful letter to a seller whose home at [ADDRESS] did not sell. It must include: an empathetic opening, one sentence on why homes in [NEIGHBORHOOD] often sit (based on this fact: [MARKET FACT]), 3 bullets on my approach ([APPROACH 1], [APPROACH 2], [APPROACH 3]), and an invitation for a free, no-pressure 20-minute consultation on [DATES]. Sign as [YOUR NAME], [PHONE]. Keep it under 180 words. Make no promises about sale price or timing.
prompts.proTip: Handwrite the envelope. It gets opened far more often than a printed one.

prompts.title: Email Asking Your Sphere for Referrals
prompts.useWhen: You want more business from people you already know (referral request, sphere of influence outreach) and hate asking.
prompts.prompt: Write a warm referral request email from me, [YOUR NAME], to friends, family, and past clients. Mention I am focusing on helping people in [AREA] with [SERVICE, like first-time buying or downsizing] this [SEASON]. Explain in 2 sentences what a good referral looks like, and make it easy with a simple reply: "Reply with a name or introduce us." Add a thank-you gift offer: [THANK-YOU GIFT]. Keep it under 130 words, personal, no pressure, and under 3 short paragraphs. Give 3 subject lines.
prompts.proTip: Send it to 20 people individually with their first name, not as one big blast.
fields: SERVICE, like first-time buying or downsizing

prompts.title: Text Follow-Up to an Online Lead
prompts.useWhen: A lead comes from Zillow, Realtor.com, or your website (internet lead, portal inquiry) and you need to reach them fast.
prompts.prompt: Write 5 short text messages for a new online lead named [LEAD FIRST NAME] who inquired about [PROPERTY ADDRESS] on [SOURCE]. Text 1: send right away with a helpful question. Text 2: 24 hours later with a new listing that fits [PRICE RANGE]. Text 3: 3 days later with an offer of a quick call. Text 4: a week later with a market tip. Text 5: a polite "should I close your file?" message. Each text under 250 characters, friendly, with an opt-out line: "Reply STOP to stop." Sign as [YOUR NAME].
prompts.proTip: Speed wins. Texting within 5 minutes can double your response rate.

prompts.title: Email Follow-Up After an Open House
prompts.useWhen: Visitors signed in at your open house (open house follow-up, sign-in sheet leads) and you want to turn them into clients.
prompts.prompt: Write two follow-up emails to send after an open house at [ADDRESS]. Email A is for visitors who are house hunting: thank them, ask what they liked and did not like, and offer to send similar homes under [PRICE RANGE]. Email B is for neighbors and casual visitors: thank them and offer a free home value estimate. Each is under 120 words with a subject line and one clear question at the end. Sign as [YOUR NAME]. Do not assume anything about visitors beyond what they told me: [NOTES FROM SIGN-IN].
prompts.proTip: Send within 24 hours. After two days, they will have forgotten the house.

prompts.title: Plan 5-Touch Follow-Up Sequence for Cold Leads
prompts.useWhen: You have leads that stopped answering (drip campaign, nurture sequence, lead cultivation) and want a repeatable plan.
prompts.prompt: Build a 5-touch follow-up plan over 30 days for a cold buyer or seller lead in [CITY]. Present it as a table with columns: Day, Channel (email, text, call, or mail), Goal, and the full message text. Include a voicemail script for one of the touches. Each message is under 80 words and offers something useful, such as [VALUE ITEM 1] or [VALUE ITEM 2]. Include opt-out language for texts and emails. Sign as [YOUR NAME].
prompts.proTip: Put your touches in your CRM so the plan runs itself.

prompts.title: Script Door Knocking and Postcard Copy for Farming
prompts.useWhen: You are farming a neighborhood (geographic farm, door knock, direct mail postcard) and need short copy that gets a response.
prompts.prompt: Write two things for farming [NEIGHBORHOOD]: (1) a 20-second door-knock script for [YOUR NAME] from [BROKERAGE], and (2) 3 postcard copy options with a headline, 2 lines of text, and a call to action. Postcard topics: a recent sale nearby ([RECENT SALE INFO]), a free home value report, or a local market fact ([MARKET FACT]). Keep the tone neighborly and respectful. Postcards must follow truthful advertising rules and include [BROKERAGE] name and my license number: [LICENSE NUMBER].
prompts.proTip: Mail the same neighborhood at least 6 times. Familiarity comes from repetition.

prompts.title: Email Re-Engaging Old Leads Who Ghosted
prompts.useWhen: A lead went silent months ago (dead lead, ghosted lead, cold database) and you want a low-pressure way to reopen the conversation.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 short re-engagement emails to leads who contacted me [NUMBER] months ago about [BUYING OR SELLING] in [AREA]. Email 1: a friendly check-in with a new market fact: [MARKET FACT]. Email 2: a helpful question, like "Has your timeline changed?" Email 3: a polite goodbye offering to keep in touch. Each is under 90 words with a subject line under 45 characters. Sound like a real person, not a robot. Sign as [YOUR NAME].
prompts.proTip: The goodbye email often gets the most replies. Give it a subject line like "Should I close your file?"

prompts.title: Response to "Your Commission Is Too High"
prompts.useWhen: A seller pushes back on your fee (commission objection, "can you lower your rate") and you want to explain your value calmly.
prompts.prompt: You are a veteran listing agent. A seller says, "Your commission is too high." Write 3 responses I can use: one for a phone call, one for a listing presentation, and one for a text. Each should acknowledge their concern, explain my value with these points: [VALUE POINT 1], [VALUE POINT 2], [VALUE POINT 3], and ask a question to keep the conversation going. My fee structure is [YOUR FEE STRUCTURE]. Never bash other agents. Stay calm, honest, and specific. Remind me that fees are negotiable and must follow my broker's policies.
prompts.proTip: Ask "What would you like to see for that fee?" Their answer shows what they truly value.

prompts.title: Response to "We Want to Wait Until Rates Drop"
prompts.useWhen: Buyers or sellers hesitate because of interest rates (mortgage rate worry, "wait for the market") and you need a fair, honest reply.
prompts.prompt: Write a respectful reply to clients who say, "We want to wait until interest rates drop." Give me a phone version (under 45 seconds spoken) and an email version (under 150 words). Explain 3 things to think about: the cost of waiting, that no one can predict rates, and the idea of refinancing later if rates change. Use [CURRENT LOCAL MARKET FACT] as support. Do not promise that rates or prices will go up or down. Suggest they talk to [LENDER NAME] for numbers. End with a question about their timeline.
prompts.proTip: Offer to run two lender payment scenarios. Numbers calm fears better than opinions.

prompts.title: Response to "Zillow Says My Home Is Worth More"
prompts.useWhen: A seller wants to list at an online estimate's price (Zestimate objection, automated valuation, overpriced expectations).
prompts.prompt: Write a friendly but clear way to explain to a seller why an online estimate (like a Zestimate) may not match what their home will sell for. Include 4 short reasons, such as updates, condition, and recent nearby sales. Add a plainlanguage example using [RECENT COMP EXAMPLE]. Offer to walk through the comps together on [DAY]. Provide a phone script (under 60 seconds) and a short email (under 130 words). Never say the seller is wrong. Keep the tone respectful and factual.
prompts.proTip: Print 3 recent comps side by side. Seeing real sold prices beats any argument.

prompts.title: Response to "I Will Use My Friend or Sell It Myself"
prompts.useWhen: A prospect says they will go with a relative, friend, or do it themselves (FSBO objection, "my cousin is an agent").
prompts.prompt: Write 3 respectful responses to a prospect who says, "I am going to use my [FRIEND, RELATIVE, OR MYSELF]." Response 1 is for keeping the door open. Response 2 highlights what I do that is different: [YOUR DIFFERENTIATOR]. Response 3 is a graceful exit that leaves a helpful resource: [RESOURCE]. Each is under 60 words. Do not criticize the other person or push. Include one question that invites them to call me back if their plans change.
prompts.proTip: Follow up in 60 days. Many friend-agent deals stall and the seller remembers you were kind.

prompts.title: Response to a Seller Who Wants to Overprice
prompts.useWhen: A seller insists on a price above the comps (price disagreement, unrealistic price, pricing conversation) and you need an honest talking plan.
prompts.prompt: I am a listing agent and my seller wants to list at [SELLER PRICE], but my analysis suggests [MY PRICE RANGE]. Write a talking plan for a respectful conversation. Include: an opening line that shows I am on their side, a simple explanation of how buyers search by price ranges, 3 supporting facts from [COMP DATA], and 2 options (list at my price, or try theirs with a set review date of [NUMBER] days). Provide a short script and a follow-up email of under 150 words. Keep it kind and honest.
prompts.proTip: Agree on a date for a price review before you list. It turns a fight into a plan.

prompts.title: Script Price Reduction Conversation
prompts.useWhen: A listing is getting showings but no offers (price drop, price adjustment, "what now" call) and the seller is frustrated.
prompts.prompt: Write a phone script and follow-up email for recommending a price reduction on [ADDRESS] to seller [SELLER FIRST NAME]. Facts: [NUMBER] days on market, [NUMBER] showings, feedback themes: [FEEDBACK THEMES], competing listings: [COMPETING LISTINGS]. Recommend reducing to [NEW PRICE] and explain why using a simple, non-blaming story. Include one alternative option, such as [ALTERNATIVE, like new photos or an incentive]. Keep the email under 180 words, calm, and supportive.
prompts.proTip: Lead with the buyer feedback. The data makes it the market's message, not yours.
fields: ALTERNATIVE, like new photos or an incentive

prompts.title: Email Comparing Multiple Offers for a Seller
prompts.useWhen: You have more than one offer (multiple offers, offer comparison, offer summary) and need to explain the choices clearly.
prompts.prompt: Create an offer comparison for my seller [SELLER FIRST NAME]. Offers: [OFFER 1 DETAILS: price, financing, down payment, contingencies, closing date, concessions], [OFFER 2 DETAILS], [OFFER 3 DETAILS]. Present a table with those columns for each offer. Then write a plain-English summary of the pros and cons of each, and a short list of questions the seller should think about. Do not pick a winner unless I ask. Remind the seller that final decisions are theirs and that legal questions go to their attorney.
prompts.proTip: Add "Now rank them by risk of falling through" for a second view.

prompts.title: Script Negotiating Repair Requests After an Inspection
prompts.useWhen: The inspection report is back (repair request, inspection negotiation, credit vs repair) and the deal is at risk.
prompts.prompt: I represent the [BUYER OR SELLER]. The inspection found: [PASTE MAJOR FINDINGS]. Help me plan a fair negotiation. Create a table that sorts items into "Safety or major," "Important," and "Cosmetic." Suggest which items to request, accept, or trade for a credit. Write a short, polite email to the other agent proposing [PROPOSED RESOLUTION], and a talking script for my client. Keep the tone firm, kind, and solution-focused. Remind me to follow our contract deadlines: [DEADLINE].
prompts.proTip: Suggest 3 to 5 key items, not 30. Long lists sink deals.

prompts.title: Email Offer Cover Letter Focused on Terms
prompts.useWhen: Your buyer is competing with other offers (offer letter, multiple offer strategy, cover letter for an offer) and you want it strong and safe.
prompts.prompt: Write a professional cover letter from me, [YOUR NAME], to the listing agent for my buyer's offer on [ADDRESS]. Highlight the strong terms: price [PRICE], financing [FINANCING], down payment [DOWN PAYMENT], closing date [DATE], and flexibility such as [FLEXIBILITY, like a rent-back]. Explain the buyer's readiness with facts only, such as pre-approval and proof of funds. Do not include personal stories, photos, or details about the buyer's family, religion, or background. Keep it under 200 words and businesslike.
prompts.proTip: Personal "love letters" can raise fair housing concerns. Let strong terms do the talking.

prompts.title: Response to a Buyer With Cold Feet
prompts.useWhen: Your buyer gets nervous after going under contract (buyer's remorse, second thoughts, "I am scared") and you need to help them decide clearly.
prompts.prompt: Write a supportive script and email for a buyer named [BUYER FIRST NAME] who has doubts after going under contract on [ADDRESS]. Their worries are: [WORRIES]. Acknowledge their feelings, help them sort real concerns from normal nerves, and outline their options under the contract in general terms, without giving legal advice. Include 4 questions I can ask them and a suggestion to talk with [ATTORNEY OR LENDER] about deadlines and details. Keep it calm and kind. Email under 180 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask "What is the worst-case and could you live with it?" This surfaces real concerns quickly.

prompts.title: Checklist Buyer Consultation Questions
prompts.useWhen: You are meeting a new buyer for the first time (buyer interview, needs analysis, intake questions) and want a smooth, professional conversation.
prompts.prompt: Create a buyer consultation guide for a first meeting in [CITY]. Include 20 questions grouped into: Timeline and motivation, Budget and financing, Must-haves and nice-to-haves, Location and commute, and Working together. Word every question neutrally so it never asks about family status, religion, or other protected traits. Add a short script to explain how I work: [YOUR PROCESS]. End with a one-page summary form I can fill out for [CLIENT FIRST NAME]. Use a table for the summary form.
prompts.proTip: Have clients rank their top 3 must-haves. It saves hours of showings later.

prompts.title: Plan Showing Day Itinerary and Route
prompts.useWhen: You are showing several homes in one day (showing schedule, tour route, home tour plan) and want it to run on time.
prompts.prompt: Build a showing day plan for buyers [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] on [DATE]. Homes: [LIST OF ADDRESSES WITH SHOWING WINDOWS]. Start time [START TIME] and lunch stop near [AREA]. Create a table with columns: Time, Address, Drive time, What to look for, and Questions to ask. Suggest the best order to save drive time, using general logic since you cannot see live maps. Add 5 tips to keep buyers focused and a closing debrief question for each home. Keep it practical.
prompts.proTip: Verify the route in your maps app. The AI cannot see live traffic or map data.
fields: LIST OF ADDRESSES WITH SHOWING WINDOWS

prompts.title: Checklist Open House Setup and Sign-In
prompts.useWhen: You are hosting an open house for the first time or want a repeatable routine (open house prep, sign-in sheet, hosting tips).
prompts.prompt: Create a complete open house checklist for [ADDRESS] on [DATE]. Include sections: 3 days before, day of setup, during the event, safety steps, and after. Add items for signs, directional signage rules in [CITY], a sign-in sheet with these fields: [SIGN-IN FIELDS], flyers, water and snacks, and a lockdown plan for valuables. Add a personal safety tip list for agents hosting alone. Use a table with a "Done" checkbox column. Keep it simple.
prompts.proTip: Have the seller remove medications, cash, and small valuables before your event.

prompts.title: Script Open House Greeting and Talking Points
prompts.useWhen: Visitors walk in and you are not sure what to say (open house script, greeting visitors, conversation starters).
prompts.prompt: Write an open house script for [YOUR NAME] at [ADDRESS]. Include: a 10-second welcome, 5 friendly questions to start conversations (about their search, not their personal life), a 30-second tour pitch highlighting [FEATURE 1], [FEATURE 2], and [FEATURE 3], and 3 replies for when someone says "I am just looking," "I have an agent," or "What is the lowest price?" Keep everything warm and natural. Include a line to invite them to sign in with [SIGN- IN METHOD]. Treat every visitor equally and welcome all guests.
prompts.proTip: Ask "What made you stop by today?" It opens the door better than "Are you working with an agent?"

prompts.title: Email Explaining Pre-Approval and Choosing a Lender
prompts.useWhen: Buyers ask "do we need to be pre-approved?" (pre-qualification vs pre-approval, mortgage lender intro) before you start showing homes.
prompts.prompt: Write an email to buyers [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] explaining why getting pre-approved before touring homes helps. Explain the difference between pre-qualified and pre-approved in simple words. List 5 documents lenders often ask for, such as [DOCUMENTS], and say that requirements vary. Introduce lender options from my trusted list: [LENDER NAME AND CONTACT], and note that they can choose any lender they like. Keep the tone friendly and under 200 words. Say I am not a lender and cannot give financial advice.
prompts.proTip: Offer more than one lender so clients can compare. It is also required in some places.

prompts.title: Analysis Comparing Homes Side by Side
prompts.useWhen: Buyers cannot decide between homes (compare properties, pros and cons list, decision help) after a day of showings.
prompts.prompt: Help my buyers compare these homes: [HOME 1 DETAILS], [HOME 2 DETAILS], [HOME 3 DETAILS]. Their top priorities are: [BUYER PRIORITIES]. Create a comparison table with rows for price, size, condition, location, monthly cost estimate factors, and how each home matches their priorities. Then write a short summary of the pros and cons of each home. Do not choose for them and do not judge neighborhoods. Add 3 questions they should think about before deciding.
prompts.proTip: Ask clients to score each home from 1 to 10 for each priority. Numbers reveal their real favorite.

prompts.title: Checklist What to Look For During a Home Showing
prompts.useWhen: Buyers ask "what should I look for when touring a house?" (viewing checklist, walkthrough tips, red flags).
prompts.prompt: Create a printable checklist for buyers touring homes in [CITY]. Sections: Outside (roof, gutters, drainage, foundation), Inside (windows, floors, smells, water stains), Kitchen and baths, Systems (HVAC, water heater, electrical panel), and Questions to ask the listing agent. For each item, add what to notice and why it matters in one short line. Include space to write notes for each home. Remind buyers a professional inspection is still needed. Use a table with checkboxes. Keep the language simple for [CLIENT FIRST NAMES].
prompts.proTip: Give this to buyers before the first showing so they know how to look.

prompts.title: Email Explaining Home Inspection Steps to Buyers
prompts.useWhen: The buyers are under contract and nervous about the inspection (inspection contingency, inspection day, what to expect).
prompts.prompt: Write an email to buyers [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] explaining what to expect at the home inspection at [ADDRESS] on [DATE AND TIME]. Explain in simple words what an inspector checks, how long it takes (about [DURATION]), whether they should attend, and how to read the report. Explain that most homes have issues and what counts as major vs minor. Mention that we have until [DEADLINE] to respond under the contract. Offer to review the report with them the same day. Under 200 words, calm and clear.
prompts.proTip: Tell buyers to expect a long list. Setting expectations early prevents panic.

prompts.title: Email Area Guide for a Relocating Buyer
prompts.useWhen: A buyer is moving from another city or state (relocation, out-of-town buyer, moving guide) and needs help learning the area.
prompts.prompt: Write a friendly area guide email for a relocating buyer named [CLIENT FIRST NAME] moving to [CITY] from [ORIGIN]. Include: how the home search will work remotely, what to expect for a video tour, key differences in the local process (such as [LOCAL PROCESS NOTE]), a list of local services to set up, and a sample 2-day visit plan. Describe places and services only, without judging neighborhoods or the people in them. Suggest a phone call on [DATE]. Under 250 words with short sections.
prompts.proTip: Offer a live video tour with your phone. It builds trust with out-of-town buyers.

prompts.title: Checklist Final Walkthrough Before Closing
prompts.useWhen: Your buyers are about to close (final walk-through, pre-closing inspection) and need to know what to check.
prompts.prompt: Create a final walkthrough checklist for buyers closing on [ADDRESS] on [DATE]. Include: check that agreed repairs are complete, test all appliances, faucets, lights, and outlets, run the HVAC, check windows and doors, confirm items that stay ([ITEMS INCLUDED]) are there, and look for new damage. Add a short section, "What to do if something is wrong," that tells them to call me before closing. Use a table with a checkbox and notes column. Remind them to bring [ITEMS TO BRING].
prompts.proTip: Book the walkthrough 24 hours before closing. That leaves time to fix issues.

prompts.title: Checklist Listing Launch SOP
prompts.useWhen: You want a repeatable list for every new listing (listing checklist, listing launch process, new listing to-do list) so nothing gets missed.
prompts.prompt: Create a standard operating procedure for launching a new listing in [STATE]. Present it as a checklist in phases: Signed and prepped, Photos and media, MLS entry, Marketing launch, and First 14 days. Assign each task to [ME], [ASSISTANT], or [VENDOR]. Include disclosure forms required in [STATE], lockbox and signage steps, and a compliance step that checks the copy for fair housing safety. Add a time estimate for each task. Format as a table so I can paste it into my task manager, [TASK TOOL].
prompts.proTip: Turn this into a template in your CRM or task tool and reuse it for every listing.

prompts.title: Checklist Contract-to-Close Timeline and Deadlines
prompts.useWhen: A deal goes under contract (transaction timeline, contingency deadlines, pending checklist) and you need a clear calendar of what is due.
prompts.prompt: Create a contract-to-close timeline for a [BUYER OR SELLER] transaction at [ADDRESS]. Contract date: [DATE]. Closing date: [DATE]. Deadlines: earnest money [DATE], inspection [DATE], financing [DATE], appraisal [DATE], and title [DATE]. Present a table with columns: Task, Due date, Who is responsible, and Status. Add reminders for 2 days before each deadline and a short script for a weekly status check with my client. Note that I must confirm all dates with the contract.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to turn the table into calendar events, then copy them into your calendar.

prompts.title: Email Introducing Your Transaction Team
prompts.useWhen: A deal is under contract and clients need to know who does what (team introduction, lender and title intro, "meet your team").
prompts.prompt: Write an email introducing the transaction team for [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] buying or selling [ADDRESS]. Team: lender [LENDER NAME], title [TITLE COMPANY], inspector [INSPECTOR NAME], and my coordinator [COORDINATOR NAME]. For each person write one line on what they do and when the client will hear from them. Add a short "How to reach me" line and a request that clients answer emails within [TIME FRAME]. Keep it friendly and under 200 words. Do not share any private details beyond names and roles.
prompts.proTip: Copy the whole team on the email so everyone has the contact info.

prompts.title: Email Requesting a Status Update From a Lender or Title Company
prompts.useWhen: You are waiting on documents (lender update request, title company follow-up, chasing paperwork) and need to nudge politely.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 versions of a polite but firm email to [LENDER OR TITLE CONTACT] asking for an update on the file for [CLIENT LAST INITIAL AND ADDRESS]. Closing is [DATE]. We are waiting on [WHAT WE ARE WAITING FOR]. Version 1 is gentle, version 2 is firm with a deadline, and version 3 is an urgent escalation copying [MANAGER NAME]. Each is under 90 words with a clear subject line and a specific request with a date. Do not include sensitive personal or financial details.
prompts.proTip: Always put the closing date in the subject line. It signals urgency without being rude.

prompts.title: SOP New Client Onboarding Process
prompts.useWhen: You want every client to get the same great start (client onboarding process, intake workflow, systems).
prompts.prompt: Write a step-by-step onboarding SOP for new [BUYER OR SELLER] clients. Include: the first call within [HOURS], a welcome email, an intake form with [FORM FIELDS], setup of [CRM NAME] and search alerts, agreement signing, and a first-week check-in. For each step list: who does it, the tool used, the deadline, and a message template name. Format as a table and add a short training note for a new assistant. Use plain language, so any new team member can follow it without asking me.
prompts.proTip: Record yourself doing the process once and ask the AI to turn the transcript into the SOP.

prompts.title: Plan Weekly Time Blocking Schedule for Agents
prompts.useWhen: Your week feels chaotic (agent schedule, daily routine, time management) and lead generation keeps slipping.
prompts.prompt: Create a weekly time-blocking schedule for a real estate agent who works [HOURS PER WEEK] and has these fixed commitments: [FIXED COMMITMENTS]. Priorities: lead generation [HOURS], client work [HOURS], marketing [HOURS], and admin [HOURS]. Present it as a Monday to Sunday table with time blocks. Protect [NUMBER] hours of lead generation before noon and include one day off. Add 5 rules to keep me on track, such as batching emails. Keep it realistic for my [SOLO OR TEAM] business.
prompts.proTip: Put your lead generation block first in the day. Everything else fits around it.

prompts.title: Email Explaining Closing Costs in Plain English
prompts.useWhen: Buyers or sellers ask "what are closing costs?" (settlement costs, fees at closing) and you want to avoid confusion or surprises.
prompts.prompt: Write an email for [BUYER OR SELLER] client [CLIENT FIRST NAME] explaining common closing costs in [STATE] in plain English. Describe these categories in one line each: lender fees, title and escrow, taxes and prepaid items, agent and transfer fees, and [OTHER CATEGORIES]. Explain that the exact amounts come from the Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure and the title company, not from me. Add a "3 questions to ask your lender" list. Under 220 words. Do not give numbers unless I supply them, and remind them this is general information.
prompts.proTip: Send this before the offer, not after. Surprises about costs can cause deals to fall apart.

prompts.title: Script Voicemail and Phone Replies for Missed Calls
prompts.useWhen: You cannot answer every call (voicemail greeting, missed call script, callback message) and want to sound professional.
prompts.prompt: Write 5 short scripts for [YOUR NAME] at [BROKERAGE]: (1) a voicemail greeting for my business line, (2) a voicemail I leave for a new lead, (3) a voicemail for a client waiting on an answer, (4) an "I am in a showing" text auto-reply, and (5) an after-hours message. Each is under 30 seconds spoken or under 250 characters in text. Include my number [YOUR PHONE] and when to expect a callback: [CALLBACK WINDOW]. Warm, clear, and professional.
prompts.proTip: Say your number twice at the end of a voicemail. It saves callbacks and confusion.

prompts.title: Checklist Listing Appointment Prep Packet
prompts.useWhen: You have a listing presentation coming up (listing appointment, seller consultation, pre-listing packet) and want to look prepared.
prompts.prompt: Create a prep checklist and packet outline for a listing appointment at [ADDRESS] with [SELLER FIRST NAMES] on [DATE]. Include what to research before (comps, tax records, neighborhood trends), what to bring (list of documents), and the packet sections: About me, My marketing plan, Pricing analysis, Timeline, Fees, and Next steps. Add a 10-question list to ask sellers during the meeting, including [SPECIFIC QUESTION]. Suggest a 45minute meeting agenda in a table. Keep everything factual and free of promises.
prompts.proTip: Send the agenda ahead of time. It makes you look organized and puts sellers at ease.

prompts.title: SOP Task Handoff to an Assistant or Transaction Coordinator
prompts.useWhen: You want to delegate (assistant handoff, hiring a virtual assistant, task delegation) and need clear written directions.
prompts.prompt: Write a clear delegation guide for handing off [TASK, like preparing a listing packet or scheduling inspections] to my assistant [ASSISTANT NAME]. Include: the goal, step-by-step instructions, tools used ([TOOLS]), where files are saved, a quality checklist, common mistakes, examples of what "done" looks like, and when to ask me for help. Keep it under 300 words with numbered steps. Write for someone who has never worked in real estate. Include one sample message they can copy and send to a client.
prompts.proTip: Have your assistant follow the guide once and mark every place it was confusing. Then update it.

prompts.title: Analysis CMA Talking Points From Comparable Sales
prompts.useWhen: You have comps and need to explain a price (CMA summary, comparable market analysis, pricing presentation) in simple words.
prompts.prompt: Act as a real estate pricing analyst. Here are the comparable sales for my subject property at [ADDRESS]: [PASTE COMPS WITH PRICE, SIZE, BEDS/BATHS, CONDITION, DATE, AND DISTANCE]. Subject facts: [SUBJECT FACTS]. Create a table of adjustments (size, condition, updates, lot) with reasons. Suggest a price range and explain it in 5 bullets a seller can understand. Point out any weak comps and why. Remind me that this is a draft for my own review and that I should verify every number against MLS data.
prompts.proTip: Ask "What would make this range higher or lower?" The answer gives you talking points for negotiation.

prompts.title: Analysis Neighborhood Market Summary From Your Data
prompts.useWhen: You want a clean report for one area (neighborhood stats, market snapshot, local trends) from numbers you already pulled.
prompts.prompt: Use only the data below to write a neighborhood market summary for [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Data: [PASTE YOUR MLS STATS, such as median price, days on market, sales count, list-to-sale ratio, and inventory for the last 3 periods]. Create: a 100-word plain-English summary, a table of the numbers with change over time, 3 takeaways for buyers, and 3 takeaways for sellers. Do not guess or add any numbers I did not give you. Do not predict future prices. Add a line stating the data source and date: [SOURCE AND DATE].
prompts.proTip: If a number looks odd, ask the AI "Which number here should I double-check?"

prompts.title: Email Explaining a Changing Market to Clients
prompts.useWhen: Prices, rates, or inventory are shifting (market update, "is it a good time to buy or sell" question) and clients are worried.
prompts.prompt: Write an email to my clients explaining that the [CITY] market is [DESCRIBE CHANGE, like slowing or heating up] in plain English. Use only these facts: [MARKET FACTS]. Explain what it means for buyers and for sellers in two short sections, and give one calm action step for each. Avoid hype and fear language. Do not predict the future or give financial advice. Keep it under 220 words with a friendly, expert tone and a clear subject line. Offer a call on [DAYS] to talk about their situation.
prompts.proTip: Reframe the news as choices, not warnings. Calm agents keep clients.
fields: DESCRIBE CHANGE, like slowing or heating up

prompts.title: Analysis Quick Screen of a Rental Investment Property
prompts.useWhen: An investor asks "does this rental make sense?" (cash flow, cap rate, rental property numbers) and you need a first look.
prompts.prompt: Act as a real estate analyst helping me explain an investment property to a client. Property: [ADDRESS]. Numbers: price [PRICE], expected rent [RENT], taxes [TAXES], insurance [INSURANCE], HOA [HOA], maintenance [MAINTENANCE PERCENT], vacancy [VACANCY PERCENT], and financing [FINANCING TERMS]. Calculate a simple monthly cash flow, cap rate, and cash-on-cash return, and show your formulas step by step. List 5 assumptions to double-check. Add a clear note that this is a rough educational estimate, not investment, tax, or legal advice.
prompts.proTip: Run three versions (best, normal, worst case) so clients see the range.

prompts.title: Plan Annual Business Plan and Goals
prompts.useWhen: You want a real plan for the year (business plan, income goals, production targets) and do not know where to start.
prompts.prompt: Help me create a one-page annual business plan for my real estate business in [CITY]. My goal is [NUMBER] closed transactions, with an average sale price of [PRICE] and commission rate of [RATE]. Work backward to show how many appointments, conversations, and leads I need each month, using conversion rates of [CONVERSION RATES OR "typical rates, please state them"]. Present a table by quarter, plus 5 weekly habits and 3 risks to watch. Note that results vary and these are estimates I should adjust with my own data.
prompts.proTip: Update your real conversion numbers every quarter and re-run the prompt.
fields: CONVERSION RATES OR "typical rates, please state them"

prompts.title: Analysis Lead Source Return on Investment Review
prompts.useWhen: You want to know which marketing works (lead source ROI, cost per lead, where to spend money) and which to cut.
prompts.prompt: Analyze my lead sources for the last [TIME PERIOD]. Data: [PASTE A TABLE WITH SOURCE, MONEY SPENT, LEADS, APPOINTMENTS, CLOSINGS, AND COMMISSION EARNED]. Calculate cost per lead, cost per closing, and return on investment for each source. Rank them best to worst and explain in plain English what the numbers suggest. Suggest what to keep, test, and stop, and 3 questions I should ask before deciding. Do not assume anything I did not provide. Show all math.
prompts.proTip: Give the AI at least 6 months of data. Small samples can mislead you.

prompts.title: Plan Marketing Budget Allocation
prompts.useWhen: You have a limited budget (marketing budget, ad spend plan, where to invest) and want a smart split.
prompts.prompt: Create a marketing budget plan for a real estate agent in [CITY] with [MONTHLY BUDGET] per month and [HOURS] hours per week to spend on marketing. My focus is [BUYERS, SELLERS, OR BOTH]. My strengths: [STRENGTHS]. Suggest a budget split across categories such as online ads, direct mail, video, events, and CRM tools, with a reason for each. Present a table with a 90-day test plan and one number to track for each item. Include free options. Do not promise any results.
prompts.proTip: Test one new channel at a time. Otherwise you will not know what worked.

prompts.title: Analysis of Competing Agents in Your Market
prompts.useWhen: You want to stand out (competitor research, agent comparison, market positioning) before a listing presentation or rebrand.
prompts.prompt: Help me compare myself with 3 competing agents in [CITY OR NEIGHBORHOOD]. Here is public information I collected: [PASTE PUBLIC INFO ABOUT EACH AGENT, such as website claims, listings, reviews, and social presence]. Build a table comparing their strengths, message, and gaps. Then suggest 5 ways I can be different, based on my strengths: [YOUR STRENGTHS]. Do not invent facts about anyone, and do not include anything unfair or private. Keep it respectful and professional.
prompts.proTip: Look for what all agents say and then say something different and true.

prompts.title: Plan Geographic Farm Area Strategy
prompts.useWhen: You want to become "the agent" in one area (farming, farm area, neighborhood marketing plan) and need a 12-month roadmap.
prompts.prompt: Create a 12-month farming plan for [NEIGHBORHOOD OR ZIP CODE] with about [NUMBER] homes. My budget is [BUDGET] per month. Present a monthly table with the activity (mailer, event, door-knock, email, social), the message, cost, and goal. Include ideas for 4 community events I can host, and how I will track results, such as [TRACKING METHOD]. Make it truthful, respectful, and fair housing safe. Add a warning to check local rules for door-knocking and mailers.
prompts.proTip: Pick a farm area of 300 to 500 homes with good turnover. Bigger areas are too costly.

prompts.title: Post Agent Bio for Your Website and Profiles
prompts.useWhen: Your "About me" is boring or outdated (agent bio, about page, professional profile) and you want clients to feel they know you.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 versions of my real estate agent bio: 50 words, 120 words, and 250 words. My details: name [YOUR NAME], brokerage [BROKERAGE], area [AREA], years in business [YEARS], specialties [SPECIALTIES], a true personal detail [PERSONAL DETAIL], and results I can prove [PROVABLE RESULTS]. Write in the first person, with a warm and confident tone. Use only facts I gave you. Avoid clichés like "passionate" and "dedicated," and avoid superlatives I cannot prove, such as "best" or "number one."
prompts.proTip: Add one small personal detail. It is what people remember and repeat.

prompts.title: Response to a Negative Online Review
prompts.useWhen: Someone leaves a bad review or one-star rating (negative review, unhappy client comment, Google or Zillow review) and you need a calm public reply.
prompts.prompt: Write a professional public reply to this negative review on [PLATFORM]: "[PASTE REVIEW]". Give me 2 versions: a short one (under 60 words) and a fuller one (under 120 words). Thank them for the feedback, take responsibility where fair, share no private client details, and invite them to talk offline at [YOUR PHONE OR EMAIL]. Do not argue, blame, or get defensive. Sign as [YOUR NAME]. Add a short note on what I should check with my broker before I post.
prompts.proTip: Wait one hour before you post. Never reply while angry.

prompts.title: Email Requesting a Review or Testimonial
prompts.useWhen: A deal just closed happily (ask for a review, testimonial request, Google review request) and you want to make it easy.
prompts.prompt: Write a review request email and text for a happy client named [CLIENT FIRST NAME] who just [BOUGHT OR SOLD] at [NEIGHBORHOOD]. Thank them for something specific: [SPECIFIC MOMENT]. Explain in one sentence why reviews help, and share the direct link: [REVIEW LINK]. Offer 3 simple prompts they can use if they are not sure what to write, such as "What was the best part?" Keep the email under 110 words and the text under 200 characters. Do not offer gifts in exchange for a review.
prompts.proTip: Ask right after a happy moment, like getting the keys. Timing beats wording.

prompts.title: Email Apologizing for a Mistake or Missed Deadline
prompts.useWhen: You made an error (apology email, missed deadline, miscommunication) and need to fix trust quickly.
prompts.prompt: Write an honest apology email to [CLIENT FIRST NAME] about this mistake: [WHAT HAPPENED]. Include: a direct apology in the first line without excuses, a clear explanation of what happened in plain words, what I am doing to fix it ([FIX STEPS]) with a timeline, and what I will change so it does not happen again. Offer a call at [TIME]. Keep it under 180 words, sincere, and calm. Do not admit legal liability or blame others. Add a reminder to review this with my broker if money or contracts are involved.
prompts.proTip: Send the apology the same day you find the mistake. Speed shows respect.

prompts.title: Email Delivering Bad News When the Appraisal Comes in Low
prompts.useWhen: The appraisal is lower than the contract price (low appraisal, appraisal gap, value shortfall) and you must explain options.
prompts.prompt: Write two emails about a low appraisal at [ADDRESS]: one to my [BUYER OR SELLER] client [CLIENT FIRST NAME], and one to the other agent, [OTHER AGENT NAME]. Facts: contract price [PRICE], appraised value [APPRAISED VALUE], deadline [DEADLINE]. In the client email, explain in plain words what happened and list general options: renegotiate, bring extra funds, challenge the appraisal, or walk away if the contract allows. Keep the tone calm. Say I am not giving legal or financial advice and suggest a lender or attorney call. Each email under 180 words.
prompts.proTip: Call the client first, then send the email. Bad news should never arrive as text alone.

prompts.title: Email When a Deal Falls Through
prompts.useWhen: A contract is canceled (deal fell through, financing denied, buyer backed out) and your client needs support and a clear next step.
prompts.prompt: Write a supportive email to my client [CLIENT FIRST NAME] after the deal on [ADDRESS] fell through because of [REASON]. Acknowledge the disappointment in one honest sentence, then explain in simple terms what happens next, such as [NEXT STEPS, like relisting or restarting the search]. Include what I will do this week and a call time on [DATE]. Keep it under 170 words, empathetic, and forward-looking. Do not blame anyone and do not promise the next deal will be smoother.
prompts.proTip: Call within an hour of the news. Clients remember who showed up when it was hard.
fields: NEXT STEPS, like relisting or restarting the search

prompts.title: Response to an Angry Client Call
prompts.useWhen: A client is upset and yelling (angry client, complaint, heated phone call) and you need a plan to calm things down.
prompts.prompt: Coach me through handling an angry [BUYER OR SELLER] client who is upset about [ISSUE]. Give me: a 5-step calm-down script with exact words to say, 5 questions to understand what they truly need, 3 phrases to avoid, and a follow-up email of under 150 words to send afterward that summarizes what we agreed to do by [DATE]. Keep the language natural and respectful. Include a note on when to bring my broker into the situation. Assume this client is stressed, not a bad person.
prompts.proTip: Say "Let me make sure I understand" and repeat their issue. Feeling heard lowers the temperature.

prompts.title: Email Ending a Client Relationship Politely
prompts.useWhen: A client is no longer a fit (firing a client, canceling a buyer agreement, "parting ways") and you need a professional exit.
prompts.prompt: Write a respectful email ending my working relationship with [CLIENT FIRST NAME]. Reason: [REASON, kept neutral and factual]. Include: a thank-you, a calm statement that I can no longer represent them effectively, what happens next under our agreement ([AGREEMENT DETAILS]), and an offer to help them find another agent. Keep it under 160 words with no blame or emotion. Add a reminder that I must check my agreement, state rules, and my broker's advice before I send anything.
prompts.proTip: Talk to your broker first. Some agreements have steps you must follow.

prompts.title: Email Coaching a Seller When Showings Are Restricted or the Listing Is Expiring
prompts.useWhen: A seller limits showings or the listing is close to expiring (no offers, stale listing, showing restrictions) and needs a firm, kind talk.
prompts.prompt: Write a caring but direct email to seller [SELLER FIRST NAME] about [ADDRESS], where [SITUATION, like showings are limited or the listing expires on DATE]. Explain how [ISSUE] affects results using these facts: [FACTS]. Offer 3 options with pros and cons, like [OPTION 1], [OPTION 2], and [OPTION 3]. Ask them to reply or call by [DATE]. Keep it under 200 words, honest, and free of blame. Do not promise sales outcomes.
prompts.proTip: Offer a call, not just an email. Tough news works better when the seller can hear your tone.

prompts.title: Email Encouraging Buyers After Losing Several Offers
prompts.useWhen: Buyers keep losing to other offers (lost bid, multiple offer fatigue, discouraged buyers) and want to give up.
prompts.prompt: Write an encouraging but realistic email to buyers [CLIENT FIRST NAMES] who lost [NUMBER] offers in a row. Include: an honest acknowledgment of how frustrating this is, a simple review of what we learned ([LESSONS]), 3 changes we can consider ([CHANGE 1], [CHANGE 2], [CHANGE 3]), and a plan for this week. Do not promise they will win the next one. Keep it under 200 words, warm, and practical. End with a question about how they are feeling about the search.
prompts.proTip: Ask about their stress level, not just their strategy. Burnout ends more searches than money does.

prompts.title: Response When a Client Asks You to Bend the Rules
prompts.useWhen: A client asks for something unethical or risky (steering request, hiding a defect, breaking a rule) and you need to say no while keeping the relationship.
prompts.prompt: A client asked me to [DESCRIBE REQUEST]. Help me say no in a respectful, professional way. Write a phone script and a short email of under 150 words that: thank them for trusting me, explain that I cannot do this because of [LAW, RULE, OR ETHICS], offer 2 legal and ethical alternatives ([ALTERNATIVE 1], [ALTERNATIVE 2]), and keep the door open. Do not lecture. Remind me to document the conversation and talk to my broker or attorney.
prompts.proTip: Write down the request and your answer the same day. A simple note protects your license.

prompts.title: Plan Full Listing Launch Package From One Fact Sheet
prompts.useWhen: You have a new listing and want every piece of marketing at once (listing launch kit, marketing package, one-click content).
prompts.prompt: You are my real estate marketing team. I will give you facts about a listing, and you will create a full launch package. Facts: address [ADDRESS], price [PRICE], beds [BEDS], baths [BATHS], size [SQFT], features [FEATURES], updates [UPDATES], nearby spots [NEARBY SPOTS], open house [OPEN HOUSE DETAILS]. Step 1: write an MLS description (900 characters). Step 2: write a website description (200 words). Step 3: write 3 Instagram captions with hashtags. Step 4: write a 30-second video script. Step 5: write a Just Listed email with 3 subject lines. Step 6: write an open house text and a Facebook event description. Step 7: review everything for fair housing risk and list any changes. Use only my facts. Describe the property, never the buyer. Label each step clearly.
prompts.proTip: Save this prompt with your facts blank, so each new listing takes 5 minutes.

prompts.title: Plan 30 Days of Content From One Neighborhood
prompts.useWhen: You want a month of posts from one area (content batch, social media month, neighborhood content series).
prompts.prompt: Act as my content strategist. I am a real estate agent focused on [NEIGHBORHOOD] in [CITY]. Facts I know: [LOCAL FACTS, PLACES, EVENTS, MARKET STATS]. Step 1: list 12 content themes based on these facts. Step 2: create a 30day calendar table with the day, platform ([PLATFORMS]), format, and topic. Step 3: write full captions for the first 10 days. Step 4: write 3 short video scripts (30 seconds each). Step 5: write one email newsletter that uses the best 3 themes. Step 6: suggest 5 local businesses I could partner with for shoutouts. Keep everything fair housing safe: describe places, not people. No claims about schools or safety. Keep it friendly and simple.
prompts.proTip: After day 10, paste in your top-performing post and ask for 10 more like it.
fields: LOCAL FACTS, PLACES, EVENTS, MARKET STATS

prompts.title: Plan 90-Day Lead Follow-Up System
prompts.useWhen: Leads keep slipping away (lead nurture system, drip campaign, follow-up plan) and you want a full done-for-you sequence.
prompts.prompt: You are a real estate lead nurture expert. Build a 90-day follow-up system for online leads in [CITY] who want to [BUY OR SELL] in the range of [PRICE RANGE]. Step 1: create a table with 12 touches across email, text, call, and mail, showing day, channel, goal, and subject. Step 2: write every email (under 120 words each) and every text (under 250 characters). Step 3: write 2 voicemail scripts. Step 4: write 3 replies for common responses like "not ready yet" and "just browsing." Step 5: suggest which touches to automate and which to do personally. Include opt-out language for texts and emails, follow TCPA and CAN-SPAM basics, and sign as [YOUR NAME].
prompts.proTip: Load the emails into your CRM once, and let the system run for every new lead.

prompts.title: Analysis Listing Presentation Builder
prompts.useWhen: You have a listing appointment and want to build a full presentation (listing pitch, seller presentation, slide outline).
prompts.prompt: Act as a listing presentation coach. I am meeting [SELLER FIRST NAMES] about their home at [ADDRESS] on [DATE]. My facts: my experience [EXPERIENCE], my marketing plan [MARKETING PLAN], my average days on market [DAYS ON MARKET], and my fee [FEE]. Step 1: create a slide-by-slide outline (12 slides) with a headline and 3 bullets for each. Step 2: write the speaking notes for each slide in 2 to 3 sentences. Step 3: list 8 likely seller questions and give me a strong, honest answer for each. Step 4: write a follow-up email to send within 2 hours after the meeting. Step 5: suggest 3 questions that will help me learn what matters to the sellers. Do not invent statistics or results. Use only my facts.
prompts.proTip: Paste in your real stats and testimonials so the deck uses your proof.

prompts.title: Plan Buyer Journey Email Series
prompts.useWhen: You want new buyers to get steady, helpful emails (buyer nurture series, email drip for homebuyers, education series).
prompts.prompt: You are an email marketing expert for real estate. Create an 8-email series for new buyer clients of [YOUR NAME] at [BROKERAGE] in [CITY]. Step 1: give me a table with email number, send timing, subject line, and goal. The topics must cover: getting pre-approved, choosing an area, what to expect at showings, making an offer, inspection, appraisal, closing costs, and moving day. Step 2: write all 8 emails, each under 200 words, at a 6thgrade level, with one clear call to action. Step 3: write a short SMS to go with emails 1, 4, and 8. Add a reminder in emails that touch on money to check with a lender or attorney. Keep the tone warm and expert.
prompts.proTip: Load this into your CRM as an automatic series triggered when a buyer signs.

prompts.title: Plan Open House Marketing Campaign
prompts.useWhen: You want a busy open house (open house promotion plan, event marketing, weekend traffic plan) with a full timeline.
prompts.prompt: Act as my event marketing manager. I am hosting an open house at [ADDRESS] on [DATE AND TIME]. Price [PRICE], key features [FEATURES]. Step 1: build a 10-day countdown plan in a table (day, channel, task). Step 2: write all the copy: 3 social posts, 1 email, 1 text to neighbors, 1 sign message, and 1 flyer text. Step 3: create a day-of checklist and a follow-up plan for visitors, including 2 follow-up emails. Step 4: write a short "thank you for coming" text. Step 5: list 5 ways to measure success, such as [SUCCESS MEASURES]. Welcome everyone equally and use fair housing safe wording only.
prompts.proTip: Invite neighbors 3 days early. They often bring friends, and they tell you who might sell.

prompts.title: Plan 12-Month Referral Campaign for Your Sphere
prompts.useWhen: You want more business from people you know (referral system, sphere of influence plan, past client marketing).
prompts.prompt: Act as a referral marketing coach. I have about [NUMBER] contacts, including [PAST CLIENTS, FRIENDS, FAMILY, OR OTHERS]. My goal is [NUMBER] referrals this year. Step 1: create a 12-month table with one touch per month (email, call, handwritten note, event, or gift), the message, and cost. Step 2: write all 12 messages. Step 3: write 3 ways to ask for referrals that feel natural. Step 4: write a thank-you plan for people who refer me. Step 5: suggest 5 ways to track results, such as [TRACKING TOOL]. Keep the tone genuine and not salesy. Follow state rules on referral fees and gifts, and remind me to check with my broker.
prompts.proTip: Put the whole plan in your calendar as recurring reminders so it happens.
fields: PAST CLIENTS, FRIENDS, FAMILY, OR OTHERS

prompts.title: Plan Business Plan With Weekly Action Steps
prompts.useWhen: You have goals but no plan (business plan, income plan, quarterly goals) and need it broken into small weekly steps.
prompts.prompt: Act as a business coach for real estate agents. My goal for the next 12 months is [GOAL, like 20 closings]. My current situation: [CURRENT SITUATION, like 8 closings last year, part-time, new agent]. My strengths: [STRENGTHS]. My weaknesses: [WEAKNESSES]. Step 1: work backward to show the numbers I need each month. Step 2: choose the 3 best lead sources for me and explain why. Step 3: give me a 4-week starter plan with daily actions.
