Step 4: set 12 monthly milestones. Step 5: list 5 risks and how to handle each. Step 6: write a weekly review checklist of 10 questions. Present in tables. State any assumptions clearly.
prompts.proTip: Run the weekly review checklist every Friday. It keeps the plan alive.

prompts.title: Plan New Agent 30-60-90 Day Launch
prompts.useWhen: You are a new agent (new agent plan, first 90 days, getting started in real estate) and need a clear path.
prompts.prompt: Act as a mentor for a new real estate agent in [CITY] who has [HOURS] hours per week and a budget of [BUDGET]. My starting network: [NETWORK DETAILS]. Step 1: build a 30-60-90 day plan with weekly goals in a table. Step 2: write 5 scripts I can use to tell people I am now an agent. Step 3: create an introduction email and 2 social posts announcing my start. Step 4: list 10 free ways to find leads. Step 5: write a list of 15 questions to ask my broker. Step 6: create a daily routine template. Keep it realistic, encouraging, and fully compliant with advertising rules, including using my brokerage name.
prompts.proTip: Show your broker this plan. Many will give feedback and hold you accountable.

prompts.title: Plan Client-for-Life Program After Closing
prompts.useWhen: You want repeat and referral business (past client program, client retention, after-sale care) instead of chasing new leads.
prompts.prompt: You are a client retention strategist for real estate agents. Build a "client for life" program for buyers and sellers who close with me, [YOUR NAME], in [CITY]. Step 1: create a 24-month touch calendar in a table (timing, touch type, message theme, cost). Step 2: write the first 8 messages, including a 1-week thank you, 30-day check-in, 6month home tip, 1-year anniversary, and market update. Step 3: write a referral request that fits the program. Step 4: suggest 5 low-cost client events or gifts under [BUDGET]. Step 5: write a short guide for tracking the program in [CRM NAME]. Never promise home values or investment returns. Keep the tone warm.
prompts.proTip: Start the program at the closing table, so no one falls through the cracks.

prompts.title: Email Explaining a Market Drop to Worried Clients
prompts.useWhen: the market falls and you need a calm, reassuring message before clients start calling in a panic about volatility or losses.
prompts.prompt: You are a communications assistant for a financial advisory firm. Write a calm, reassuring email to clients about the recent market decline of [PERCENTAGE OR DESCRIPTION]. My firm's philosophy is [YOUR INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY, E.G., LONG- TERM, DIVERSIFIED, GOALS-BASED]. Remind clients why their plan was built for moments like this, without predicting the market or promising any outcome. Keep it under 200 words, warm but professional, and end by inviting them to [CALL/BOOK A MEETING] if they want to talk. Do not use jargon.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version for clients within 5 years of retirement; they need a different kind of reassurance.

prompts.title: Email Requesting Missing Documents From a Client
prompts.useWhen: you are chasing paperwork a client still has not sent and want a friendly nudge that actually gets a response.
prompts.prompt: Write a short, friendly email to my client [CLIENT FIRST NAME] requesting these missing documents: [LIST OF DOCUMENTS]. We need them by [DATE] so we can [WHAT YOU'RE DOING FOR THEM, E.G., FILE THEIR RETURN, FINISH THEIR PLAN]. Make it easy to act: include a numbered list of exactly what to send and how to send it ([PORTAL/EMAIL/DROP-OFF]). Keep the tone helpful, not scolding. Under 120 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a follow-up version "with a gentle deadline warning" to send one week later if they still have not replied.

prompts.title: Plain-English Explanation of a Financial Term or Concept
prompts.useWhen: a client asks what something means (Roth conversion, amortization, cost basis, escrow) and you want a simple definition without dumbing it down.
prompts.prompt: Explain [FINANCIAL TERM OR CONCEPT] to a client with no financial background. Use everyday language, one short analogy, and a concrete example with round numbers like [EXAMPLE AMOUNT]. Keep it under 150 words. Then give me a one-sentence version I can say out loud in a meeting. Avoid any language that sounds like a recommendation; this is education only.
prompts.proTip: Add "explain it for a [AGE]-year-old client thinking about [THEIR GOAL]" to make the example feel personal.

prompts.title: Email Announcing a Fee Increase to Existing Clients
prompts.useWhen: you are raising prices or changing your fee schedule and need to notify clients without triggering an exodus.
prompts.prompt: Write an email announcing a fee change to my existing clients. Current fee: [CURRENT FEE]. New fee: [NEW FEE], effective [DATE]. Reasons: [E.G., EXPANDED SERVICES, RISING COSTS, FIRST INCREASE IN X YEARS]. Lead with the value they receive, state the change clearly and confidently (no over-apologizing), explain what stays the same, and invite questions. Professional and warm, under 250 words. Give me 2 versions: one for long-time clients and one for newer clients.
prompts.proTip: Ask it to also draft 3 likely client pushback questions with suggested short answers.

prompts.title: Reply to a Client Asking for Advice Outside Your Scope
prompts.useWhen: a client asks about something you do not handle (legal questions, insurance you don't sell, crypto tips) and you need a graceful redirect or referral.
prompts.prompt: Write a brief, kind email to a client who asked me about [TOPIC OUTSIDE YOUR SCOPE]. I am a [YOUR ROLE, E.G., CPA, FINANCIAL PLANNER] and this falls outside my services/licensing. Thank them for trusting me, explain in one sentence why I can't advise on it, and refer them to [TYPE OF PROFESSIONAL OR SPECIFIC NAME]. Offer to coordinate with that professional if helpful. Keep it under 100 words so it feels effortless, not defensive.
prompts.proTip: Keep a saved version for each of the 3 topics clients ask you about most.
fields: YOUR ROLE, E.G., CPA, FINANCIAL PLANNER
TYPE OF PROFESSIONAL OR SPECIFIC NAME

prompts.title: Quarterly Check-In Email for Clients You Have Not Talked To
prompts.useWhen: you want a low-pressure touch-base message for quiet clients so they feel remembered, not sold to.
prompts.prompt: Write a warm quarterly check-in email for clients I have not spoken with recently. My services: [YOUR SERVICES]. Season/context: [E.G., MID-YEAR, POST TAX SEASON, YEAR-END]. Include one useful seasonal reminder (like [TOPIC, E.G., RMD DEADLINES, ESTIMATED PAYMENTS, BENEFITS ENROLLMENT]), one open question about changes in their life, and an easy way to book time with me: [BOOKING LINK OR PHONE]. Under 150 words. No hard sell.
prompts.proTip: Generate all four quarters at once by adding "give me a version for each quarter of the year."
fields: E.G., MID-YEAR, POST TAX SEASON, YEAR-END

prompts.title: Email Explaining an IRS or State Tax Notice to a Client
prompts.useWhen: a client forwards a scary letter from the IRS or state and you need to translate it and lay out next steps before they spiral.
prompts.prompt: Help me explain a tax notice to my client. Notice type: [NOTICE NUMBER/ TYPE, E.G., CP2000]. What it says: [BRIEF SUMMARY]. What we plan to do: [YOUR PLANNED RESPONSE]. Write an email that (1) tells them not to panic and why, (2) explains the notice in plain English in 2-3 sentences, (3) lists what I need from them, and (4) states the deadline [DATE]. Reassuring, professional, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a phone script version too; anxious clients often call before they read.

prompts.title: Holiday and Milestone Greeting Messages for Clients
prompts.useWhen: you want short, personal-feeling notes for birthdays, holidays, retirements, new babies, or business anniversaries, without sounding like a greeting card rack.
prompts.prompt: Write [NUMBER] short greeting messages I can send clients for [OCCASION, E.G., THANKSGIVING, A RETIREMENT, A BUSINESS ANNIVERSARY]. My relationship with clients is [FORMAL/FRIENDLY/LONG-TERM]. Each message should be 2-4 sentences, feel personal rather than corporate, avoid religious assumptions unless I say otherwise, and never pitch services. Vary the wording so no two feel identical. Give them to me as a numbered list.
prompts.proTip: Paste in one detail about the specific client ("just became a grandparent") and ask it to weave that in.

prompts.title: Email Summarizing a Client Meeting and Next Steps
prompts.useWhen: you just finished a client meeting or review call and need a same-day recap email with action items while it is fresh.
prompts.prompt: Turn my rough meeting notes into a polished recap email for my client [CLIENT NAME]. Notes: [PASTE YOUR NOTES]. Structure it as: a one-line thank you, "What we discussed" (3-5 bullets), "What I will do" with dates, "What you will do" with dates, and "Our next meeting: [DATE]". Keep my wording where it is clear, fix grammar, and keep the whole email under 250 words. Professional but warm.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a 2-line internal file note version at the same time for your CRM or workpapers.

prompts.title: Reusable Answer to a Question Clients Ask Over and Over
prompts.useWhen: you keep typing the same reply (FAQ) from scratch, like "when will my refund arrive" or "should I worry about this statement."
prompts.prompt: Help me build a reusable answer to a question my clients constantly ask: "[THE QUESTION]". My typical answer, roughly: [YOUR ROUGH ANSWER]. Turn it into a clear, friendly email template with a [BLANK] placeholder anywhere the answer changes per client. Keep it under 150 words, add one sentence inviting follow-up questions, and suggest a subject line. Also give me a 2-sentence short version for text or portal messages.
prompts.proTip: Run this once for your top 10 questions and you have a personal template library in an afternoon.

prompts.title: Email Introducing a New Team Member to Your Clients
prompts.useWhen: you hired an associate, admin, or junior accountant and want clients to trust and actually use the new person.
prompts.prompt: Write an email introducing our new team member to clients. Name and role: [NAME, ROLE]. Background highlights: [2-3 CREDENTIALS OR EXPERIENCE POINTS]. What they will handle for clients: [TASKS]. What stays with me: [TASKS]. Frame this as a service upgrade (faster responses, more attention), not a handoff. Include one human detail about them: [HOBBY OR FUN FACT]. Warm, confident, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a short version the new hire can use to introduce themselves when they first reply to a client.

prompts.title: Boundary-Setting Reply to After-Hours or Constant Messages
prompts.useWhen: a client texts at 9 pm, emails daily, or expects instant answers, and you need to reset expectations without souring the relationship.
prompts.prompt: Write a kind but firm reply to a client who [DESCRIBE BEHAVIOR, E.G., TEXTS AT NIGHT, EMAILS MULTIPLE TIMES A DAY]. Reassure them their needs matter, then clearly state my communication policy: response time of [YOUR RESPONSE WINDOW], business hours [YOUR HOURS], and the best channel [EMAIL/PORTAL/SCHEDULED CALLS]. Explain the benefit to them (focused, accurate work). No apologies for having boundaries. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a positive "policy welcome blurb" version to give all new clients so you rarely need this email again.

prompts.title: Welcome Email Sequence for a New Client
prompts.useWhen: someone just signed on and you want a 3-email onboarding welcome series instead of one info-dump message.
prompts.prompt: Write a 3-email welcome sequence for a new client of my [TYPE OF PRACTICE, E.G., TAX FIRM, ADVISORY PRACTICE]. Email 1 (day 1): warm welcome, what happens next, one action for them: [FIRST ACTION]. Email 2 (day 3): how we work: communication policy [YOUR POLICY], portal/tools [YOUR TOOLS], who to contact for what. Email 3 (day 7): what great results look like by [TIMEFRAME] and how to reach me: [CONTACT]. Each under 150 words, friendly and confident. Label each with its send day and subject line.
prompts.proTip: Paste the finished sequence into your email tool once and onboarding runs itself.
fields: TYPE OF PRACTICE, E.G., TAX FIRM, ADVISORY PRACTICE

prompts.title: New Client Intake Questionnaire
prompts.useWhen: you need an intake form or discovery questionnaire that gathers real information without overwhelming a new client.
prompts.prompt: Create a new client intake questionnaire for my [TYPE OF PRACTICE] serving [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS, PRE-RETIREES]. Organize it into sections: contact and household basics, current financial picture, goals and worries, past experience with [ADVISORS/ACCOUNTANTS], and logistics. Use a mix of short-answer and multiple-choice. Maximum [NUMBER] questions total, worded warmly (ask about "concerns," not "problems"). Flag which 5 questions matter most if I need a short version.
prompts.proTip: Ask it to convert the final version into a fillable format for Google Forms with question types labeled.
fields: CLIENT TYPE, E.G., SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS, PRE-RETIREES

prompts.title: Checklist of Documents Needed From a New Client
prompts.useWhen: you are sending a document request list (tax docs, statements, policies) and want it organized so clients actually complete it.
prompts.prompt: Create a document checklist for a new [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., 1040 TAX CLIENT, FINANCIAL PLANNING CLIENT]. Services involved: [YOUR SERVICES]. Group documents by category (income, accounts, insurance, legal, business), mark each item as Required or If Applicable, and add a plain-English note for anything clients commonly misunderstand, like [COMMONLY CONFUSED ITEM]. Format as a clean checklist I can paste into an email or PDF, with a friendly 2-sentence intro and a due date of [DATE].
prompts.proTip: Ask for a "where to find this" hint next to the 3 items clients most often cannot locate.

prompts.title: Agenda for a First Discovery Meeting With a Prospect
prompts.useWhen: you have an initial consultation booked and want a structured agenda that builds trust and surfaces whether you two are a fit.
prompts.prompt: Build a [LENGTH]-minute agenda for a first meeting with a prospective client. My practice: [WHAT YOU DO]. The prospect's situation, as far as I know: [WHAT YOU KNOW]. Structure: warm open (2 min), their story and goals (the longest block, with 5 open questions for me to ask), how I work and pricing overview, fit check both ways, clear next step. For each section give the time, purpose, and one suggested phrase to open it. Keep the whole thing on one page.
prompts.proTip: Ask it to add the one question you should NOT forget based on their situation.

prompts.title: Script for Explaining Your Services and Process to a New Client
prompts.useWhen: you stumble through "so here's how this works" and want a tight, confident explanation of your process and what clients get.
prompts.prompt: Write a spoken script (not an email) explaining how my service works, for use in meetings. My service: [SERVICE]. My process steps: [LIST YOUR STEPS]. Timeline: [TYPICAL TIMELINE]. What clients get: [DELIVERABLES]. What I need from them: [CLIENT RESPONSIBILITIES]. Make it 90 seconds when read aloud, conversational, confident, and free of jargon. End with a natural check-in question, not "any questions?"
prompts.proTip: Practice it out loud twice, then ask the AI to shorten whatever felt clunky when you said it.

prompts.title: Annual Review Meeting Agenda and Prep Questions
prompts.useWhen: yearly review or planning meetings are coming up and you want a repeatable agenda plus questions that get clients talking.
prompts.prompt: Create an annual review meeting agenda for my [ADVISORY/TAX/ ACCOUNTING] clients. Meeting length: [LENGTH]. Cover: wins and changes since last year, review of [WHAT YOU REVIEW, E.G., PORTFOLIO, TAX RESULT, FINANCIALS], life or business changes ahead, and next-year priorities. Include 6 open-ended prep questions to send the client one week before, worded so a busy person can answer in 5 minutes. Format the agenda with time blocks and the prep questions as a separate short email.
prompts.proTip: Reuse the same agenda every year; consistency makes reviews feel like a premium service.
fields: WHAT YOU REVIEW, E.G., PORTFOLIO, TAX RESULT, FINANCIALS

prompts.title: Reusable Meeting Recap Template
prompts.useWhen: you want one fill-in-the-blank recap template your whole office can use after any client meeting or call.
prompts.prompt: Create a fill-in-the-blank meeting recap template for my [TYPE OF FIRM]. It should work for any client meeting. Sections: meeting date and attendees, key topics ([BLANK] bullets), decisions made, action items split into "our tasks" and "client tasks" with owners and due dates, and next meeting date. Add a short professional opening and closing line that stays the same every time. Keep the template under one page and label every blank clearly in [BRACKETS].
prompts.proTip: Save this in your notes app; pair it with Prompt #9 to auto-fill it from raw notes.

prompts.title: Client Expectations One-Pager: How We Work Together
prompts.useWhen: you want a "working with us" welcome document that prevents 90% of future friction about response times, deadlines, and scope.
prompts.prompt: Write a one-page "How We Work Together" document for new clients of my [TYPE OF PRACTICE]. Include: what we do (and don't do): [SCOPE]; communication: response time [WINDOW], channels [CHANNELS]; deadlines and what happens if documents arrive late: [YOUR POLICY]; fees and billing basics: [BILLING APPROACH]; and how to get the best results from us (3 tips). Friendly and clear, zero legal-sounding language, under 400 words with short headers.
prompts.proTip: Send it with every engagement letter; it answers the questions clients feel awkward asking.

prompts.title: Discovery Questions About Goals, Money History, and Risk
prompts.useWhen: you want deeper conversation starters for understanding a client's real goals, fears, and risk comfort, beyond the standard questionnaire.
prompts.prompt: Give me 12 open-ended discovery questions for a meeting with a [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., NEW RETIREE COUPLE, RESTAURANT OWNER]. Goal of the meeting: [GOAL]. Organize them into three groups: their history with money, what they want life or the business to look like in [TIMEFRAME], and how they feel about risk and uncertainty. Word each question conversationally, the way I would actually say it, and add a one-line note on what each question helps me learn.
prompts.proTip: Pick your favorite 5; twelve questions is a menu, not a script.
fields: CLIENT TYPE, E.G., NEW RETIREE COUPLE, RESTAURANT OWNER

prompts.title: Offboarding Email and Checklist for a Departing Client
prompts.useWhen: a client is leaving (moving, switching firms, closing a business) and you want a graceful exit that protects the relationship and covers the transfer details.
prompts.prompt: Write a professional offboarding email for a client leaving my practice because [REASON, IF KNOWN]. Include: a gracious thank-you for their trust, a checklist of what happens next (final [DELIVERABLES/RETURNS/REPORTS], records they will receive and how [FORMAT/PORTAL], any final invoice [AMOUNT/TIMING], and what I will send their new [ADVISOR/ACCOUNTANT] with their authorization), and a warm door-open closing. No guilttripping. Under 250 words, plus a 5-item internal checklist for my team.
prompts.proTip: Departing clients still refer people; ask for one closing sentence that plants that seed naturally.

prompts.title: Month of LinkedIn Post Ideas for Your Practice
prompts.useWhen: your content calendar is empty and you need 30 days of social media ideas tailored to your niche, not generic finance fluff.
prompts.prompt: Act as a content strategist for financial professionals. Generate 20 LinkedIn post ideas for a [YOUR ROLE, E.G., CPA, WEALTH ADVISOR] serving [YOUR NICHE, E.G., DENTISTS, YOUNG FAMILIES]. Mix these types: myth-busting, seasonal reminders tied to [CURRENT MONTH], client-question answers, behind-the-scenes of my work, and simple how-tos. For each idea give a hook line (first sentence) and a 1-line summary. No investment performance claims, no guarantees, nothing that promises specific results. Present as a numbered list.
prompts.proTip: Say "write out ideas 3, 7, and 12 as full posts" to turn the best ones into finished content instantly.
fields: YOUR ROLE, E.G., CPA, WEALTH ADVISOR
YOUR NICHE, E.G., DENTISTS, YOUNG FAMILIES

prompts.title: LinkedIn Post Explaining a Money Topic in Plain English
prompts.useWhen: you want one finished social post that teaches a concept simply and positions you as the approachable expert.
prompts.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post explaining [TOPIC, E.G., WHY TAX REFUNDS AREN'T FREE MONEY, WHAT AN EMERGENCY FUND REALLY COVERS] for [AUDIENCE]. Structure: a scroll-stopping first line, a short story or relatable example, 3 quick takeaways, and a soft closing question to invite comments. Under 200 words, short paragraphs, no hashtag spam (3 max), 6th-grade reading level. Educational tone only: no advice to buy or sell anything, no performance promises. Give me 2 versions with different hooks.
prompts.proTip: The hook is 80% of the result; ask for 5 alternative first lines and pick the one you'd stop for.

prompts.title: Email Newsletter Draft From One Topic
prompts.useWhen: your monthly client newsletter is due and you have a topic but no time to write it.
prompts.prompt: Write my [MONTHLY/QUARTERLY] client newsletter. Main topic: [TOPIC]. My audience: [CLIENT TYPE]. Structure: a 2-sentence personal opening from me (context: [WHAT'S NEW WITH YOU OR THE SEASON]), the main article (300 words, plain English, one practical takeaway), a "dates and deadlines" box with [UPCOMING DEADLINES], and a one-line reminder of a service: [SERVICE]. Include a subject line and preview text. Warm and helpful, never salesy, no market predictions.
prompts.proTip: Keep every issue's structure identical; readers skim familiar layouts and actually finish them.
fields: WHAT'S NEW WITH YOU OR THE SEASON

prompts.title: Lead Magnet Ideas and Outline (Checklist, Guide, or Worksheet)
prompts.useWhen: you want a freebie download to capture emails, like a tax prep checklist or retirement readiness guide, and need ideas plus a full outline.
prompts.prompt: Suggest 5 lead magnet ideas for a [YOUR ROLE] who wants to attract [IDEAL CLIENT]. Each idea: a title, the format (checklist, short guide, worksheet, calculator walkthrough), and why this audience would trade their email for it. Then take the strongest idea and write a complete outline: sections, key points per section, and a title plus subtitle for the cover. It must be doable as a [LENGTH]-page PDF and require no ongoing updates for at least a year.
prompts.proTip: Ask it to draft the full text of the winning lead magnet next; you are one prompt away from finished.

prompts.title: Website Homepage Copy for Your Practice
prompts.useWhen: your website reads like everyone else's ("comprehensive solutions for your financial needs") and you want copy that speaks to your actual clients.
prompts.prompt: Rewrite my website homepage copy. My practice: [WHAT YOU DO]. Ideal client: [WHO]. Their biggest worry: [PAIN POINT]. What makes me different: [DIFFERENTIATOR]. Write: a headline focused on the client's outcome (not my services), a subheadline, 3 short service blurbs with benefit-first titles, a 100-word "why work with me" section, and a call to action for [NEXT STEP, E.G., FREE CONSULTATION]. Confident, warm, no clichés like "comprehensive" or "holistic," no guarantees of results.
prompts.proTip: Paste your current homepage text and add "here's my old copy; keep anything that's working."

prompts.title: Google Business Profile Description and Posts
prompts.useWhen: local clients find you through Google and your profile is empty, outdated, or missing regular updates (also works for Yelp and directories).
prompts.prompt: Write content for my Google Business Profile. Business: [NAME], a [TYPE OF PRACTICE] in [CITY] serving [CLIENT TYPE]. First, a 750-character business description packed with the phrases locals actually search, like [SEARCH TERMS, E.G., "TAX PREPARER NEAR ME," "FEE-ONLY ADVISOR [CITY]"]. Then 4 short update posts (one per week for a month): a seasonal tip, a service spotlight on [SERVICE], a FAQ answer, and a friendly office update. Each post under 100 words with a clear call to action.
prompts.proTip: Refresh the 4 posts monthly with this same prompt; active profiles rank higher in local results.

prompts.title: Script for a 60-Second Educational Video or Reel
prompts.useWhen: you want to try short video (Reels, Shorts, TikTok) and need a tight script that teaches one thing without rambling.
prompts.prompt: Write a 60-second video script for [PLATFORM] where I explain [ONE NARROW TOPIC, E.G., THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A W-2 AND A 1099]. My audience: [AUDIENCE]. Format: a 3-second hook that names their problem, the explanation in 3 simple beats with a concrete number example, and a closing line inviting them to [FOLLOW/ COMMENT/DOWNLOAD MY GUIDE]. Write it word-for-word as I would speak, about 140 words total, with [PAUSE] markers. No jargon, no promises about results.
prompts.proTip: Ask for 4 more scripts on related micro-topics; batch-record them all in one 30-minute sitting.

prompts.title: Seminar or Webinar Promotion Email and Social Posts
prompts.useWhen: you are hosting an educational event (webinar, lunch-and-learn, tax workshop) and need the full promo kit to fill seats.
prompts.prompt: Create a promotion kit for my upcoming event: [EVENT NAME] on [DATE/TIME] about [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. Registration: [LINK OR METHOD]. Write: an invitation email (under 200 words, benefit-led subject line), a reminder email for 2 days before, 3 social posts with different angles (what they'll learn, who it's for, seats limited: [CAPACITY]), and a 50word blurb for partners to share. Educational framing throughout; attendees should expect learning, not a sales pitch.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a "sorry we missed you" replay email too; half your leads come from people who didn't show.

prompts.title: Client Review and Testimonial Request Message
prompts.useWhen: you want more Google reviews or testimonials and need a comfortable way to ask happy clients without pressuring them.
prompts.prompt: Write a short message asking a happy client for a review. Context: we just [RECENT WIN, E.G., FINISHED THEIR RETURN, COMPLETED THEIR PLAN]. Where to review: [GOOGLE/PLATFORM LINK]. Make the ask feel optional and easy: mention it takes 2 minutes, suggest they mention what the experience was like working with us (service, communication, clarity), and thank them either way. Under 100 words. Note for me: list 2 sentences on common review-solicitation compliance cautions for [YOUR PROFESSION] I should verify with my compliance resource.
prompts.proTip: Advisors: testimonial rules changed under the SEC Marketing Rule; confirm your firm's policy before sending any review request.

prompts.title: Blog Post on a Tax or Money Deadline
prompts.useWhen: a deadline is approaching (filing day, RMDs, open enrollment, estimated payments) and you want a helpful, search-friendly article.
prompts.prompt: Write a 600-word blog post about the upcoming [DEADLINE, E.G., APRIL 15 FILING DEADLINE, DECEMBER 31 RMD DEADLINE] for [AUDIENCE]. Include: why this deadline matters in plain English, the [NUMBER] most common mistakes people make, a short "what to do this week" action list, and when to get professional help. SEO title and meta description included, target phrase: [SEARCH PHRASE]. Reading level: 7th grade. End with a soft call to action for [YOUR SERVICE]. No fear-mongering; helpful and calm.
prompts.proTip: Change the deadline and audience and this one prompt becomes a year of blog content.

prompts.title: Tax Season Countdown Social Posts
prompts.useWhen: tax season is approaching and you want a series of posts that build urgency for early filing and early document drop-off.
prompts.prompt: Write a 6-post social media countdown series for tax season. My firm: [FIRM NAME/TYPE] serving [CLIENT TYPE]. Key dates: documents due to us by [YOUR INTERNAL DEADLINE], filing deadline [DATE]. Posts: 8 weeks out (get organized), 6 weeks (documents checklist teaser), 4 weeks (early-bird benefits), 3 weeks (our cutoff is coming), 2 weeks (extension explainer, no shame), deadline week (last call + what to do if you missed it). Each under 80 words, friendly urgency, no panic language.
prompts.proTip: Ask for matching email subject lines so your inbox campaign and social feed reinforce each other.

prompts.title: Compliance-Safe Rewrite of Marketing Copy
prompts.useWhen: you have drafted marketing text and want a sweep for guarantees, performance promises, or overreaching claims before it goes out (advertising review helper).
prompts.prompt: Review this marketing copy for a [YOUR ROLE, E.G., INVESTMENT ADVISOR, CPA]: [PASTE COPY]. Flag anything that (1) promises or implies specific results or returns, (2) uses superlatives I can't prove ("best," "guaranteed," "always saves you money"), (3) could mislead about my credentials or services, or (4) states opinions as facts. For each flag, explain the problem in one sentence and suggest a compliant rewrite that keeps the persuasive punch. Then output the full cleaned-up version.
prompts.proTip: This is a helpful first screen, not a compliance approval; your compliance officer or state board rules always get the final word.
fields: YOUR ROLE, E.G., INVESTMENT ADVISOR, CPA

prompts.title: Cold Outreach Email to a Small Business Owner
prompts.useWhen: you are reaching out to a business owner who has never heard of you and want a first-touch email that gets a reply, not a delete.
prompts.prompt: Write a cold outreach email to [PROSPECT TYPE, E.G., A LOCAL RESTAURANT OWNER, A DENTAL PRACTICE OWNER] from me, a [YOUR ROLE]. The specific reason I'm reaching out: [PERSONALIZED HOOK, E.G., THEY JUST OPENED A SECOND LOCATION]. One problem I solve for businesses like theirs: [PROBLEM]. Under 90 words, no attachments mentioned, one clear low-commitment ask: [ASK, E.G., 15-MINUTE CALL]. Sound like a helpful local professional, not a marketing agency. Give me 3 subject lines under 6 words.
prompts.proTip: One genuinely specific detail about their business beats every clever template line; always fill the hook.
fields: PERSONALIZED HOOK, E.G., THEY JUST OPENED A SECOND LOCATION

prompts.title: Follow-Up Email After a Networking Event
prompts.useWhen: you met someone at a chamber event, conference, or BNI meeting and want to follow up within 48 hours without being awkward.
prompts.prompt: Write a follow-up email to [NAME], whom I met at [EVENT]. What we talked about: [CONVERSATION DETAIL]. Their situation: [WHAT YOU LEARNED]. My goal: [GOAL, E.G., COFFEE MEETING, STAY ON THEIR RADAR, INTRO TO THEIR CLIENTS]. Reference our conversation naturally in the first line, offer something useful (an article, an intro, a quick answer) before asking anything, and keep it under 120 words. Friendly and specific, zero sales pressure.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a calendar reminder message to yourself for 3 weeks later if they don't respond.

prompts.title: Referral Request Email to Happy Clients
prompts.useWhen: you want more clients like your best ones and need a comfortable way to ask for introductions and word-of-mouth.
prompts.prompt: Write a referral request email to a client who recently said [POSITIVE FEEDBACK THEY GAVE]. My ideal referral: [WHO YOU WANT TO MEET, E.G., OTHER PHYSICIANS, BUSINESS OWNERS NEARING RETIREMENT]. Make it specific ("if you know someone who [SITUATION]...") rather than "anyone you know." Explain in one sentence how I treat referred people (no pressure, [FREE CONSULT/CONVERSATION FIRST]). Give an effortless way to connect us: [METHOD, E.G., FORWARD THIS EMAIL, REPLY WITH THEIR NAME]. Under 130 words, grateful but not gushing.
prompts.proTip: Send within a week of a client thanking you; gratitude has a short shelf life.
fields: METHOD, E.G., FORWARD THIS EMAIL, REPLY WITH THEIR NAME

prompts.title: Outreach to Referral Partners: Attorneys, Realtors, and Lenders
prompts.useWhen: you want a referral relationship with centers of influence (estate attorneys, realtors, mortgage brokers, bankers) who serve your same clients.
prompts.prompt: Write an outreach email to a [PROFESSIONAL TYPE, E.G., ESTATE ATTORNEY] proposing a referral relationship. My practice: [WHAT YOU DO] for [CLIENT TYPE]. Why the partnership helps THEIR clients: [BENEFIT, E.G., THEIR CLIENTS NEED TAX GUIDANCE AFTER SETTLING AN ESTATE]. Suggest a specific low-effort first step: [COFFEE, 20-MINUTE CALL]. Make 70% of the email about their clients and their practice, 30% about mine. Under 150 words, peer-to-peer tone, plus 2 subject line options.
prompts.proTip: Mention one real way you've helped a mutual client type; specificity is what separates you from every other "let's connect" email they get.

prompts.title: Follow-Up Sequence for a Prospect Who Went Quiet
prompts.useWhen: a promising lead ghosted after a consultation or proposal and you need a polite re-engagement drip that isn't desperate.
prompts.prompt: Write a 3-email follow-up sequence for a prospect who went silent after [LAST INTERACTION, E.G., OUR INITIAL MEETING, RECEIVING MY PROPOSAL]. Their situation: [WHAT THEY NEEDED]. Email 1 (1 week later): friendly check-in with one new helpful thought about their situation. Email 2 (2 weeks later): a short relevant resource or example of how I've helped someone similar, no pressure. Email 3 (4 weeks later): a graceful "door stays open" close that makes it easy to say no or come back later. Each under 100 words.
prompts.proTip: The permission-to-say-no email gets the most replies; never skip email 3.

prompts.title: Response to a Price-Shopping Prospect
prompts.useWhen: someone's first question is "what do you charge?" (fee shopping) and you want to answer honestly while shifting the conversation to value and fit.
prompts.prompt: Write a reply to a prospect who asked only about my fees. My pricing: [YOUR PRICING OR RANGE]. My typical client: [CLIENT TYPE]. Answer the price question directly in the first two sentences (hiding it feels evasive), then briefly explain what that fee includes: [WHAT'S INCLUDED], and one sentence on the cost of getting this wrong: [COMMON COSTLY MISTAKE]. End by offering a [FREE CALL/MEETING] to see if we're a fit. Confident, never defensive about my prices. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Track how many price-shoppers convert after this email; it will make you braver about stating fees plainly.

prompts.title: Re-Engagement Email for Past Clients
prompts.useWhen: former or one-time clients (a single tax return, a one-off project) have drifted and you want to win them back or reactivate them.
prompts.prompt: Write a re-engagement email to past clients I haven't worked with since [TIMEFRAME]. What we did together: [PAST SERVICE]. What's changed that makes now a good time to reconnect: [TRIGGER, E.G., NEW TAX RULES, MY EXPANDED SERVICES, YEAR-END PLANNING SEASON]. Acknowledge the gap without apologizing for it, lead with something useful to them, and offer a specific next step: [OFFER, E.G., 15-MINUTE CATCH- UP CALL]. Under 130 words, plus a subject line that doesn't look like a mass email.
prompts.proTip: Personalize the first line for your top 10 past clients and send the generic version to the rest.

prompts.title: Pitch to Speak, Guest on a Podcast, or Teach a Class
prompts.useWhen: you want visibility through speaking gigs, podcast interviews, or community classes and need a pitch that gets a yes.
prompts.prompt: Write a pitch email to [TARGET, E.G., A LOCAL PODCAST HOST, THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, A LIBRARY PROGRAM COORDINATOR] offering myself as a [SPEAKER/GUEST/INSTRUCTOR]. My expertise: [YOUR SPECIALTY]. Proposed topic: [TOPIC] with 3 takeaways their audience would care about because [AUDIENCE RELEVANCE]. Include one line of credibility: [CREDENTIAL OR EXPERIENCE], and make me easy to say yes to (flexible dates, I'll promote it too). Under 150 words. Give 2 alternative topic angles at the end.
prompts.proTip: Pitch topics about the audience's problems ("5 money leaks in a restaurant"), never about your services.

prompts.title: Proposal Follow-Up Email That Is Not Pushy
prompts.useWhen: you sent a proposal or engagement letter days ago, heard nothing, and want to nudge the decision without pestering.
prompts.prompt: Write a follow-up email about the proposal I sent to [PROSPECT NAME] on [DATE] for [SERVICE]. Assume they're busy, not uninterested. Briefly restate the one outcome they cared about most: [THEIR PRIORITY], ask if anything in the proposal needs clarifying, and offer to adjust [SCOPE/TIMING/PHASING] if the fit isn't right. One clear question they can answer in a single reply. Under 100 words, warm and unhurried, with a subject line referencing our conversation, not "following up."
prompts.proTip: "Following up" subject lines get skipped; reference their goal instead ("your question about quarterly taxes").

prompts.title: Objection Response: "I Can Just Do This Myself With Software"
prompts.useWhen: a prospect says TurboTax, robo-advisors, or QuickBooks can do what you do, and you want an honest, non-defensive answer.
prompts.prompt: Help me respond to a prospect who said they can handle [WHAT THEY'D DIY, E.G., THEIR TAXES WITH SOFTWARE, INVESTING WITH A ROBO-ADVISOR] themselves. Write a response that genuinely agrees software is fine for simple situations, then describes the 3 specific situations where professional help changes the outcome, using their circumstances: [THEIR SITUATION]. No trash-talking the software, no fear tactics, no guaranteed savings claims. End with an easy offer: [OFFER, E.G., A SECOND-LOOK REVIEW OF LAST YEAR'S RETURN]. Under 150 words, spoken-conversation tone.
prompts.proTip: The "second look" offer converts DIYers better than any argument; lead with it when you can.
fields: OFFER, E.G., A SECOND-LOOK REVIEW OF LAST YEAR'S RETURN

prompts.title: Client-Friendly Summary of a Financial Plan
prompts.useWhen: you finished a financial plan and need a one-page executive summary the client will actually read (instead of the 40-page PDF).
prompts.prompt: Turn my financial plan notes into a one-page client summary. Client situation: [BRIEF SITUATION]. Their top goals: [GOALS]. Key recommendations we discussed: [YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS]. Structure: "Where you stand today" (3 bullets), "Where you're headed" (2-3 sentences), "What we agreed to do" (numbered action steps with owners and timing), and "What we'll watch" (2 bullets). Plain English, encouraging but honest, under 300 words. No new advice: only restate what I've listed.
prompts.proTip: Add "write at a level my client's teenager could follow"; clients share these summaries with family.

prompts.title: Retirement Readiness Talking Points From Client Numbers
prompts.useWhen: you are prepping a retirement conversation and want clear talking points that turn projections into a story (retirement planning meeting prep).
prompts.prompt: Help me prepare talking points for a retirement readiness meeting. Client ages: [AGES]. Target retirement: [AGE/YEAR]. Current savings picture: [SUMMARY]. Key finding from my analysis: [ON TRACK / GAP OF X / AHEAD]. Draft: an opening that frames the conversation around their life (not numbers), 3 talking points explaining the situation with simple comparisons, 2 trade-off options I want to present: [OPTIONS], and one question to end on that invites their reaction. Conversational phrasing I can say naturally. This is a communication draft; the analysis and advice are mine.
prompts.proTip: Ask for "the gentle version and the direct version" of the gap conversation and choose based on the client.
fields: ON TRACK / GAP OF X / AHEAD

prompts.title: Explanation of Investment Concepts for a Nervous Beginner
prompts.useWhen: a first-time investor client is anxious or confused and you want simple explanations of diversification, risk, or compounding that calm rather than lecture.
prompts.prompt: Write a short explanation of [CONCEPT, E.G., DIVERSIFICATION, DOLLAR- COST AVERAGING, WHY MARKETS FLUCTUATE] for a nervous first-time investor who is [CLIENT CONTEXT, E.G., 55 AND JUST INHERITED MONEY, 25 AND STARTING A 401(K)]. Use one everyday analogy (not the usual "eggs in baskets" if you can find better), a small numeric example, and one sentence acknowledging that feeling nervous is normal. Under 150 words, kind and steady in tone, no predictions or return promises.
prompts.proTip: Collect these into a "first-year investor" welcome packet; nervous clients reread them after every scary headline.

prompts.title: Risk Tolerance Conversation Guide
prompts.useWhen: the risk questionnaire says one thing but the client's behavior says another, and you need a real conversation about risk comfort.
prompts.prompt: Create a conversation guide for discussing risk tolerance with [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., A COUPLE WHO DISAGREE ABOUT RISK, A CLIENT WHO PANICS IN DOWNTURNS]. Give me: 5 scenario-based questions that reveal how they'd actually behave (framed in dollars, like "if your [ACCOUNT VALUE] dropped to [LOWER VALUE] in three months..."), 2 questions separating their need for risk from their comfort with it, and phrases for naming a mismatch kindly. End with a summary sentence I can use to reflect back what I heard.
prompts.proTip: Use real dollar amounts from their accounts, not percentages; "down 20%" and "down $180,000" get very different reactions.

prompts.title: Scenario Comparison Table for a Client Decision
prompts.useWhen: a client faces a fork in the road (pay off the mortgage vs. invest, lump sum vs. pension, Roth vs. traditional) and you want a clean side-by-side comparison to discuss.
prompts.prompt: Build a side-by-side comparison table for a client deciding between [OPTION A] and [OPTION B]. Their relevant details: [KEY FACTS, E.G., AGE, TAX BRACKET, TIMELINE, BALANCES]. Rows: how each option works in one sentence, potential upsides, potential downsides, what has to be true for it to win, tax considerations to explore further, and emotional/lifestyle factors. Fill in general educational points only and mark anything requiring my professional analysis with [ADVISOR TO CONFIRM]. Close with 3 questions I should discuss with the client.
prompts.proTip: The [ADVISOR TO CONFIRM] flags are the point: the table structures the meeting, and your expertise fills the gaps.
fields: KEY FACTS, E.G., AGE, TAX BRACKET, TIMELINE, BALANCES

prompts.title: Savings Roadmap Outline for a Big Goal
prompts.useWhen: a client wants to save for college, a home, a sabbatical, or a business launch and you want a motivating goal roadmap to walk through.
prompts.prompt: Outline a savings roadmap for a client goal: [GOAL] costing about [AMOUNT] in [TIMEFRAME]. Their capacity: roughly [MONTHLY SAVINGS ABILITY]. Structure: the goal restated in motivating language, 3 milestone checkpoints with target amounts and dates, general account-type considerations to discuss (mark specifics as [DISCUSS OPTIONS]), what could knock the plan off course and the pre-agreed response, and a celebration marker at each milestone. Encouraging coach's tone, one page, plain English.
prompts.proTip: Clients hit milestones they can visualize; ask for the roadmap as a simple timeline graphic description they can pin up.

prompts.title: Talking Points for a Market Volatility Phone Call
prompts.useWhen: a specific client calls scared during a downturn and you have five minutes to prepare for the conversation (panic call prep).
prompts.prompt: Prepare talking points for a call with a worried client during market volatility. Client context: [AGE, GOAL, TIME HORIZON, ROUGH ALLOCATION APPROACH]. Their specific fear, as expressed: "[WHAT THEY SAID]". Give me: an opening that validates the feeling before any facts, 3 points connecting their plan design to this exact situation, one question that shifts them from headlines to their own timeline, and what NOT to say (dismissive phrases to avoid). No market predictions. Format as brief cue-card bullets I can glance at mid-call.
prompts.proTip: Lead with "that makes sense, tell me more" and let them empty the worry first; the talking points land better second.
fields: AGE, GOAL, TIME HORIZON, ROUGH ALLOCATION APPROACH

prompts.title: Estate and Beneficiary Checkup Conversation Checklist
prompts.useWhen: you want to prompt clients to review wills, beneficiaries, and estate documents (legacy planning checkup) without practicing law.
prompts.prompt: Create an estate readiness conversation checklist for my meeting with [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., A RECENTLY REMARRIED CLIENT, NEW PARENTS, A WIDOWED CLIENT]. Cover: beneficiary designations to verify ([ACCOUNT TYPES THEY HOLD]), documents to ask about (will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives), life changes since last review: [KNOWN CHANGES], and conversation starters for sensitive topics like [SENSITIVE AREA, E.G., UNEQUAL INHERITANCES, BLENDED FAMILY]. Note clearly where "refer to estate attorney" is the right answer. Warm, non-morbid phrasing throughout.
prompts.proTip: Beneficiary mismatches are the most common (and cheapest to fix) estate mistake; always start the meeting there.
fields: SENSITIVE AREA, E.G., UNEQUAL INHERITANCES, BLENDED FAMILY

prompts.title: Insurance and Protection Gap Discussion Outline
prompts.useWhen: you need to raise life, disability, or umbrella coverage (risk protection review) with a client who finds insurance boring or salesy.
prompts.prompt: Outline a protection review conversation for a client: [SITUATION, E.G., SOLE EARNER WITH TWO KIDS, BUSINESS OWNER WITH A PARTNER]. Frame it around what they're protecting (income, family, business), not products. Include: 4 discovery questions about what would happen if [RISK SCENARIO], a plain-English explainer of the coverage types relevant to them: [TYPES TO COVER], common gaps for people like them, and how to discuss amounts as a range to analyze rather than a quote. One page. Note where I should involve [A LICENSED SPECIALIST / THEIR AGENT] per my licensing.
prompts.proTip: "If your income stopped for a year, what breaks first?" opens this conversation better than any product mention.

prompts.title: Client Education Handout on a Planning Topic
prompts.useWhen: you want a leave-behind or portal upload explaining a planning topic (Social Security timing, HSAs, 529 basics) in your voice.
prompts.prompt: Write a one-page client education handout titled "[TOPIC], Explained Simply" for my [CLIENT TYPE] clients. Cover: what it is in 2 sentences, why it matters to people like them, 3-5 key things to know (with a small example using [EXAMPLE NUMBERS]), common misconceptions, and 3 questions to bring to our next meeting. Footer disclaimer: educational only, not personal advice, situations vary. Reading level: 7th grade. Friendly, confident, zero sales language.
prompts.proTip: Build one handout per month; in a year you own a client education library competitors can't match.

prompts.title: Tax Season Kickoff Email With Document Checklist
prompts.useWhen: it is January and you need the annual "tax season is here" email that gets organizers back fast (tax prep announcement).
prompts.prompt: Write my tax season kickoff email to clients. Firm: [FIRM NAME]. Key dates: send us documents by [INTERNAL DEADLINE], filing deadline [DATE]. Include: a warm 2sentence opening, what's new this year: [CHANGES, E.G., NEW PORTAL, RATE CHANGES, NEW STAFF], a short document checklist for [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., INDIVIDUALS, S- CORPS], how to send documents: [METHOD], and what happens if documents arrive after our deadline: [YOUR POLICY]. Encouraging, organized, under 300 words, plus a subject line that isn't "Tax Season 2026."
prompts.proTip: State your internal cutoff 3+ weeks before the real deadline and repeat it in every touchpoint; it's the single best workload-smoothing tool you have.
fields: CHANGES, E.G., NEW PORTAL, RATE CHANGES, NEW STAFF
CLIENT TYPE, E.G., INDIVIDUALS, S- CORPS

prompts.title: Escalating Reminder Emails for Late Tax Documents
prompts.useWhen: clients still have not sent their tax documents and you need three chasing emails that escalate from friendly to firm.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 escalating reminder emails for clients who haven't sent tax documents. Our cutoff: [DATE]. Filing deadline: [DATE]. Email 1 (friendly): quick nudge with the checklist link [LINK/METHOD]. Email 2 (direct): specific consequence: after [CUTOFF] we file an extension per our policy, here's what an extension does and doesn't mean. Email 3 (final): clear statement that we're now filing an extension, what they owe by when to avoid penalties: [GENERAL GUIDANCE TO VERIFY], and next steps. Each under 120 words. Firm but never shaming.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a text-message version of each; late-document clients often ignore email but answer texts.

prompts.title: Plain-English Explanation of a Client's Tax Result
prompts.useWhen: a return is done and you want a cover note explaining the refund or balance due so clients understand it instead of just signing.
prompts.prompt: Write a short cover note explaining a client's tax result. Outcome: [REFUND/ BALANCE DUE OF AMOUNT]. The main drivers this year: [2-3 REASONS, E.G., WITHHOLDING CHANGE, CAPITAL GAINS, NEW CREDIT]. Explain each driver in one plain-English sentence, state what happens next ([E-FILE TIMING, PAYMENT OPTIONS/ DUE DATE]), and add one forward-looking sentence about what we might adjust for next year: [ADJUSTMENT TO DISCUSS]. Under 180 words, no jargon, calm and clear. I will verify all numbers before sending.
prompts.proTip: Clients who understand their result argue less about fees; send this with every single return.
fields: E-FILE TIMING, PAYMENT OPTIONS/ DUE DATE

prompts.title: Estimated Quarterly Tax Reminder Emails
prompts.useWhen: self-employed and business clients keep missing estimated payments and you want reminders for all four quarterly due dates.
prompts.prompt: Write 4 estimated tax reminder emails, one per quarterly due date: [LIST THE FOUR DATES FOR THE CURRENT YEAR]. Audience: my self-employed and small business clients. Each email: the deadline in the subject line, a 2-sentence reminder of who this applies to, how to pay ([IRS DIRECT PAY/VOUCHER/STATE PORTAL]), a note to contact us if income changed a lot this quarter, and one seasonal money tip for business owners: [OPTIONAL TIP TOPIC]. Under 100 words each, so clients actually read them. Vary the openings so they don't feel copy-pasted.
prompts.proTip: Schedule all four in your email tool today; this is an hour of work that prevents a year of penalty conversations.
fields: LIST THE FOUR DATES FOR THE CURRENT YEAR

prompts.title: Tax Deadline Countdown Communication Plan
prompts.useWhen: you want a full timeline of client touchpoints from January through the filing deadline (busy season communication calendar).
prompts.prompt: Build a tax season communication calendar for my firm from [START DATE] to [FILING DEADLINE]. Clients: [MIX, E.G., 60% INDIVIDUALS, 40% SMALL BUSINESS]. Map week by week: what message goes out (kickoff, checklist, early-bird push, cutoff warnings, extension explainer, deadline week, post-season thank you), the channel (email/text/social), and the goal of each touch. Mark the 3 highest-impact messages I should prioritize if I only have time for three. Format as a table: Week, Message, Channel, Goal.
prompts.proTip: Feed each row of this calendar into Prompts #55, #56, and #33 to generate the actual messages.

prompts.title: Explanation of a Bookkeeping Cleanup Project and Its Cost
prompts.useWhen: a prospect's books are a mess (catch-up bookkeeping, un-reconciled accounts) and you need to explain the cleanup, the price, and why it's worth it.
prompts.prompt: Write an email explaining a bookkeeping cleanup project to a prospect. What I found in their books: [ISSUES, E.G., 14 MONTHS UNRECONCILED, PERSONAL EXPENSES MIXED IN, DUPLICATE ENTRIES]. The risk of leaving it: [CONSEQUENCES, E.G., WRONG TAX FILINGS, NO USABLE REPORTS, LOAN APPLICATION PROBLEMS]. My proposed fix: [SCOPE] for [PRICE OR RANGE], taking [TIMELINE]. Explain it like a contractor explaining a repair: what's broken, what fixing it involves, what "done" looks like. No shaming their past bookkeeping. Under 250 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a one-line "monthly service after cleanup" transition sentence; cleanup clients are your best recurring revenue.

prompts.title: Monthly Bookkeeping Close Checklist
prompts.useWhen: you want a standardized month-end close process (reconciliation checklist) for yourself or to train staff.
prompts.prompt: Create a monthly close checklist for a bookkeeping practice using [SOFTWARE, E.G., QUICKBOOKS ONLINE, XERO]. Client type: [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., SERVICE BUSINESSES, RESTAURANTS, ECOMMERCE]. Organize into phases: gather (statements, receipts, payroll reports), reconcile (list each account type), review (uncategorized transactions, negative balances, owner draws, loan balances), report (which reports to send: [REPORTS]), and communicate (client summary email). Add typical time estimates per phase and mark steps a trained assistant can own versus steps I should review. Checklist format with checkboxes.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a "client-caused delays" section: the 5 things clients don't send that stall your close, with chase-up one-liners.

prompts.title: Email Explaining Why a Client Owes More Tax Than Last Year
prompts.useWhen: a client is upset about a higher balance due (or smaller refund) and you need to explain the difference without getting defensive.
prompts.prompt: Write an email to a client upset that they owe [AMOUNT] this year versus [LAST YEAR'S RESULT]. The actual reasons: [DRIVERS, E.G., SIDE INCOME WITH NO WITHHOLDING, LOST A CREDIT, BONUS PUSHED THEM UP A BRACKET]. Acknowledge the frustration first, explain each driver in one plain sentence with its rough dollar impact, make clear the return reflects the law (not our choices), and pivot to prevention: [FIX, E.G., WITHHOLDING ADJUSTMENT, QUARTERLY ESTIMATES] with an offer to set it up. Steady, non-defensive, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: The prevention pivot turns an angry email into a planning engagement; always include a concrete next step.
fields: FIX, E.G., WITHHOLDING ADJUSTMENT, QUARTERLY ESTIMATES

prompts.title: Client Alert About a New Tax Law or Rule Change
prompts.useWhen: a tax law changes and you want to alert affected clients before they read a confusing headline about it (tax update announcement).
prompts.prompt: Write a client alert about a tax rule change. The change, as I understand it: [PASTE YOUR SUMMARY OF THE CHANGE]. Who in my client base it affects: [AFFECTED GROUP]. Structure: what changed in 2 sentences, who needs to care (and who can ignore it), what we recommend doing about it: [YOUR RECOMMENDED ACTION], and by when: [TIMING]. Headline-style subject line without hype. Under 200 words. Include a line that details are still settling and we'll confirm specifics as guidance is issued, if applicable.
prompts.proTip: You supply the facts of the change from your professional sources; never let the AI fill in the rule's details from memory.
fields: PASTE YOUR SUMMARY OF THE CHANGE

prompts.title: Email Explaining Why Filing an Extension Is Okay
prompts.useWhen: a client is panicking about going on extension and you need to calm the stigma ("extensions aren't audits") while being clear about payment.
prompts.prompt: Write an email to a client we're placing on extension. Reason: [REASON, E.G., DOCUMENTS ARRIVED LATE, AWAITING A K-1]. Explain in plain English: an extension gives more time to FILE, not more time to PAY; it is routine and does not by itself raise audit risk; what they should pay by [DEADLINE] based on our estimate: [ESTIMATE OR "WE WILL PROVIDE"], and what happens between now and final filing: [TIMELINE]. Reassuring but honest about any interest/penalty exposure on unpaid amounts. Under 180 words.
prompts.proTip: Send this proactively in early April to every likely extension client; the pre-emptive version prevents the panicked calls.
fields: REASON, E.G., DOCUMENTS ARRIVED LATE, AWAITING A K-1

prompts.title: Client Guide to Business Expense Categories and Receipts
prompts.useWhen: business clients keep handing you shoeboxes and miscategorized expenses and you want a simple recordkeeping guide in your voice.
prompts.prompt: Write a one-page expense and receipt guide for my [CLIENT TYPE, E.G., CONTRACTOR, THERAPIST, FOOD TRUCK] clients. Include: the expense categories I want them to use: [YOUR CATEGORY LIST OR "SUGGEST STANDARD ONES"], the 5 expenses this client type most often gets wrong (like [KNOWN TROUBLE AREA, E.G., MEALS, MILEAGE, HOME OFFICE]) with a one-line rule of thumb for each, what receipts to keep and for how long, and the easiest capture habit: [YOUR PREFERRED METHOD/APP]. Friendly, practical, zero lecture tone. Note that specific deductibility depends on their situation and current rules.
prompts.proTip: Make one version per client industry you serve; "for food trucks" feels custom and gets followed.
fields: CLIENT TYPE, E.G., CONTRACTOR, THERAPIST, FOOD TRUCK
YOUR CATEGORY LIST OR "SUGGEST STANDARD ONES"
KNOWN TROUBLE AREA, E.G., MEALS, MILEAGE, HOME OFFICE

prompts.title: Talking Points for an Entity Structure Conversation
prompts.useWhen: a client asks "should I become an S-corp?" (LLC, sole prop, entity election questions) and you want a structured conversation, not a lecture.
prompts.prompt: Prepare talking points for an entity structure conversation with a client. Their situation: [BUSINESS TYPE, PROFIT LEVEL, STATE, CURRENT STRUCTURE]. Frame it as education for our discussion: how their current structure works in 2 sentences, the general trade-offs of the alternative they asked about ([ALTERNATIVE]) across taxes, paperwork, payroll requirements, and costs, the 4 questions whose answers drive this decision, and what analysis I'll run before we decide: [YOUR ANALYSIS]. Mark every number as illustrative. Conversational bullets, one page. Final decision requires my professional analysis of their specifics.
prompts.proTip: Clients remember the "4 questions" framework long after the meeting; keep it identical across all these conversations.
fields: BUSINESS TYPE, PROFIT LEVEL, STATE, CURRENT STRUCTURE

prompts.title: Service Proposal for a New Client Engagement
prompts.useWhen: a prospect said "send me a proposal" and you need a professional engagement proposal (quote) that sells the outcome, not a task list.
prompts.prompt: Write a service proposal for a prospective client. Their situation and goals: [WHAT THEY NEED AND WHY]. My proposed services: [SERVICES]. Fee: [FEE AND BILLING STRUCTURE]. Timeline: [TIMELINE]. Structure: their situation restated in their words (so they feel heard), the outcome we're aiming for, what's included (grouped by benefit, not just task names), what's not included: [EXCLUSIONS], investment and payment terms, and next step to start: [NEXT STEP]. Confident, client-focused, 1-2 pages. No hedging language like "we hope" or "we'll try."
prompts.proTip: Restating their words in the opening paragraph is the highest-converting sentence in any proposal; fill that placeholder carefully.

prompts.title: Three-Tier Pricing Packages for Your Services
prompts.useWhen: you are moving from hourly billing to packages (or productizing services) and need well-structured good/better/best tiers.
prompts.prompt: Help me design 3 pricing tiers for my [SERVICE, E.G., MONTHLY BOOKKEEPING, ONGOING PLANNING]. What I can include: [LIST EVERYTHING YOU COULD OFFER]. My cost floor / minimum viable price: [MINIMUM]. Target clients per tier: [WHO EACH TIER IS FOR]. Build: a named tier structure (names that signal value, not "basic/premium"), what's in each tier and why, a price anchor strategy making the middle tier the obvious choice, and a one-line pitch for each. Then list 3 things I should NOT include in the cheapest tier and why.
prompts.proTip: Ask "what would make the top tier worth 3x the bottom tier?" and let the answer stretch your pricing courage.
fields: SERVICE, E.G., MONTHLY BOOKKEEPING, ONGOING PLANNING

prompts.title: Plain-English Summary of an Engagement Letter
prompts.useWhen: you want a friendly cover summary for your engagement letter or contract so clients sign faster and understand what they agreed to.
prompts.prompt: Write a plain-English summary to accompany my engagement letter. The engagement covers: [SERVICES]. Key terms to highlight: fee [FEE], term [PERIOD], what we're responsible for, what the client is responsible for: [CLIENT DUTIES], and how either side can end the engagement: [TERMINATION BASICS]. Format: "Here's what this letter says, in normal words" with 5-6 short bullets, plus one sentence encouraging them to read the full letter and ask questions. Under 200 words. Note: this summarizes but doesn't replace the letter's legal language.
prompts.proTip: Send the summary in the email body with the letter attached; signed engagement letters come back twice as fast when the email itself explains the deal.

prompts.title: Response to a Scope Creep Request From a Client
prompts.useWhen: a client asks for extra work outside the agreement ("can you also just quickly...") and you need to say yes-for-a-fee or no gracefully.
prompts.prompt: Write a response to a client requesting work outside our engagement scope. What they asked for: [THE REQUEST]. What our engagement covers: [CURRENT SCOPE]. My preferred outcome: [ADD IT FOR A FEE OF X / DECLINE / FOLD INTO A BIGGER PACKAGE]. Affirm the relationship, note kindly that this falls outside our current agreement, present the path forward with clear pricing or alternatives, and make saying yes easy. No apologizing for charging. Under 150 words. Give me a firmer second version if they push back.
prompts.proTip: "That's a great question, and it deserves real work rather than a quick guess" reframes the boundary as quality, not gatekeeping.
fields: ADD IT FOR A FEE OF X / DECLINE / FOLD INTO A BIGGER PACKAGE

prompts.title: Client-Friendly Monthly or Quarterly Report Summary
prompts.useWhen: you send financial statements or portfolio reports and want a short narrative summary on top, because clients read the note and skip the numbers.
prompts.prompt: Write a client-facing summary paragraph for a [MONTHLY FINANCIAL/ QUARTERLY PORTFOLIO] report. The key numbers this period: [3-5 KEY FIGURES OR CHANGES]. What drove them: [DRIVERS]. Anything needing the client's attention or decision: [ACTION ITEM OR "NONE"]. Write: a 3-sentence "what happened and why" in plain English, one "what this means for you" sentence, and one "what to watch next period" sentence. No jargon, no alarm, no rosy spin: just clear and honest. Under 120 words total.
prompts.proTip: Keep the three-part structure every period; clients start reading reports when the summary is predictable and short.

prompts.title: Year-End Client Summary Letter
prompts.useWhen: the year is closing and you want a wrap-up letter covering the year's work, results, and what's ahead (annual client letter).
prompts.prompt: Write my year-end letter to clients. This year at the firm: [FIRM MILESTONES, E.G., NEW SERVICE, TEAM GROWTH]. What the year looked like for clients generally: [THEMES, E.G., RATE CHANGES, NEW TAX RULES, MARKET SWINGS] (described factually, no predictions). What's coming next year: [KNOWN CHANGES OR DEADLINES]. Include a sincere thank-you that doesn't sound like a form letter, and one action item for January: [ACTION]. Warm, human, under 350 words. Give me a P.S. line offering [REFERRAL/REVIEW/MEETING] softly.
prompts.proTip: Mail this one physically if you can; a printed year-end letter gets kept on refrigerators, and emails don't.
fields: FIRM MILESTONES, E.G., NEW SERVICE, TEAM GROWTH
THEMES, E.G., RATE CHANGES, NEW TAX RULES, MARKET SWINGS

prompts.title: Value Recap: What We Did for You This Year
prompts.useWhen: renewal or fee conversations are coming and you want a personalized "here's everything we handled" recap that makes your fee feel obvious.
prompts.prompt: Turn my notes into a "year in review" value recap for client [CLIENT NAME]. What we did: [LIST: RETURNS FILED, MEETINGS HELD, ISSUES RESOLVED, SAVINGS FOUND, DEADLINES MANAGED, QUESTIONS ANSWERED]. Organize into: "By the numbers" (counts of deliverables and touchpoints), "Moments that mattered" (2-3 short narratives from my list), and "Set up for next year" (what's in place now that wasn't before). Factual and specific, no self-congratulation, no invented outcomes: only items from my list. One page.
prompts.proTip: Track these items in a simple log all year; the recap writes itself in minutes and renewals stop being negotiations.

prompts.title: Explaining the ROI of Your Fees to a Hesitant Client
prompts.useWhen: a client or prospect says you're expensive and you need to justify your fee with honest value framing, not desperation discounts.
prompts.prompt: Help me respond to a client questioning my fee of [FEE] for [SERVICE]. The concrete value elements: [WHAT YOU DELIVER: TIME SAVED, ERRORS PREVENTED, PLANNING OPPORTUNITIES, PEACE OF MIND, SPECIFIC PAST WINS]. Write a response that: acknowledges fee questions are fair, walks through what the fee covers in outcome terms, gives an honest cost-of-mistakes comparison relevant to their situation: [RELEVANT RISK], and holds the price without discounting. Offer one flexibility option that isn't a discount: [E.G., PHASED SCOPE, DIFFERENT TIER]. Under 200 words, steady and unapologetic.
prompts.proTip: Never send this while annoyed; ask the AI to "make it 20% warmer" and it will read better tomorrow.

prompts.title: Honest Comparison of Your Service vs. DIY Software
prompts.useWhen: you want a comparison sheet for prospects weighing you against TurboTax, QuickBooks-alone, or a robo-advisor (works as a website page or leave-behind).
prompts.prompt: Create an honest comparison guide: working with [YOUR PRACTICE TYPE] versus using [DIY ALTERNATIVE]. Format as a table with rows: cost, time required from them, what's covered, what happens when things get complicated ([COMPLICATION EXAMPLES FOR YOUR NICHE]), who catches mistakes, and support when [STRESSFUL SCENARIO, E.G., AN IRS LETTER, A MARKET DROP] happens. Be fair: state plainly when DIY is the sensible choice. Close with "you might be a fit for us if..." (3 bullets). No fear tactics, no trash talk.
prompts.proTip: The honesty is the persuasion; prospects trust the comparison because you conceded the DIY cases.
fields: STRESSFUL SCENARIO, E.G., AN IRS LETTER, A MARKET DROP

prompts.title: SOP for a Recurring Task in Your Practice
prompts.useWhen: a process lives only in your head (client onboarding, return assembly, monthly close) and you need a written procedure someone else could follow.
prompts.prompt: Turn my rough description into a formal SOP. Task: [TASK NAME]. How I do it, roughly: [BRAIN-DUMP THE STEPS, MESSY IS FINE]. Tools involved: [SOFTWARE/ TOOLS]. Format: purpose (1 sentence), when this SOP triggers, step-by-step numbered instructions with the software clicks spelled out, quality checks before it counts as done, common mistakes to avoid, and who to ask when stuck: [ESCALATION PERSON]. Write it so a smart new hire could follow it on day one without asking questions.
prompts.proTip: Read the SOP and do the task exactly as written once; every spot you deviate is an edit the AI can make in seconds.
fields: BRAIN-DUMP THE STEPS, MESSY IS FINE

prompts.title: Job Posting for an Admin or Junior Hire
prompts.useWhen: you are hiring your first admin, bookkeeper, or junior associate and need a job ad that attracts the right applicants (help wanted listing).
prompts.prompt: Write a job posting for a [ROLE, E.G., PART-TIME ADMIN, JUNIOR BOOKKEEPER] at my [TYPE OF PRACTICE] in [LOCATION/REMOTE]. Key duties: [MAIN TASKS]. Must-haves: [REQUIREMENTS]. Nice-to-haves: [PREFERENCES]. Pay range: [RANGE]. Hours: [SCHEDULE]. Open with what makes this job good (variety, stability, learning, [YOUR SELLING POINTS]), describe a realistic typical day, and be honest about busy season: [BUSY SEASON REALITY]. Warm and specific, no corporate clichés like "fastpaced environment." Include 2 screening questions for applicants.
prompts.proTip: The busy-season honesty filters out the people who would have quit in March anyway.
fields: ROLE, E.G., PART-TIME ADMIN, JUNIOR BOOKKEEPER

prompts.title: Training Checklist for a New Assistant
prompts.useWhen: someone new is starting and you need a first-30-days onboarding and training plan so they ramp up without shadowing you all day.
prompts.prompt: Create a 30-day training plan for my new [ROLE]. They'll eventually own: [THEIR RESPONSIBILITIES]. Our tools: [SOFTWARE LIST]. Week 1: setup, security and confidentiality basics for a financial practice, observing [CORE PROCESS]. Week 2: doing [FIRST OWNED TASK] with review. Weeks 3-4: adding [NEXT TASKS], first solo client interactions ([WHICH KIND]). Format as a weekly checklist with clear "you're ready to own this when..." criteria per task, plus 3 check-in questions for our Friday reviews.
prompts.proTip: Pair each checklist item with its SOP from Prompt #76; training plans without written procedures just create better questions.

prompts.title: Starter Library of Email Subject Lines and Snippets
prompts.useWhen: you want a grab-and-go library of subject lines and reusable sentences (canned responses) for the messages you send constantly.
prompts.prompt: Build me a reusable email snippet library for a [TYPE OF PRACTICE]. Create: 10 subject lines for common messages (document requests, meeting scheduling, deadline reminders, [YOUR FREQUENT MESSAGE TYPES]), 5 polished opening lines that aren't "I hope this finds you well," 5 closing lines that prompt action without pressure, and 5 onesentence transitions for delivering mixed news. Match my tone: [DESCRIBE YOUR TONE, E.G., WARM BUT BRIEF]. Present in labeled groups I can paste into my email template tool.
prompts.proTip: Load these into your email signatures or text-expander tool; two hours of setup saves a sentence-staring minute fifty times a week.
fields: DESCRIBE YOUR TONE, E.G., WARM BUT BRIEF

prompts.title: Weekly Priorities Plan From Your To-Do List
prompts.useWhen: your task list is a swamp of client work, admin, and marketing, and you want a realistic weekly plan (time blocking help).
prompts.prompt: Organize my week. My open tasks: [PASTE YOUR FULL LIST, MESSY IS FINE]. Hard deadlines: [DEADLINES]. My available work hours this week: [HOURS], and my protected time: [MEETINGS/COMMITMENTS]. Sort everything into: Must happen this week (with suggested day), Should happen if the musts go well, Can wait (with a suggested future week), and Delegate or drop (with one-line reasoning). Flag anything I've likely underestimated, like [TASK TYPE YOU ALWAYS UNDERESTIMATE]. Keep the "must" list honest: max [NUMBER] items.
prompts.proTip: Run this every Monday morning with fresh input; the 10-minute ritual replaces the 3 pm Wednesday overwhelm spiral.
fields: PASTE YOUR FULL LIST, MESSY IS FINE

prompts.title: Out-of-Office and Busy-Season Auto-Reply Messages
prompts.useWhen: you are heading into vacation, a conference, or deep busy-season focus mode and need auto-replies that manage expectations kindly.
prompts.prompt: Write [NUMBER] auto-reply messages for me: (1) vacation from [DATES] with [BACKUP CONTACT/PLAN] for urgent items and a clear definition of urgent, (2) busy-season mode: I'm heads-down on client filings, expect replies within [RESPONSE WINDOW], here's how to send documents in the meantime: [METHOD], and (3) [OTHER SCENARIO, E.G., CONFERENCE, PARENTAL LEAVE]. Each under 80 words, warm, and firm about the boundary without apologizing for it. Include a subject-line-style first sentence since many people only read the preview.
prompts.proTip: Define "urgent" explicitly in the message ("an IRS deadline within 5 days"); otherwise everything becomes urgent.
fields: OTHER SCENARIO, E.G., CONFERENCE, PARENTAL LEAVE

prompts.title: Agenda for Your Weekly Team Meeting
prompts.useWhen: your staff meetings ramble or don't happen at all, and you want a tight recurring agenda (team huddle) that ends on time.
prompts.prompt: Design a [LENGTH]-minute weekly team meeting agenda for my practice of [TEAM SIZE] people. Standing sections: wins from last week (5 min), workload and capacity check (who's underwater on [CURRENT SEASON WORK]), client issues needing decisions (with a rule: issues come with a proposed solution), deadlines in the next 2 weeks, and one process improvement: [FOCUS AREA]. Include time boxes, a rotating facilitator note, and 3 ground rules that keep it short. Add a 5-line async update template for weeks we skip the meeting.
prompts.proTip: The "come with a proposed solution" rule cuts meeting length by a third; enforce it warmly but always.

prompts.title: Client FAQ Page for Your Website or Welcome Packet
prompts.useWhen: you answer the same logistics questions daily (pricing basics, timing, what to bring) and want an FAQ page that deflects them politely.
prompts.prompt: Write an FAQ page for my [TYPE OF PRACTICE]. Answer these questions I get constantly: [LIST YOUR REAL QUESTIONS, E.G., WHAT DO YOU CHARGE, HOW LONG DOES A RETURN TAKE, DO YOU WORK WITH PEOPLE IN OTHER STATES, WHAT DO I NEED TO BRING]. My answers, roughly: [YOUR ROUGH ANSWERS]. Polish each into 2-4 friendly sentences, ordered from most-asked to least, with honest answers (including price ranges: [RANGES]) rather than "it depends" dodges. Add 2 questions I should include that similar practices get asked.
prompts.proTip: Every honest answer on this page saves a discovery call with a mismatched prospect; the price range question earns its spot.

prompts.title: Response to a Negative Online Review
prompts.useWhen: a bad Google or Yelp review just landed (unfair or fair) and you need a public reply that protects your reputation and confidentiality.
prompts.prompt: Write a public response to this negative review of my practice: [PASTE REVIEW]. What actually happened, for my context only: [YOUR SIDE]. Requirements: never confirm they are or were a client (confidentiality), never share any details of their situation, acknowledge their frustration genuinely, state my practice's standards in one sentence, and invite them to continue offline: [CONTACT METHOD]. No defensiveness, no rebuttal of specifics, under 100 words. Then give me a private message version for if they contact us.
prompts.proTip: Remember the real audience is future prospects reading the exchange, not the reviewer; write for them.

prompts.title: Email to a Client Who Is Angry About a Bill or Fee
prompts.useWhen: a client is disputing an invoice or shocked by a bill and you want to deescalate while standing behind fair charges.
prompts.prompt: Write a response to a client upset about their bill of [AMOUNT] for [SERVICE]. Why the bill is what it is: [BREAKDOWN, E.G., EXTRA HOURS FROM LATE DOCUMENTS, EXPANDED SCOPE, COMPLEXITY]. My position: [HOLD FIRM / OFFER PARTIAL ADJUSTMENT OF X / PAYMENT PLAN]. Open by taking the concern seriously, explain the charges factually with the breakdown, connect the work to what it accomplished for them, then state my position clearly and kindly. If offering flexibility, frame it as goodwill, not admission of overcharging. Under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Include the itemized breakdown even if they didn't ask; surprise is usually the real complaint, not the amount.
fields: HOLD FIRM / OFFER PARTIAL ADJUSTMENT OF X / PAYMENT PLAN

prompts.title: Script for Ending a Relationship With a Difficult Client
prompts.useWhen: it is time to fire a client (disengagement) who is abusive, chronically late, refuses advice, or just isn't worth it, and you want a clean, professional exit.
prompts.prompt: Write a client disengagement letter. The situation, for context: [WHY YOU'RE ENDING IT]. Effective date: [DATE]. Requirements: state the decision clearly in the first paragraph without detailed justification or blame, cover the practical transition (final deliverables: [WHAT YOU'LL COMPLETE], records transfer process, any refund or final balance: [AMOUNT]), recommend they engage a new [ADVISOR/ACCOUNTANT] promptly given [UPCOMING DEADLINE, IF ANY], and close with professional well-wishes. Neutral, firm, kind, under 250 words. Also give me a 3-sentence phone version.
prompts.proTip: Never list the grievances in the letter; the decision needs no defense, and documentation of issues belongs in your files, not theirs.

prompts.title: Escalating Late Payment Reminder Emails
prompts.useWhen: an invoice is overdue (past-due accounts receivable) and you need a politeto-firm collection sequence that preserves the relationship where possible.
prompts.prompt: Write a 3-stage late payment reminder sequence for an invoice of [AMOUNT] due on [DUE DATE]. Stage 1 (a few days late): friendly assumption it slipped their mind, payment link/method: [METHOD]. Stage 2 (2-3 weeks late): direct but respectful, restate terms [YOUR TERMS], ask if something's wrong and offer a payment plan option. Stage 3 (30+ days): firm statement of next steps: [YOUR POLICY, E.G., PAUSING WORK, LATE FEES PER AGREEMENT], with a final date. Each under 100 words, professional throughout, never sarcastic.
prompts.proTip: Stage 2's "is something wrong?" question resolves most cases; financial hardship answers honestly when asked kindly.
fields: YOUR POLICY, E.G., PAUSING WORK, LATE FEES PER AGREEMENT

prompts.title: Talking a Client Out of a Panic Decision
prompts.useWhen: a client wants to do something rash (sell everything, drain retirement accounts, ignore an IRS notice, fire their bookkeeper mid-close) and you need to slow them down without commanding them.
prompts.prompt: Help me prepare for a conversation with a client about to make a rushed decision: [THE DECISION]. What's driving it: [THEIR STATED REASON/FEAR]. What I want them to consider first: [KEY CONSIDERATIONS]. Draft: an opening that respects their autonomy (it's their money/business), 3 questions that surface consequences without lecturing, a way to propose a pause: [E.G., 72-HOUR WAIT, RUNNING THE NUMBERS FIRST], and language for documenting my advice if they proceed anyway. Calm, respectful, zero condescension. Cue-card bullet format.
prompts.proTip: Questions beat warnings; "what would need to be true for this to work out?" does more than any caution you can state.
fields: E.G., 72-HOUR WAIT, RUNNING THE NUMBERS FIRST

prompts.title: Apology Email for a Mistake or Missed Deadline on Your Side
prompts.useWhen: your firm made an error (wrong figure, missed filing, lost document) and you need to own it, fix it, and keep the client's trust.
prompts.prompt: Write an email owning a mistake we made. What happened: [THE ERROR]. The impact on the client: [IMPACT, E.G., AMENDED RETURN NEEDED, PENALTY OF X, DELAY]. Our fix, already underway: [CORRECTIVE STEPS AND TIMELINE]. What we're covering: [E.G., PENALTY REIMBURSEMENT, FEE WAIVED, IF APPLICABLE]. What we've changed so it doesn't recur: [PROCESS CHANGE]. Requirements: apologize once, clearly, without groveling; no excuses or blame-shifting; lead with the fix. Under 200 words, plus a subject line that's honest but not alarming.
prompts.proTip: One clean apology plus a visible fix builds MORE trust than an error-free year; clients remember how you handled it.
