fields: IMPACT, E.G., AMENDED RETURN NEEDED, PENALTY OF X, DELAY
E.G., PENALTY REIMBURSEMENT, FEE WAIVED, IF APPLICABLE

prompts.title: Response to a Client Threatening to Leave
prompts.useWhen: a client says they're switching firms (or a competitor is courting them) and you want a response that addresses the real issue without begging.
prompts.prompt: Write a response to a client considering leaving my practice. Their stated reason: [THEIR REASON, E.G., FEES, RESPONSIVENESS, A COMPETITOR'S PITCH]. What I know about the underlying situation: [CONTEXT]. My honest position: [FIGHT TO KEEP THEM / LET THEM GO GRACEFULLY / FIX A LEGITIMATE ISSUE]. Draft a response that: thanks them for telling me directly, addresses their actual concern specifically (not generically), states what I can and can't change, and gives them a genuine choice without pressure or guilt. Under 180 words. If keeping them requires a change on my side, ask me first whether I'm truly willing to sustain it.
prompts.proTip: A retained client on unsustainable terms leaves anyway within a year; only promise changes you'll still be glad about in March.

prompts.title: Turn One Client Question Into a Month of Content
prompts.useWhen: you want a full content batch (newsletter, social posts, video script, FAQ) built from a single real question a client asked you.
prompts.prompt: You are my content repurposing engine. A client recently asked me: "[THE REAL QUESTION A CLIENT ASKED]". My answer, in short: [YOUR ANSWER IN 3-5 SENTENCES]. My audience: [CLIENT TYPE]. My tone: [TONE]. Now produce, in order: (1) a 300-word newsletter article answering the question, (2) three LinkedIn posts, each taking a different angle (the misconception, the story, the checklist), (3) a 60-second video script with a hook, (4) a polished FAQ entry for my website, and (5) a 2-sentence portal message version I can send to clients this applies to. Keep facts limited to my stated answer; add no advice I didn't give. Label each piece clearly.
prompts.proTip: Run this every time a client asks something good and your content calendar fills itself with material you know your audience wants.
fields: THE REAL QUESTION A CLIENT ASKED

prompts.title: Build Your Full Tax Season Communication System
prompts.useWhen: you want the entire busy-season client communication package (kickoff to wrap-up) generated in one sitting.
prompts.prompt: Act as the communications manager for my [TAX/ACCOUNTING] firm. Details: firm name [NAME], document cutoff [DATE], filing deadline [DATE], document submission method [PORTAL/METHOD], extension policy: [POLICY]. Build my complete season system: (1) kickoff email with document checklist for [CLIENT TYPES], (2) two reminder emails escalating politely, (3) a "we're filing an extension" email, (4) deadline-week social post and email, (5) a post-season thank-you email with one planning-season offer: [OFFER], and (6) a one-page internal cheat sheet listing what goes out when. Keep every client email under 250 words, warm and organized. Number and label everything.
prompts.proTip: Do this in November, load it all into your email scheduler, and January-you will want to hug December-you.

prompts.title: Complete New Client Onboarding Kit in One Go
prompts.useWhen: you want your entire onboarding package (welcome sequence, checklist, questionnaire, expectations doc) created as one consistent set.
prompts.prompt: Build a complete onboarding kit for my [TYPE OF PRACTICE]. My services: [SERVICES]. My process after signing: [YOUR STEPS]. My communication policy: [RESPONSE TIME, CHANNELS]. My tools: [PORTAL/SOFTWARE]. Produce: (1) a 3-email welcome sequence (days 1, 3, 7), (2) a document checklist grouped by category with Required/If Applicable labels, (3) a client intake questionnaire under [NUMBER] questions, (4) a one-page "How We Work Together" expectations sheet, and (5) a 30-day internal checklist of what MY team does for each new client. Use one consistent voice across all five pieces: [TONE]. Label each piece and keep the whole kit skimmable.
prompts.proTip: Ask it to "review the five pieces for contradictions" as a follow-up; consistency between documents is what makes a kit feel professional.

prompts.title: Annual Client Review Package: Prep, Agenda, and Follow-Up
prompts.useWhen: annual review season is starting and you want the full meeting system: prep email, agenda, recap template, and next-year plan format.
prompts.prompt: Create my annual review meeting system for [ADVISORY/TAX/ACCOUNTING] clients. Meeting length: [LENGTH]. What I review: [WHAT YOU COVER]. Produce: (1) a prep email sent 1 week ahead with 5 quick questions and a document ask: [DOCUMENTS], (2) a time-blocked meeting agenda, (3) a fill-in-the-blank recap email template with action items split between us and the client, (4) a one-page "next year priorities" worksheet the client and I fill in together at the end, and (5) a 6-month mini check-in email to schedule as follow-up. Keep everything reusable across clients with [BRACKETS] where I personalize.
prompts.proTip: The 6-month mini check-in is the piece most practices skip and the one clients mention most when they refer you.

prompts.title: New Service Launch Bundle: Pricing, Proposal, and Promotion
prompts.useWhen: you are adding a service (advisory add-on, CFO package, planning subscription) and need pricing, positioning, and launch materials together.
prompts.prompt: Help me launch a new service: [SERVICE DESCRIPTION] for [TARGET CLIENT]. The problem it solves: [PROBLEM]. My cost/time to deliver: [ESTIMATE]. Competing alternatives clients have: [ALTERNATIVES]. Build the launch bundle: (1) positioning statement and 3 name options for the service, (2) suggested pricing with reasoning (single price or tiers, your call, but explain it), (3) a 150-word description for my website, (4) an announcement email to existing clients, (5) three social posts, and (6) a oneparagraph pitch script for mentioning it in meetings. Flag any claims I should soften for compliance in financial services.
prompts.proTip: Launch to existing clients two weeks before the public; their questions will sharpen the public materials.

prompts.title: Difficult Conversation Rehearsal: Role-Play the Client, Then Debrief
prompts.useWhen: a hard conversation is coming (fee increase, firing a client, a big mistake, talking someone off a ledge) and you want to practice against a realistic opponent first.
prompts.prompt: Let's rehearse a difficult client conversation. The situation: [DESCRIBE IT]. The client's personality: [E.G., CONFLICT-AVOIDANT, AGGRESSIVE, ANXIOUS, VERY ANALYTICAL]. What I need to communicate: [YOUR MESSAGE]. My worst fear about this conversation: [FEAR]. You play the client, realistically but not cartoonishly difficult; I'll play myself. Stay in character until I say "DEBRIEF." Then step out of character and give me: what I did well, where I got defensive or vague, the one sentence I should say earlier next time, and a stronger phrasing for my 2 weakest moments.
prompts.proTip: Rehearse twice: once against the difficult version, once against the sad version; real conversations usually contain both.

prompts.title: Ideal Client Profile and 90-Day Content Calendar
prompts.useWhen: your marketing is scattered and you want a defined ideal client persona plus a full quarter of planned content that speaks to them.
prompts.prompt: Act as my marketing strategist. My practice: [WHAT YOU DO]. My best current clients look like: [DESCRIBE 2-3 FAVORITE CLIENTS]. My revenue goal for this segment: [GOAL]. Step 1: build an ideal client profile (their situation, top 3 money worries, where they spend attention online, what they'd search when looking for someone like me). Step 2: from that profile, create a 90-day content calendar: one weekly theme, with a newsletter topic, two social post ideas, and one client-outreach action per week. Step 3: mark the 4 highest-impact weeks if I only manage one week per month. Format the calendar as a table.
prompts.proTip: Generate month one's actual content immediately (Prompts #24, #25) while the strategy is fresh; calendars without drafts die by week three.

prompts.title: Fee Increase Rollout Plan: Analysis, Letters, and Objection Handling
prompts.useWhen: you know you're undercharging and want the complete fee-raise package: segmentation, announcement letters, FAQ, and pushback responses.
prompts.prompt: Help me plan a fee increase across my practice. Current pricing: [CURRENT FEES BY SERVICE]. Target: [NEW FEES OR PERCENTAGE]. Client mix: [ROUGH SEGMENTS, E.G., LONG-TERM LOYAL, NEWER, UNDERPRICED LEGACY]. Build: (1) a rollout strategy (who to notify first, timing across [TIMEFRAME], whether to grandfather anyone and the trade-offs), (2) announcement letters for each segment in a confident, valuefirst tone, (3) an internal FAQ: the 6 likely objections with short spoken responses, (4) a script for the "I'll leave over this" conversation, and (5) a break-even note: how many clients I could lose at the new pricing and still come out ahead, using [CLIENT COUNT AND AVERAGE FEE].
prompts.proTip: Run the break-even math first; realizing you can lose 15% of clients and still earn more is what gives the letters their calm confidence.

prompts.title: Practice SOP Manual Starter: Interview Me, Then Draft Five SOPs
prompts.useWhen: nothing in your practice is documented and you want the AI to interview you, extract your processes, and write the first five SOPs.
prompts.prompt: You are an operations consultant documenting my practice. My practice: [TYPE AND SIZE]. The 5 processes that most need documenting: [LIST THEM, E.G., NEW CLIENT SETUP, MONTHLY CLOSE, RETURN REVIEW AND DELIVERY, BILLING, DOCUMENT REQUESTS]. Interview me about each process ONE AT A TIME: ask me 4-6 specific questions (triggers, steps, tools, checks, failure points), wait for my answers, then draft that SOP in a standard format (purpose, trigger, numbered steps, quality checks, escalation) before moving to the next process. At the end, produce a table of contents for my new operations manual and a list of the next 5 SOPs I should write.
prompts.proTip: Answer the interview questions by voice dictation while walking; you'll give richer answers talking than typing.

prompts.title: Year-End Client Value Report Generator
prompts.useWhen: you want to turn your scattered notes about a client's year into a polished value report plus a next-year meeting agenda (client annual report).
prompts.prompt: Build a year-end value report for my client [CLIENT NAME/TYPE]. Everything we did this year, from my notes: [PASTE YOUR LIST: DELIVERABLES, MEETINGS, PROBLEMS SOLVED, DEADLINES MET, SAVINGS OR OPPORTUNITIES FOUND]. Their goals when we started the year: [GOALS]. Produce: (1) a one-page client-facing report: "Your Year in Review" with sections By the Numbers, What We Accomplished Together, and Ready for [NEXT YEAR], written warmly and factually with nothing invented beyond my notes, (2) a cover email inviting them to their annual review, and (3) my internal agenda for that review meeting, including one expansion opportunity to raise: [SERVICE THEY DON'T USE YET]. Label the three pieces.
prompts.proTip: Send the report BEFORE the renewal invoice, not with it; value should arrive first and alone.

prompts.title: Email: Personal Thank-You Note for a New Gift
prompts.useWhen: A gift just came in and you need a thank-you (also called a gift acknowledgment) that doesn't sound like a form letter.
prompts.prompt: Act as a development officer at [ORGANIZATION NAME], a nonprofit focused on [MISSION AREA]. Write a warm, personal thank-you note for a donor named [DONOR NAME] who just gave [GIFT AMOUNT] to support [PROGRAM OR FUND NAME]. Mention one specific, concrete way this gift will be used — not vague language like "makes a difference." Keep the tone [TONE, e.g., heartfelt but not overly formal]. Length: under 150 words. End with a specific next step, like an invitation to visit or a link to see impact updates.
prompts.proTip: Paste in one real detail from your program (a number, a name, a recent story) so the AI has something specific to anchor the thank-you to — generic gratitude is the #1 reason thank-you notes get ignored.
fields: TONE, e.g., heartfelt but not overly formal

prompts.title: Email: Lapsed Donor Win-Back Message
prompts.useWhen: You're pulling a lapsed-donor or LYBUNT list (donors who haven't given in 12-18 months) and need to re-engage them without guilt-tripping.
prompts.prompt: Write a "we miss you" re-engagement email to a donor who last gave to [ORGANIZATION NAME] [TIME SINCE LAST GIFT] ago, supporting [PROGRAM OR FUND NAME]. The tone should feel like a genuine check-in, not a guilt trip. Briefly share one update on what's changed at the organization since their last gift, then invite them back with a low-pressure ask (a specific small gift amount or just "reconnect with us"). Subject line + body, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI for 2 subject line options — one curiosity-based, one direct — and A/B test them if your email platform allows it.

prompts.title: Email: Convert a One-Time Donor to a Monthly Sustainer
prompts.useWhen: You want to upgrade a one-time gift into recurring giving (also called a sustainer or monthly donor program).
prompts.prompt: Write a short, friendly email inviting a donor who has given [NUMBER] one-time gifts to [ORGANIZATION NAME] to convert to a monthly giving program called [MONTHLY GIVING PROGRAM NAME]. Explain in plain terms why monthly gifts matter more to the organization's stability than the raw dollar amount. Suggest a specific monthly amount based on their past giving of [AVERAGE GIFT AMOUNT]. Keep it under 150 words and end with one clear call to action.
prompts.proTip: Suggest a monthly amount roughly 1/12th of their average annual gift — it feels small to the donor but adds up to real recurring revenue for you.

prompts.title: Plan: Major Donor Cultivation Touchpoint Ideas
prompts.useWhen: You need a reason to reach out to a major or mid-level donor (a cultivation touch) without asking for money.
prompts.prompt: I'm a fundraiser at [ORGANIZATION NAME] and want to strengthen my relationship with a major donor named [DONOR NAME] who cares about [DONOR'S STATED INTEREST/CAUSE AREA]. Suggest 5 non-ask touchpoint ideas I could use this quarter to cultivate the relationship (e.g., sharing relevant articles, program invites, handwritten notes). For each idea, give me a one-sentence script or message I could send. Format as a numbered list.
prompts.proTip: Tell the AI what season or upcoming event is coming up (year-end, program launch, anniversary) so the touchpoints feel timely instead of random.

prompts.title: Letter: Year-End Appeal / Annual Fund Ask
prompts.useWhen: You're writing your biggest fundraising ask (annual appeal or year-end appeal) of the year.
prompts.prompt: Write a year-end appeal letter for [ORGANIZATION NAME], a nonprofit working on [MISSION AREA]. Open with a short story about [ONE SPECIFIC PERSON OR OUTCOME THE ORG HELPED], connect it to the bigger need, and close with a specific dollar ask of [SUGGESTED GIFT AMOUNT] tied to a tangible outcome that amount funds. Use a warm, urgent-but-not-desperate tone. 300-400 words, formatted for direct mail or email.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a P.S. line separately — appeal letters get read bottom-up as often as top-down, so a strong P.S. with the ask restated performs disproportionately well.
fields: ONE SPECIFIC PERSON OR OUTCOME THE ORG HELPED

prompts.title: Email: Donor Impact Update With No Ask
prompts.useWhen: It's been a few months since a gift and you want to show stewardship — what the gift funded — with zero fundraising ask attached.
prompts.prompt: Write a pure "impact update" email (no fundraising ask) to donors who gave to [PROGRAM OR CAMPAIGN NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Share [1-2 SPECIFIC RESULTS OR NUMBERS] from the program since their gift, and thank them again for making it possible. Close by saying more updates are coming — do not ask for another gift in this email. Under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Send at least one pure-impact, zero-ask update between every two appeals — donors who only ever hear "give again" churn faster than donors who see their money working.

prompts.title: Note: Donor Giving-Anniversary or Birthday Message
prompts.useWhen: You want to acknowledge a donor's giving anniversary or a personal milestone like a birthday.
prompts.prompt: Write a short, genuine note to a donor named [DONOR NAME] celebrating [MILESTONE, e.g., their 5th year giving to ORGANIZATION NAME / their birthday]. Reference their history of support in one sentence without listing exact dollar amounts. Keep it warm and personal, under 100 words, no ask included.
prompts.proTip: Pull the "years given" field from your donor CRM (Bloomerang, DonorPerfect, Little Green Light) so this feels personal rather than templated — even one accurate detail changes the whole tone.

prompts.title: Email: Employer Matching Gift Reminder
prompts.useWhen: You want to boost gift value by reminding donors their employer might offer a corporate match.
prompts.prompt: Write a short, friendly reminder email or social caption for [ORGANIZATION NAME] donors, letting them know many employers match charitable donations dollar-for-dollar (or more). Explain in 2-3 plain-English sentences how matching gifts typically work and where they'd check with their employer. Include a light call to action to look into it before [DEADLINE, e.g., year-end]. Under 120 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version formatted as a social media caption too — matching gift reminders work well as short posts, not just emails.

prompts.title: Plan: Donor Segmentation by Giving Level
prompts.useWhen: You have one donor list and need to message different giving tiers (segments) differently instead of a single blast.
prompts.prompt: I run fundraising for [ORGANIZATION NAME] and have donors across these giving levels: [LIST GIVING TIERS, e.g., under $100, $100-$999, $1,000+]. Suggest how I should segment my messaging for each tier for an upcoming [CAMPAIGN NAME] appeal — including tone, ask amount, and one thing that should differ in each version. Present as a table with columns: Tier, Tone, Suggested Ask, Key Message Difference.
prompts.proTip: Feed this table back into the AI afterward and ask it to draft the actual email for just one tier at a time — trying to write all tiers in one shot usually blurs the differences. 2. Grant Writing & Fundraising Proposals

prompts.title: Letter: Letter of Inquiry (LOI) to a Funder
prompts.useWhen: A foundation requires a short letter of inquiry, or LOI, before you can submit a full grant proposal.
prompts.prompt: Write a 1-page letter of inquiry to [FOUNDATION/FUNDER NAME] on behalf of [ORGANIZATION NAME], requesting [GRANT AMOUNT] to support [PROGRAM NAME]. Include: the problem we address, our approach, why our organization is positioned to do this work, and the specific outcomes this grant would fund. Match the funder's stated priorities of [FUNDER'S STATED PRIORITIES, from their website or guidelines]. Keep it under 500 words, professional but not stiff.
prompts.proTip: Paste in 2-3 sentences directly from the funder's mission statement or guidelines — proposals that mirror a funder's own language in the right places score noticeably better with reviewers.
fields: FUNDER'S STATED PRIORITIES, from their website or guidelines

prompts.title: Section: Statement of Need for a Grant Proposal
prompts.useWhen: You need the "statement of need" (also called a needs statement or problem statement) section of a grant proposal and are staring at a blank page.
prompts.prompt: Write a needs statement for a grant proposal from [ORGANIZATION NAME] addressing [PROBLEM/ ISSUE] in [GEOGRAPHIC AREA/COMMUNITY]. Use these facts and statistics: [PASTE 2-4 STATS OR DATA POINTS]. Structure it as: the scope of the problem, who it affects most, why current solutions fall short, and how it connects to our program. 250-350 words, cite data inline in plain language (not academic citation format).
prompts.proTip: If you don't have current stats, ask the AI to list 3-4 credible national or state data sources (like Census, CDC, or a relevant national nonprofit) where you could look up numbers — don't let it invent statistics for you.

prompts.title: Section: Program Description for a Grant Application
prompts.useWhen: A grant application asks you to describe your program in detail.
prompts.prompt: Write a program description for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME] for a grant proposal. Cover: who we serve (target population and rough numbers served per year), what activities the program includes, how long participants are typically involved, and what staff/partners deliver it. Base this on: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES ABOUT THE PROGRAM]. Write in clear, funder-friendly language, 300-400 words, no jargon.
prompts.proTip: Give the AI your messiest bullet-point notes rather than trying to write clean sentences first — it's much better at organizing rough information than you might expect.
fields: PASTE ROUGH NOTES ABOUT THE PROGRAM

prompts.title: Table: Logic Model / Theory of Change Draft
prompts.useWhen: A funder wants a logic model and you've never built one from scratch.
prompts.prompt: Help me build a simple logic model for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Our inputs/ resources are: [LIST RESOURCES]. Our main activities are: [LIST ACTIVITIES]. Structure a logic model as a table with columns: Inputs, Activities, Outputs, Short-Term Outcomes, Long-Term Outcomes/Impact. Fill in reasonable outputs and outcomes based on what I've given you, and flag anywhere you had to guess so I can confirm it.
prompts.proTip: Always review the "flagged guesses" line by line before submitting — logic models are one place where funders can tell instantly if the connections between activities and outcomes are handwavy.

prompts.title: Narrative: Grant Budget Line-Item Justification
prompts.useWhen: You need to explain grant budget line items (a budget narrative) in plain language.
prompts.prompt: Write a budget narrative explaining these grant budget line items for [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s [PROGRAM NAME]: [PASTE LINE ITEMS AND AMOUNTS]. For each line item, write 1-2 sentences justifying the cost and connecting it to program delivery. Keep the tone factual and specific, avoiding vague phrases like "as needed." Format as a short paragraph per line item.
prompts.proTip: Round numbers make budget narratives look padded — if a line item is oddly specific (like $4,283), ask the AI to reflect that precision in the justification instead of smoothing it over.

prompts.title: Summary: Grant Proposal Executive Summary
prompts.useWhen: You've finished a full grant proposal and need a tight 1-paragraph summary (also called an abstract) at the top.
prompts.prompt: Here is my full grant proposal for [PROGRAM NAME]: [PASTE FULL PROPOSAL OR KEY SECTIONS]. Write a 150-word executive summary that a busy program officer could read in 30 seconds and understand: the need, our solution, the amount requested, and the expected outcome. No filler sentences.
prompts.proTip: Write the executive summary last, always — it's the section funders read first but should be the section you write after everything else is finalized.
fields: PASTE FULL PROPOSAL OR KEY SECTIONS

prompts.title: Report: Grant Outcomes Report to a Funder
prompts.useWhen: A funder requires a grant report (also called an outcomes report or final report) on how their money was used.
prompts.prompt: Write a grant outcomes report to [FUNDER NAME] covering their [GRANT AMOUNT] gift to [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], for the period [REPORTING PERIOD]. Use these results: [PASTE OUTCOMES/NUMBERS/STORIES]. Structure it as: brief recap of the grant's purpose, key outcomes achieved (with numbers), one short story or quote illustrating impact, and any challenges or lessons learned. Professional, honest tone — including one honest challenge builds more trust than a report that sounds perfect. 400-500 words.
prompts.proTip: Always include one genuine challenge or adjustment you made — funders trust reports more when they're not 100% rosy, and it sets up your next ask more credibly.

prompts.title: Analysis: Funder Prospect Research Summary
prompts.useWhen: You've found a new foundation and need to quickly vet the fit (funder prospecting) before spending hours on a proposal.
prompts.prompt: I'm evaluating whether [FOUNDATION/FUNDER NAME] is a good fit for [ORGANIZATION NAME], which works on [MISSION AREA]. Based on this information about the funder: [PASTE WHAT YOU KNOW — website text, past grantee list, focus areas], summarize in a short brief: their apparent priorities, whether our program aligns, red flags or unclear fit, and 2-3 questions I should try to answer before applying (like typical grant size or geographic restrictions).
prompts.proTip: Don't ask the AI to guess a funder's typical grant size or deadlines from memory — those change yearly and it may be wrong; have it flag that you need to verify those on the funder's current site.

prompts.title: Case: Multi-Year Funding Request
prompts.useWhen: You're asking a funder to commit to multiple years (multi-year or general operating support) instead of a one-time gift.
prompts.prompt: Write the case for multi-year funding as part of a proposal to [FUNDER NAME] for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Explain why a [NUMBER]-year commitment of [ANNUAL AMOUNT] per year produces better outcomes than a single one-time grant of the same total — focus on program stability, ability to hire/retain staff, and long-term outcome measurement. 200-250 words, direct and confident tone.
prompts.proTip: Lead with what instability costs the program (staff turnover, interrupted services) rather than what stability would be nice to have — funders respond more to concrete risk than to aspiration. 3. Social Media & Content Marketing

prompts.title: Post: Impact Story Social Media Caption
prompts.useWhen: You have a program success story and need it turned into a scroll-stopping social post.
prompts.prompt: Write an Instagram/Facebook caption for [ORGANIZATION NAME] sharing this story: [PASTE ROUGH STORY DETAILS OR NOTES]. Open with a hook in the first line (not "We're excited to share..."). Keep it under 150 words, end with a soft call to action to [DESIRED ACTION, e.g., visit our website, donate, share]. Include a suggestion for 5 relevant hashtags.
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 different opening-line options and pick the one that would make YOU stop scrolling — the first sentence does 80% of the work on social media.
fields: PASTE ROUGH STORY DETAILS OR NOTES
DESIRED ACTION, e.g., visit our website, donate, share

prompts.title: Post: Behind-the-Scenes "Day in the Life" Caption
prompts.useWhen: You want to humanize your organization with behind-the-scenes content instead of another "big ask" post.
prompts.prompt: Write a behind-the-scenes social media caption showing what a typical day looks like for [ROLE, e.g., a case manager / a volunteer / a program staff member] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Base it on: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES ABOUT THEIR DAY]. Keep the tone light, human, and specific — avoid generic phrases like "making a difference every day." Under 120 words.
prompts.proTip: Behind-the-scenes content consistently outperforms polished announcement posts — schedule one of these for every 3-4 promotional posts.
fields: PASTE ROUGH NOTES ABOUT THEIR DAY

prompts.title: Post: Volunteer Spotlight Social Media Post
prompts.useWhen: You want to publicly recognize a volunteer and drive more volunteer signups at the same time.
prompts.prompt: Write a volunteer spotlight social media post for [ORGANIZATION NAME] featuring a volunteer named [VOLUNTEER NAME] who [WHAT THEY DO/HOW LONG]. Include one quote-style line that sounds like something they might say about why they volunteer. End with a call to action for others to sign up to volunteer, linking to [VOLUNTEER SIGNUP LINK/PAGE]. Under 130 words.
prompts.proTip: Send the draft to the volunteer for approval before posting — even an AI-written "quote" attributed to a real person should get their sign-off.

prompts.title: Post: Awareness Statistic / Shareable Stat Caption
prompts.useWhen: You want to raise awareness about the issue you work on using a shareable statistic or fact.
prompts.prompt: Write a short, shareable social media caption built around this statistic: [PASTE STATISTIC AND SOURCE]. Make the stat the hook in the first sentence, briefly explain why it matters, and connect it to what [ORGANIZATION NAME] is doing about it. End with a specific call to action. Under 100 words, written for a graphic/carousel post, not a long-form caption.
prompts.proTip: Always double-check any statistic before posting — ask the AI to flag if it's unsure of the source, and verify the number yourself against the original source before it goes live.

prompts.title: Plan: Repurpose One Piece of Content Into 5 Social Posts
prompts.useWhen: You have one piece of long content (a blog post, newsletter, or report) and need to stretch it into multiple social posts.
prompts.prompt: Here is a piece of content from [ORGANIZATION NAME]: [PASTE BLOG POST, NEWSLETTER SECTION, OR REPORT EXCERPT]. Turn it into 5 separate social media posts for different platforms: 2 for Instagram/Facebook (short, visual-friendly), 2 for LinkedIn (slightly more professional tone), and 1 for a short-form video script (30 seconds, spoken). Format each clearly labeled by platform.
prompts.proTip: Repurposing one piece of content into 5 posts is the single highest-leverage prompt in this pack for a time-strapped comms team — use it on every newsletter and blog post you publish.
fields: PASTE BLOG POST, NEWSLETTER SECTION, OR REPORT EXCERPT

prompts.title: Plan: Giving Tuesday / Campaign Countdown Post Series
prompts.useWhen: You're running a time-bound campaign like Giving Tuesday and need a week of countdown posts at once.
prompts.prompt: Write a 5-post social media countdown series leading up to [CAMPAIGN NAME, e.g., Giving Tuesday] for [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Our goal is [CAMPAIGN GOAL, e.g., raise $10,000 for PROGRAM]. Each post should build urgency without being repetitive — vary the angle (a story, a stat, a matching gift mention, a countdown reminder, a final push). Label each post by day (5 days out, 3 days out, day-of, etc.) with caption text for each.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the final "day-of" post to be written twice — once for morning, once for evening — so you have a natural reason to post about the campaign twice on the actual day.
fields: CAMPAIGN GOAL, e.g., raise $10,000 for PROGRAM

prompts.title: Post: LinkedIn Thought Leadership Post for Your ED
prompts.useWhen: Your executive director or program lead wants to build credibility and visibility on LinkedIn.
prompts.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post in the voice of [NAME/TITLE, e.g., Executive Director] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], sharing a perspective on [TOPIC/TREND RELATED TO YOUR MISSION]. Base it on this rough take: [PASTE ROUGH THOUGHTS OR NOTES]. Open with a strong first line, include one specific example or data point, and end with a question to invite comments. Under 200 words, confident but not preachy tone.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the post to end with an open-ended question rather than a call to action — LinkedIn's algorithm favors posts that generate comments, and questions outperform "click here" asks.

prompts.title: Calendar: Monthly Social Media Content Calendar
prompts.useWhen: You need a full month of social content planned out but only have a few program updates to work with.
prompts.prompt: Build a 4-week social media content calendar for [ORGANIZATION NAME], posting [NUMBER] times per week. We have these upcoming events/updates: [LIST 3-5 THINGS HAPPENING THIS MONTH]. Fill in the remaining slots with a mix of: impact stories, behind-the-scenes, educational/ awareness content, and volunteer or donor recognition. Format as a table: Week, Day, Content Type, Caption Idea (1 sentence).
prompts.proTip: Once you have the calendar, come back and run each row through Prompt #19 or #20 one at a time to get the full caption — the calendar is your outline, not your finished copy.

prompts.title: Response: Reply to a Negative Social Media Comment
prompts.useWhen: Someone leaves a critical or hostile comment on a social post and you need a calm, public-facing reply.
prompts.prompt: Someone left this comment on our social media post: [PASTE COMMENT]. Write a calm, professional public reply from [ORGANIZATION NAME] that doesn't sound defensive, acknowledges any valid point without over-apologizing, and redirects to a private channel if the issue needs more discussion. Keep it under 60 words. Do not argue or get pulled into a back-and-forth tone.
prompts.proTip: Have a teammate read the reply before posting if the comment touches anything sensitive or political — a second set of eyes catches tone problems the writer is too close to see. 4. Email Campaigns & Newsletters

prompts.title: Newsletter: Monthly Email Newsletter Draft
prompts.useWhen: It's e-newsletter time and you have scattered updates but no draft yet.
prompts.prompt: Write a monthly email newsletter for [ORGANIZATION NAME] covering these updates: [LIST 3-5 UPDATES/STORIES/UPCOMING EVENTS]. Structure it as: a short opening note (2-3 sentences), then each update as its own short section with a header, then a closing call to action to [DESIRED ACTION]. Keep the overall tone [TONE, e.g., warm and conversational]. Include a suggested subject line.
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 subject line options ranked by likely open rate, and note that questions and specific numbers in subject lines typically outperform generic phrases like "Newsletter - March."

prompts.title: Email: Event Invitation
prompts.useWhen: You need to promote an upcoming event to your email list.
prompts.prompt: Write an email inviting [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s email list to [EVENT NAME] happening on [DATE] at [LOCATION]. The event is for [PURPOSE, e.g., fundraising gala / volunteer appreciation / community open house]. Include why they should attend, what to expect, and a clear registration call to action linking to [REGISTRATION LINK]. Under 200 words, include a subject line.
prompts.proTip: Plan for 3 emails per event (save-the-date, invitation, last-chance reminder) rather than one — ask the AI to draft all three in one go so you can schedule them in advance.

prompts.title: Email: Welcome Message for New Subscribers or Donors
prompts.useWhen: Someone just joined your email list or made their first gift and needs an automated welcome message.
prompts.prompt: Write a welcome email for someone who just [SUBSCRIBED TO OUR NEWSLETTER / MADE THEIR FIRST GIFT] to [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Introduce our mission in 2 sentences, tell them what to expect from us (how often we email, what kind of content), and include one easy next step they could take (follow on social, share with a friend, etc.). Warm, welcoming tone, under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: This is a "set it and forget it" email — write it once, load it into your email platform's automation, and it'll work in the background for every new subscriber going forward.
fields: SUBSCRIBED TO OUR NEWSLETTER / MADE THEIR FIRST GIFT

prompts.title: Email: Program Update With No Ask
prompts.useWhen: You want to keep supporters informed about a specific program without a fundraising ask attached.
prompts.prompt: Write an email update on [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME] for our supporter email list. Share these updates: [PASTE PROGRAM NOTES/NUMBERS/MILESTONES]. Keep the tone informative and proud without being salesy. No donation ask in this email — the goal is just to keep people engaged and informed. Under 250 words.
prompts.proTip: Rotate pure-update emails with ask emails roughly 2-to-1 — supporters who only ever receive fundraising asks unsubscribe at a noticeably higher rate.

prompts.title: Email: Re-Engagement for Inactive Subscribers
prompts.useWhen: You want to clean your list by re-engaging people (a win-back or list-cleaning email) who haven't opened emails in a while.
prompts.prompt: Write a re-engagement email for subscribers to [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s email list who haven't opened an email in [TIME PERIOD]. Ask directly if they'd like to keep hearing from us, share one compelling update to remind them why they signed up, and include a clear option to stay subscribed or update their preferences. Friendly, no-guilt tone, under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Anyone who doesn't engage with this email is a candidate to remove from your list — a smaller, engaged list improves your deliverability and open rates for everyone else.

prompts.title: Email: Survey or Feedback Request
prompts.useWhen: You want input (a survey or feedback form) from donors, volunteers, or program participants.
prompts.prompt: Write a short email asking [AUDIENCE, e.g., donors / volunteers / program participants] of [ORGANIZATION NAME] to fill out a [LENGTH]-minute survey about [SURVEY TOPIC]. Explain briefly why their input matters and how it will be used. Include a placeholder link to the survey. Keep it under 100 words — people are more likely to respond to a short ask.
prompts.proTip: Mention a specific, believable time estimate ("takes about 3 minutes") — vague asks like "a quick survey" get skipped more often than ones with a concrete number attached.
fields: AUDIENCE, e.g., donors / volunteers / program participants

prompts.title: Sequence: 4-Email Fundraising Campaign Series
prompts.useWhen: You're launching a campaign and need a full email sequence or drip series, not just one message.
prompts.prompt: Write a 4-email sequence for a fundraising campaign called [CAMPAIGN NAME] with a goal of [GOAL AMOUNT] to support [PROGRAM/PURPOSE]. Email 1: launch announcement. Email 2: a story-driven email midway through. Email 3: a progress update showing how close we are to goal. Email 4: final urgency/deadline email. Give each a subject line and full body, under 200 words each.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to reference the previous email's theme in each new one ("as I mentioned last week...") so the sequence feels like a connected story instead of four separate asks.

prompts.title: Email: "Ask a Question" Engagement Email
prompts.useWhen: You want to boost email replies and engagement without asking for money.
prompts.prompt: Write a short email from [ORGANIZATION NAME] asking our supporters a genuine question related to [TOPIC, e.g., what they'd like to see more of / their connection to our cause]. Make it feel like a real question, not a survey. Invite them to just hit reply. Under 100 words, casual and conversational tone.
prompts.proTip: Actually read and respond to a few replies personally — this prompt works because it feels human, and a canned auto-response undoes that trust immediately.

prompts.title: Email: End-of-Campaign Thank-You and Results
prompts.useWhen: A campaign just wrapped and you need to report final results and say thank you.
prompts.prompt: Write a campaign results email for [CAMPAIGN NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. We raised [FINAL AMOUNT] against a goal of [GOAL AMOUNT] from [NUMBER] donors. Thank supporters, share the final number with genuine excitement (or honest framing if the goal wasn't fully met), and tell them one specific next step for how the funds will be used. Under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: If you fell short of the goal, ask the AI specifically for language that stays honest and forward-looking rather than apologetic — donors respond better to "here's what we'll still accomplish" than to an email that sounds like a failure report. 5. Volunteer Recruitment & Management

prompts.title: Post: Volunteer Recruitment Post or Email
prompts.useWhen: You need to fill volunteer shifts or open roles and want a compelling recruitment ask.
prompts.prompt: Write a volunteer recruitment post/email for [ORGANIZATION NAME] promoting a role called [ROLE NAME]. The role involves [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF TASKS], requires [TIME COMMITMENT], and is a good fit for someone who [TYPE OF PERSON/SKILLS]. Include what makes this role meaningful (not just what's required) and a clear signup call to action linking to [SIGNUP LINK]. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Lead with the impact of the role, not the time commitment — "help 20 kids learn to read" recruits better than "2 hours every Tuesday," even though both facts belong in the post.

prompts.title: Description: Volunteer Role Description
prompts.useWhen: You're creating a formal volunteer job description for a new position.
prompts.prompt: Write a volunteer role description for [ROLE NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Include: a short role summary, key responsibilities (bullet list), time commitment, any required skills or qualifications, what training or support is provided, and who they'll report to. Base it on these rough notes: [PASTE NOTES ABOUT THE ROLE]. Format for posting on a volunteer matching site like VolunteerMatch or Idealist.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a "why this role matters" sentence at the top separate from the responsibilities list — role descriptions that lead with duties instead of purpose get fewer applicants.

prompts.title: Email: Volunteer Onboarding Welcome Message
prompts.useWhen: A new volunteer just signed up and needs a warm, clear first message.
prompts.prompt: Write a welcome message for a new volunteer joining [ORGANIZATION NAME] as a [ROLE NAME]. Cover: a warm welcome, what to expect for their first day/shift, any paperwork or training they still need to complete, and who to contact with questions. Friendly and organized tone, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for this to be formatted with a short checklist at the end — new volunteers retain "what do I do next" information far better as a checklist than as a paragraph.

prompts.title: Message: Volunteer Appreciation Note
prompts.useWhen: You want to thank volunteers, individually or as a group, for their time.
prompts.prompt: Write a volunteer appreciation message for [ORGANIZATION NAME] to send to volunteers who contributed [NUMBER] hours / helped with [SPECIFIC EVENT OR PROGRAM]. Acknowledge specifically what their time made possible, not just "thank you for your service." Keep it genuine and under 120 words. Suggest this works as an email, but note it could also be adapted for a printed card.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version that names a specific outcome ("because of you, 40 families got groceries this month") — specific appreciation is remembered longer than general appreciation.

prompts.title: Reminder: Volunteer Shift Reminder
prompts.useWhen: You need a quick, friendly reminder before a scheduled volunteer shift.
prompts.prompt: Write a short reminder text or email for volunteers signed up for [SHIFT/EVENT NAME] on [DATE/ TIME] at [LOCATION]. Include what to bring or wear if relevant, where to check in, and a quick line of appreciation for them showing up. Under 60 words, casual and friendly tone.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a text-message-length version separately from the email version — reminders sent as texts have much higher read rates than reminder emails for same-day shifts.

prompts.title: Message: Volunteer Exit and Feedback Request
prompts.useWhen: A long-term volunteer is stepping away and you want to close the loop well.
prompts.prompt: Write a message to a volunteer named [VOLUNTEER NAME] who is stepping away from their role as [ROLE NAME] after [LENGTH OF SERVICE] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Thank them warmly and specifically, invite honest feedback about their experience, and leave the door open for them to return or stay connected as a donor/supporter in the future. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Always include the "door open" line — a volunteer who leaves on a warm note is one of your best future donor or return-volunteer prospects.

prompts.title: Pitch: Corporate or Group Volunteer Day Pitch
prompts.useWhen: You're trying to recruit a company or group for a team volunteer day (corporate social responsibility, or CSR, outreach).
prompts.prompt: Write a pitch email to a local business or company proposing a corporate volunteer day with [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Describe 2-3 possible volunteer projects that would work well for a group of [GROUP SIZE], explain the impact, and note any logistics (timing, location, what we'd provide). Include a professional but enthusiastic tone, aimed at an HR or CSR contact. Under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Mention that you can provide photos, a recap, or social media recognition for the company afterward — many corporate CSR programs need that content to justify the day internally, and offering it upfront makes you easier to say yes to.

prompts.title: Outline: Volunteer Training / Orientation Script
prompts.useWhen: You need a script or outline to run a volunteer orientation or training session.
prompts.prompt: Build a 30-minute volunteer orientation outline for new volunteers at [ORGANIZATION NAME] joining as [ROLE TYPE]. Cover: welcome/mission overview (5 min), role expectations and logistics (10 min), safety/policy essentials (10 min), and Q&A (5 min). For each section, give me 3-4 bullet talking points based on: [PASTE KEY POLICIES/DETAILS TO COVER].
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to flag which sections should be handouts versus spoken content — orientation sessions run more smoothly when policy details are given as a leave-behind rather than read aloud.

prompts.title: Newsletter: Volunteer-Only Update
prompts.useWhen: You want to keep your active volunteer base informed and engaged between shifts.
prompts.prompt: Write a short volunteer-only newsletter update for [ORGANIZATION NAME] covering: [LIST 2-3 UPDATES, e.g., upcoming shifts needed, a recent win, a volunteer shoutout]. Keep the tone like an update from a teammate, not a formal announcement. Under 200 words, include a section header for each update.
prompts.proTip: Include one open volunteer need with a direct signup link in every issue — a volunteer newsletter is one of your highest-converting channels for filling last-minute shifts. 6. Board & Stakeholder Communication

prompts.title: Agenda: Board Meeting Agenda
prompts.useWhen: You need to build a clear agenda ahead of a board of directors meeting.
prompts.prompt: Build a board meeting agenda for [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s [QUARTERLY/MONTHLY] board meeting on [DATE]. We need to cover: [LIST TOPICS, e.g., financial update, program report, upcoming event, ED report]. Allocate reasonable time blocks for a [MEETING LENGTH]-minute meeting, and note which items are informational versus require a board vote. Format as a numbered agenda with time estimates.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to flag any agenda item that seems too big to cover in its allotted time — packed agendas are the #1 reason board meetings run long and important items get rushed.

prompts.title: Report: Executive Director's Report to the Board
prompts.useWhen: You need to summarize the last quarter or month for your board (an ED report).
prompts.prompt: Write an Executive Director's report to the board of [ORGANIZATION NAME] covering [TIME PERIOD]. Include these updates: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES ON PROGRAMS, FINANCES, STAFFING, CHALLENGES]. Structure it as: key wins, challenges/risks the board should know about, financial snapshot, and 1-2 decisions or input needed from the board. Clear, direct, no filler. 400-500 words.
prompts.proTip: Always include the "challenges/risks" section honestly — boards that only hear good news can't help you when you actually need them, and it erodes trust when problems surface later that weren't flagged.

prompts.title: Pitch: Board Member Recruitment Message
prompts.useWhen: You're recruiting a new board member and need to explain the opportunity (board development).
prompts.prompt: Write a board recruitment message for [ORGANIZATION NAME], inviting a prospective board member named [NAME] to consider joining. Explain our mission in 2 sentences, what we're looking for in this board seat (e.g., [SKILL/EXPERTISE NEEDED]), the time commitment ([MEETINGS PER YEAR, GIVE/GET EXPECTATION IF ANY]), and why we think they'd be a great fit based on [WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT THEM]. Warm, respectful tone, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Name the specific skill gap you're filling ("we need someone with financial oversight experience") rather than a generic pitch — people are more likely to say yes when they understand exactly why they were asked.
fields: MEETINGS PER YEAR, GIVE/GET EXPECTATION IF ANY

prompts.title: Minutes: Board Meeting Minutes Cleanup
prompts.useWhen: You have rough, messy notes from a board meeting and need clean, official minutes.
prompts.prompt: Here are my rough notes from [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s board meeting on [DATE]: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES]. Turn these into clean, professional board meeting minutes. Include: attendance, items discussed, any motions made and their outcomes (pass/fail/tabled), and action items with owners. Use standard nonprofit board minutes formatting.
prompts.proTip: Always have the board chair or secretary review AI-cleaned minutes against their own notes before they're filed — minutes are a legal record, and any motion or vote detail needs to be verified for accuracy, not assumed correct.

prompts.title: Update: Stakeholder Update for a Government or Institutional Partner
prompts.useWhen: You need to update a government agency, school district, or institutional funder/ partner on a partnership's progress.
prompts.prompt: Write a formal update to [PARTNER ORGANIZATION/AGENCY NAME] on the progress of our partnership around [PARTNERSHIP PURPOSE]. Cover: what's been accomplished since [LAST UPDATE DATE], any challenges or delays, and what's planned next. Use a professional, straightforward tone appropriate for [TYPE OF INSTITUTION, e.g., a school district administrator]. 250-300 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version with a one-line executive summary at the top — institutional readers often forward these to people who won't read the full update, and a strong summary line ensures the key point survives.
fields: TYPE OF INSTITUTION, e.g., a school district administrator

prompts.title: Section: Annual Report "Year in Review" Narrative
prompts.useWhen: You're pulling together your annual report and need the narrative section written.
prompts.prompt: Write the "Year in Review" narrative section of [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s annual report for [YEAR]. Use these highlights: [PASTE KEY NUMBERS, MILESTONES, STORIES]. Structure it as an engaging but factual 300-400 word summary covering our impact, what changed this year, and a forward-looking closing line about what's next. Written for a mixed audience of donors, board members, and community partners.
prompts.proTip: Draft this section before the design/layout process starts, not during — annual reports read much better when the writing drives the design instead of getting squeezed to fit a template.

prompts.title: Talking Points: Media or Public Statement Prep
prompts.useWhen: Your ED or a spokesperson needs quick talking points before an interview or public comment (media prep).
prompts.prompt: Prepare 5 talking points for [SPOKESPERSON NAME/TITLE] at [ORGANIZATION NAME] ahead of [OCCASION, e.g., a local news interview / a community forum] about [TOPIC]. Each talking point should be one clear, quotable sentence backed by a specific fact or example we can point to: [PASTE RELEVANT FACTS/CONTEXT]. Keep the tone confident and on-message, avoiding anything that sounds defensive.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version of each talking point trimmed to under 15 words — the shorter version is what actually gets quoted, and it's easier to remember on the spot.
fields: OCCASION, e.g., a local news interview / a community forum

prompts.title: Charter: Board Committee Charter / Terms of Reference
prompts.useWhen: You're formalizing a board committee (finance, governance, development) and need a clear charter.
prompts.prompt: Draft a committee charter for the [COMMITTEE NAME, e.g., Finance Committee] of [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s board. Include: purpose, key responsibilities, membership composition and term length, meeting frequency, and how it reports back to the full board. Base this on standard nonprofit governance practice, and flag anywhere our specific bylaws should be checked instead of assuming a default.
prompts.proTip: Always cross-check the draft against your actual bylaws before adopting it — committee structure and authority often need to align with language already baked into your governing documents.

prompts.title: Message: Thank-You to an Outgoing Board Member
prompts.useWhen: A board member's term is ending and they deserve a proper send-off.
prompts.prompt: Write a thank-you message (suitable for a card or a short speech) to an outgoing board member named [NAME] who served [LENGTH OF TERM] on the board of [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Reference 1-2 specific contributions they made: [PASTE SPECIFIC CONTRIBUTIONS]. Warm and genuine tone, under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for both a written card version and a shorter spoken version — you'll likely want to say something out loud at their final meeting in addition to giving them something in writing. 7. Program Design & Impact Reporting

prompts.title: Summary: Program Outcomes Summary From Raw Data
prompts.useWhen: You need to translate raw program data into a readable outcomes (impact) summary.
prompts.prompt: Turn this raw program data into a clear outcomes summary for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], covering [TIME PERIOD]: [PASTE RAW NUMBERS/DATA]. Distinguish clearly between outputs (what we did — e.g., number served) and outcomes (what changed for participants — e.g., skills gained, conditions improved). Format as a short summary followed by 3-5 key stats presented as bullet points.
prompts.proTip: If your data only shows outputs (people served, sessions held) and no outcomes, ask the AI to suggest 2-3 simple outcome questions you could start tracking — funders increasingly expect outcomes, not just activity counts.

prompts.title: Story: Client or Participant Success Story Write-Up
prompts.useWhen: A staff member shares a great client story and you need it turned into a polished, appropriately anonymized write-up.
prompts.prompt: Turn these rough notes about a program participant into a polished success story for [ORGANIZATION NAME]: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES]. Change identifying details to protect privacy (use a first name only or a pseudonym, and note this in brackets). Structure it as: their situation before, what our program provided, and where they are now. Warm, respectful, non-exploitative tone — avoid "poverty porn" framing that reduces the person to their hardship. 200-300 words.
prompts.proTip: Always get informed consent from the participant (or guardian) before publishing their story anywhere, even with a changed name — ask the AI to include a placeholder reminder line to confirm consent was obtained.

prompts.title: Design: Program Evaluation Survey Questions
prompts.useWhen: You need to design a participant survey to measure program outcomes (an evaluation instrument).
prompts.prompt: Design a [NUMBER]-question survey to measure outcomes for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Our program is intended to improve [SPECIFIC OUTCOME, e.g., job readiness / reading level / food security]. Include a mix of scaled (1-5) and open-ended questions, and suggest whether each should be asked before, during, or after program participation. Format as a table: Question, Type, Timing.
prompts.proTip: Keep the survey under 10 questions for participant surveys — completion rates drop sharply past that point, and a shorter survey you actually get filled out beats a thorough one that gets abandoned.

prompts.title: Memo: Program Options Comparison Memo
prompts.useWhen: Your team is deciding between a few program design options and needs a cleareyed comparison.
prompts.prompt: I'm deciding between these program approaches for [PROGRAM GOAL]: [LIST 2-3 OPTIONS WITH BRIEF DESCRIPTIONS]. Write a comparison memo covering the pros, cons, rough cost implications, and staffing implications of each option. End with a neutral recommendation of what questions we should answer before deciding, rather than picking for us. Format as a table plus a short summary paragraph.
prompts.proTip: Explicitly ask the AI not to pick a "winner" — its job here is to organize the tradeoffs clearly so your team can decide, not to make the call for you.

prompts.title: Case: Case for Support for Program Expansion
prompts.useWhen: You're making the internal or funder-facing case to expand or add a new program.
prompts.prompt: Write a case for support for expanding [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME] to [NEW SCOPE, e.g., a second location / a new age group / double the current capacity]. Cover: the evidence this program works (based on [CURRENT OUTCOMES/DATA]), the unmet need that justifies expansion, what expansion would require (staffing, budget, timeline), and the expected impact. 350-450 words, confident and evidence-based tone.
prompts.proTip: Lead with your existing program's proof points before making the case for expansion — funders and boards are far more willing to fund "more of what's already working" than an untested new idea.

prompts.title: Rewrite: Client Intake Form Plain-Language Cleanup
prompts.useWhen: Your intake forms are clunky, jargon-heavy, or intimidating to the people filling them out.
prompts.prompt: Here is our current client intake form language for [PROGRAM NAME]: [PASTE CURRENT FORM TEXT]. Rewrite it in plain, warm, 6th-grade reading level language that would feel approachable to someone accessing services for the first time. Keep all the same required information fields, just simplify the wording and framing around each one.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the rewritten form to be reviewed specifically for anything that could feel judgmental or bureaucratic (e.g., "explain your situation") and softened — intake language shapes whether people feel safe enough to actually complete the form.

prompts.title: Outline: New Program Staff Training Plan
prompts.useWhen: You're onboarding new program staff and need a structured first-week training plan.
prompts.prompt: Build a first-week training outline for a new [STAFF ROLE, e.g., case manager] joining [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Cover: program overview and mission alignment (day 1), key policies and required trainings (days 1-2), shadowing/hands-on practice (days 2-4), and a check-in/ Q&A (day 5). For each day, list 3-4 specific topics based on: [PASTE KEY PROGRAM POLICIES/ PROCEDURES].
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to flag which topics involve compliance or safety requirements (like mandated reporting) — those sections should be reviewed by someone with the right expertise, not finalized from an AI draft alone.

prompts.title: Summary: Plain-Language External Evaluation Report Summary
prompts.useWhen: You have a dense external evaluation report and need a plain-language summary for your board or newsletter.
prompts.prompt: Here is an excerpt from an external evaluation report on [PROGRAM NAME]: [PASTE REPORT EXCERPT]. Summarize the key findings in plain, non-academic language suitable for a board update or newsletter. Focus on: what the evaluation found worked well, what it found needs improvement, and 1-2 recommended next steps. Under 300 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a separate one-paragraph version specifically for a public-facing newsletter, since board updates can include more nuance and caveats than what you'd want to share externally.

prompts.title: Narrative: Theory of Change Narrative
prompts.useWhen: You need to explain, in plain language, why your program's approach should lead to the outcomes you claim.
prompts.prompt: Write a plain-language theory of change narrative for [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s work on [MISSION AREA]. Structure it as: if we do [KEY ACTIVITIES], then [SHORT-TERM CHANGES] will happen, which leads to [LONG-TERM IMPACT], because [UNDERLYING ASSUMPTION/EVIDENCE]. Base this on: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES ON YOUR APPROACH AND WHY YOU BELIEVE IT WORKS]. Write it as a short narrative paragraph, not just a diagram, suitable for a website "our approach" page.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the "underlying assumption" to be stated explicitly and separately — funders and evaluators increasingly want to see that you know why you believe your approach works, not just that you believe it. 8. Event Planning & Promotion

prompts.title: Plan: Event Run-of-Show Schedule
prompts.useWhen: You're planning a fundraising or community event and need a structured minute-byminute outline.
prompts.prompt: Build a run-of-show for [EVENT NAME], a [EVENT TYPE, e.g., fundraising gala / community open house] for [ORGANIZATION NAME] on [DATE], expecting [NUMBER] attendees. Include a timed schedule from doors-open to close, covering: welcome/arrival, program elements (speeches, ask, entertainment), and wrap-up. Base the program elements on: [LIST WHAT NEEDS TO HAPPEN, e.g., ED remarks, live ask, silent auction close]. Format as a table: Time, Activity, Owner.
prompts.proTip: Build in 10-15 minutes of built-in buffer time somewhere in the middle of the run-of-show — events almost always run behind, and having planned slack prevents the ending from getting rushed.
fields: EVENT TYPE, e.g., fundraising gala / community open house

prompts.title: Outline: Event Sponsorship Pitch Deck
prompts.useWhen: You're seeking event sponsors and need to outline the pitch.
prompts.prompt: Outline a sponsorship pitch for [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], targeting local businesses. Include suggested sponsorship tiers (e.g., [TIER NAMES/AMOUNTS]) and what benefits each tier would receive (logo placement, mentions, tickets, etc.). Structure as a one-page outline: event overview, audience/reach, sponsorship tiers table, and a closing reason a business should say yes now.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the audience/reach section to only include numbers you can actually verify (past attendance, email list size, social following) — inflated reach claims are the fastest way to lose a sponsor's trust for next year.

prompts.title: Description: Auction Item Descriptions
prompts.useWhen: You need compelling item descriptions for a live or silent auction catalog.
prompts.prompt: Write auction item descriptions for [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s [EVENT NAME] auction. Here are the items: [LIST ITEMS WITH BASIC DETAILS AND DONOR NAMES]. For each item, write a 2-3 sentence description that makes it sound appealing, includes the estimated value, and credits the donor. Format as a numbered catalog.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the highest-value items to get a slightly longer, more vivid description than smaller items — bidders spend more time reading (and bidding on) items that are described with more detail.
fields: LIST ITEMS WITH BASIC DETAILS AND DONOR NAMES

prompts.title: Speech: Fundraising Ask Speech for an Event
prompts.useWhen: You need remarks for the live ask (paddle raise or fund-a-need) moment at a gala or event.
prompts.prompt: Write a 3-minute fundraising ask speech for [SPEAKER NAME/ROLE] to deliver at [EVENT NAME] for [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Include a brief story to open (about [STORY TOPIC]), a clear statement of what we're raising money for and why it matters right now, and a specific, confident ask amount of [ASK AMOUNT] with a clear instruction on how to give in the room. Conversational, spoken-word tone — not written like an essay.
prompts.proTip: Read the speech out loud once before finalizing — AI-written text often has sentences that look fine on paper but are awkward to actually say; ask for a rewrite of any line that trips up the speaker.

prompts.title: Email: Post-Event Thank-You and Recap
prompts.useWhen: An event just wrapped and you need to thank attendees and share results.
prompts.prompt: Write a post-event thank-you email to attendees of [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Thank them for coming, share the results (raised [AMOUNT], [NUMBER] attendees, or other key outcome), include a couple of specific highlights or moments from the event, and end with what's next. Warm and celebratory tone, under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a separate, shorter thank-you specifically for sponsors and top donors who attended — they deserve a more personal acknowledgment than the general attendee email.

prompts.title: Sheet: Day-Of Volunteer or Staff Briefing Sheet
prompts.useWhen: You need to brief day-of volunteers or staff on their roles at an event.
prompts.prompt: Create a day-of briefing sheet for volunteers/staff working [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Include: arrival time and check-in location, a summary of the event schedule, each role's specific responsibilities based on [LIST ROLES AND TASKS], and a contact number for day-of issues. Format as a clean, easy-to-scan one-pager.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the most important logistics (arrival time, check-in spot, emergency contact) to be pulled into a bolded box at the top — volunteers skim these sheets fast, and the critical info needs to be impossible to miss.

prompts.title: Announcement: Save-the-Date Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You're announcing next year's event date early to build anticipation.
prompts.prompt: Write a short save-the-date announcement for [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], happening [DATE] at [LOCATION]. Keep it brief and exciting — this isn't the full invitation, just enough to get people to hold the date. Suitable for both email and a social media caption version. Under 60 words for each version.
prompts.proTip: Send the save-the-date at least 8-10 weeks before the event for anything requiring travel or formal wear — people need real lead time to plan around a gala-style event.

prompts.title: FAQ: Event FAQ Page
prompts.useWhen: You're getting repeated questions about an upcoming event and want a self-serve answer page.
prompts.prompt: Write an FAQ section for [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], answering these common questions: [LIST QUESTIONS YOU'VE BEEN GETTING, e.g., parking, dress code, ticket refunds, accessibility]. Keep each answer short (1-3 sentences), friendly, and clear. Format as a Q&A list suitable for a website page.
prompts.proTip: Always include an accessibility question and answer even if no one's asked yet (parking, seating, dietary accommodations) — it signals inclusivity and heads off individual emails asking the same thing.

prompts.title: Memo: Event Budget Line-Item Justification
prompts.useWhen: You need to justify event expenses to your board or a funder covering event costs.
prompts.prompt: Write a short justification memo for these event expenses for [EVENT NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]: [PASTE LINE ITEMS AND AMOUNTS]. For each major line item, explain why the cost is reasonable and how it supports the event's fundraising or mission goals. Include a closing note on projected net revenue (total raised minus total costs). Professional, concise tone.
prompts.proTip: Always present the net revenue number, not just gross funds raised — boards and funders want to see that event costs are proportionate to what the event actually nets the organization. 9. Difficult Conversations & Crisis Comms

prompts.title: Response: Declined Grant Follow-Up to a Funder
prompts.useWhen: A funder turned you down (a grant rejection) and you want to keep the relationship warm for next time.
prompts.prompt: Write a gracious response to [FUNDER NAME] after being declined for a grant supporting [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Thank them for considering us, ask (politely) if they'd be open to feedback on the proposal or a future conversation, and express interest in applying again in the future. Keep it short, professional, and free of any disappointment or defensiveness. Under 120 words.
prompts.proTip: Always ask for feedback in this email, even if you don't expect a detailed answer — funders remember grantees who handle "no" gracefully and ask good questions, and it often improves your odds next cycle.

prompts.title: Response: Reply to an Upset or Complaining Donor
prompts.useWhen: A donor is upset or filing a complaint about how their gift was used, a mistake in acknowledgment, or a program decision.
prompts.prompt: A donor named [DONOR NAME] is upset about [SITUATION, e.g., a delayed thank-you letter / how funds were used / a program change]. Write a response that acknowledges their concern genuinely (without being overly apologetic if we didn't actually do anything wrong), explains the situation clearly, and offers a specific next step to resolve or address it. Calm, respectful, non-defensive tone. Under 200 words.
prompts.proTip: Have someone senior review this before sending if the donor is a major or long-term giver — the stakes of getting the tone right go up significantly with your most important relationships.

prompts.title: Announcement: Program Cut or Change Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You need to announce a program is ending, shrinking, or changing significantly, to staff, participants, or the community.
prompts.prompt: Write an announcement that [ORGANIZATION NAME] is [ENDING/CHANGING] [PROGRAM NAME], intended for [AUDIENCE, e.g., program participants / the community / staff]. Explain the reason honestly in plain language (without excessive corporate-speak), what this means for people currently affected, and what support or alternatives are available. Compassionate, direct, and honest tone — avoid vague language that obscures what's actually happening. 200-300 words.
prompts.proTip: Never let an AI-drafted version of this go out without a human who deeply understands the situation reviewing every sentence — the framing of a program cut affects real people's trust in your organization, and precision matters more than speed here.
fields: AUDIENCE, e.g., program participants / the community / staff

prompts.title: Statement: Response to Public Criticism or a Negative News Story
prompts.useWhen: Your organization is facing public criticism, a negative article, or online backlash and needs a press statement.
prompts.prompt: Draft a public response statement from [ORGANIZATION NAME] addressing [SITUATION/ CRITICISM, briefly describe]. The statement should acknowledge the concern raised, provide factual context or correction where needed (using: [PASTE RELEVANT FACTS]), and state what we're doing in response if applicable. Calm, non-defensive, factual tone — avoid language that sounds dismissive or combative. 150-200 words.
prompts.proTip: Treat this as a first draft only — for anything involving real reputational risk, have this reviewed by your ED, board chair, and (for serious situations) legal counsel before it goes anywhere public.

prompts.title: Communication: Layoff or Restructuring Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You need to communicate a staff layoff or organizational restructuring, internally or to stakeholders.
prompts.prompt: Write an internal announcement to staff at [ORGANIZATION NAME] about [RESTRUCTURING/ LAYOFF SITUATION, briefly describe]. Explain the reason for the change honestly, what it means for the team, and what support is being offered to those affected. Compassionate, clear, and direct — no corporate euphemisms. Separately, draft a short external version for board/funders that respects affected staff's privacy while being transparent about organizational changes.
prompts.proTip: Have HR and legal review any layoff communication before it's sent — this is one of the highest-stakes communications a nonprofit sends, and an AI draft should only ever be a starting point here, never the final version.

prompts.title: Notification: Data Breach or Privacy Incident Notice
prompts.useWhen: A privacy or data incident has occurred and you need to notify affected individuals.
prompts.prompt: Draft a notification to [AFFECTED GROUP, e.g., donors / program participants] about [INCIDENT DESCRIPTION, briefly describe what happened]. Explain what happened in plain language, what information may have been affected, what we're doing about it, and what steps they can take to protect themselves. Serious, transparent, non-alarmist tone. 200-250 words.
prompts.proTip: This communication likely has legal notification requirements depending on your state and the type of data involved — treat this prompt as a drafting starting point only, and have legal counsel confirm both the content and the timing before anything is sent.
fields: AFFECTED GROUP, e.g., donors / program participants
INCIDENT DESCRIPTION, briefly describe what happened

prompts.title: Response: Donor Request to Redirect or Refund a Gift
prompts.useWhen: A donor is requesting their gift be redirected to a different program or refunded entirely.
prompts.prompt: A donor named [DONOR NAME] has asked to [REDIRECT THEIR GIFT TO A DIFFERENT PROGRAM / HAVE IT REFUNDED], originally given to [ORIGINAL PROGRAM/FUND]. Write a response addressing their request professionally, explaining our policy on gift redirection/refunds ([DESCRIBE YOUR ACTUAL POLICY]), and offering the appropriate next step based on that policy. Respectful and solution-oriented tone, under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Know your restricted-gift policy before writing this — if the original gift was restricted to a specific fund, redirecting it may have real accounting and donor-intent implications that need a policy answer, not just a friendly one.

prompts.title: Apology: Apology for an Organizational Mistake
prompts.useWhen: Your organization made a genuine mistake (a missed deadline, an error in communication, a service failure) and owes someone a real apology.
prompts.prompt: Write a sincere apology to [RECIPIENT, e.g., a donor / a partner organization / a program participant] for [MISTAKE, briefly describe what happened]. Take clear ownership without over-explaining or making excuses, state specifically what we're doing to fix it or prevent it from happening again, and keep the tone humble and direct. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Cut any sentence that starts with "unfortunately" or shifts blame to circumstances — a real apology owns the mistake in the first sentence, and the AI will sometimes soften into passive language unless you specifically ask it to avoid that.

prompts.title: Script: Difficult Conversation Prep Script
prompts.useWhen: You need to prepare for an in-person difficult conversation, like addressing underperformance or a board conflict.
prompts.prompt: Help me prepare for a difficult conversation with [PERSON'S ROLE, e.g., a staff member / a board member] about [ISSUE, briefly describe]. Give me a simple script structure: how to open the conversation, 2-3 key points I need to make clearly, how to invite their perspective, and how to close with clear next steps. Keep the tone direct but respectful — this is a private prep tool, not something I'll read verbatim.
prompts.proTip: Practice this out loud once before the actual conversation — scripts read differently than they sound, and saying it aloud once will surface anything that feels stiff or unnatural so you can adjust before the real conversation.
fields: PERSON'S ROLE, e.g., a staff member / a board member

prompts.title: Plan: One Program Description Into a Month of Content
prompts.useWhen: You have one solid program description and need a full month of marketing material from it.
prompts.prompt: I'm going to give you a description of one program at [ORGANIZATION NAME]: [PASTE PROGRAM DESCRIPTION]. From this single description, generate: (1) 4 social media captions (one per week, different angles: a stat, a story, a behind-the-scenes moment, and a call to volunteer/donate), (2) one newsletter section (150 words), (3) one email appeal tied to this program (200 words), and (4) 3 possible headlines for a blog post about it. Label each piece clearly.
prompts.proTip: Run this once per program per quarter — it turns your existing program knowledge into an entire content backlog in one sitting instead of writing everything from scratch each time you need a post.

prompts.title: Draft: Full Grant Proposal Builder
prompts.useWhen: You have your program facts gathered and need a complete first-draft proposal, not just one section.
prompts.prompt: I'm applying for a grant from [FUNDER NAME] for [PROGRAM NAME] at [ORGANIZATION NAME], requesting [AMOUNT]. Here's what you need to know: [PASTE MISSION, PROGRAM DETAILS, TARGET POPULATION, OUTCOMES DATA, BUDGET NOTES]. Draft a full first-pass proposal with these sections in order: executive summary, statement of need, program description, goals and measurable outcomes, budget narrative, and organizational capacity. Flag any section where you had to make assumptions so I can fill in real details.
prompts.proTip: Don't submit this draft as-is — use it as a skeleton to fill in with your organization's verified facts, and always match the final structure to the funder's actual required sections and word limits.

prompts.title: Kit: Full Fundraising Campaign Kit
prompts.useWhen: You're launching a campaign and need every piece of collateral at once — not just emails.
prompts.prompt: I'm launching a fundraising campaign called [CAMPAIGN NAME] with a goal of [GOAL AMOUNT] to fund [PURPOSE], running from [START DATE] to [END DATE]. Build me a full campaign kit: (1) a campaign one-line pitch, (2) a 4-email sequence (launch, story, progress update, final push), (3) 5 social media captions spaced across the campaign timeline, (4) a website/landing page paragraph, and (5) a thank-you email template for when someone gives. Label each clearly and keep messaging consistent across all pieces.
prompts.proTip: Save this entire output as one document per campaign — reusing last year's campaign kit as a starting point for this prompt cuts your planning time dramatically on annual campaigns like Giving Tuesday or year-end.

prompts.title: Generator: Annual Report Content Generator
prompts.useWhen: It's annual report season and you need most of the narrative content drafted from raw numbers and notes.
prompts.prompt: Help me draft the core content for [ORGANIZATION NAME]'s [YEAR] annual report. Here's our raw data and notes: [PASTE KEY NUMBERS, PROGRAM HIGHLIGHTS, FINANCIAL SUMMARY NOTES, ONE OR TWO STORIES]. Generate: (1) a "Year in Review" narrative (300 words), (2) a "By the Numbers" section formatted as 5-6 standalone stats with one-line context each, (3) a donor/ funder thank-you section, and (4) a forward-looking closing statement about next year's priorities. Keep tone consistent and factual throughout.
prompts.proTip: Gather all your raw numbers and stories into one document before running this prompt — the quality of an annual report draft depends entirely on how complete the input data is, not on how the prompt is worded.

prompts.title: Package: New Program Launch Package
prompts.useWhen: You're launching a brand-new program and need everything from the pitch to the promotion built at once.
prompts.prompt: [ORGANIZATION NAME] is launching a new program called [PROGRAM NAME] to address [PROBLEM/NEED], serving [TARGET POPULATION]. Here's what we know so far: [PASTE PROGRAM DETAILS, HOW IT WORKS, WHO RUNS IT]. Generate: (1) a one-paragraph program description for our website, (2) a launch announcement email to our supporter list, (3) a launch social media post, (4) an internal one-pager for staff/board explaining the program, and (5) 3 potential outcome metrics we could start tracking from day one.
