prompts.proTip: Use the outcome metrics list (item 5) as a starting point for a conversation with your program team about what you'll actually measure — deciding this before launch, not six months in, makes your first grant report or annual report far easier to write.
fields: PASTE PROGRAM DETAILS, HOW IT WORKS, WHO RUNS IT

prompts.title: Sequence: Full-Year Donor Journey Email Series
prompts.useWhen: You want a complete automated email sequence covering a donor's entire first year, not just one email.
prompts.prompt: Build a full first-year donor journey email sequence for a new donor to [ORGANIZATION NAME] who just made their first gift of [TYPICAL FIRST GIFT AMOUNT]. Include: (1) immediate thank-you (send day 1), (2) impact update with no ask (send ~6 weeks), (3) a second touchpoint — a story or update (send ~4 months), (4) a soft ask to become a monthly donor (send ~7 months), (5) a year-end/ anniversary appeal (send ~11-12 months). For each, give the send timing, subject line, and full email body.
prompts.proTip: Load this sequence into your email platform's automation once, tied to "date of first gift," and every new donor going forward automatically gets a thoughtful first year of stewardship without you writing a single extra email.

prompts.title: Package: Board Meeting Prep Package
prompts.useWhen: You need everything ready for an upcoming board meeting — not just the agenda.
prompts.prompt: I have a board meeting for [ORGANIZATION NAME] on [DATE]. Here's what's happened since our last meeting: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES ON PROGRAMS, FINANCES, FUNDRAISING, CHALLENGES]. Generate: (1) a full agenda with time blocks, (2) the ED's written report to the board, (3) 3 discussion questions to pose to the board on our biggest open decision, and (4) a short premeeting email to send the board with these materials attached. Keep everything consistent and pulling from the same set of facts.
prompts.proTip: Send the pre-meeting materials at least 3-5 days ahead of the actual meeting — board members who receive materials the day before rarely read them closely, and your meeting quality drops as a result.

prompts.title: Plan: Crisis Communication Response Plan
prompts.useWhen: A situation has just broken (negative press, an internal incident, a public complaint) and you need a full response plan fast, not just one statement.
prompts.prompt: A situation has come up at [ORGANIZATION NAME]: [DESCRIBE THE SITUATION HONESTLY AND IN DETAIL]. Help me build a response plan: (1) a short internal message to staff/board explaining what happened and how we're handling it, (2) a public statement (if one is warranted) that's factual and non-defensive, (3) a list of 3-5 questions we should expect from media, donors, or the public, with a one-line answer to each, and (4) a recommendation on which audiences need to hear from us directly versus only if asked.
prompts.proTip: Treat every output from this prompt as a draft for your leadership team and, for serious situations, legal counsel to review — the value here is having a fast, organized starting point under pressure, not a final answer to publish unreviewed.
fields: DESCRIBE THE SITUATION HONESTLY AND IN DETAIL

prompts.title: Combo: Grant Report Plus Renewal Ask
prompts.useWhen: You're writing a required grant report and want to use the same momentum to make the case for renewed funding.
prompts.prompt: I need to write a grant outcomes report to [FUNDER NAME] for their [AMOUNT] gift to [PROGRAM NAME], and I also want to lay groundwork for asking them to renew or increase support next cycle. Here's our data: [PASTE OUTCOMES, CHALLENGES, NUMBERS]. Draft: (1) the formal outcomes report (400-500 words, following standard report structure), and (2) a separate, shorter closing paragraph I could add or mention in a follow-up conversation that makes a soft case for continued or increased support based on the results shown in the report.
prompts.proTip: Keep the renewal language out of the formal report itself unless the funder's report template explicitly invites it — use it instead in a follow-up call or cover email so the report reads as accountability, not a pitch.

prompts.title: Package: New Employee First-Week Orientation
prompts.useWhen: You're onboarding a new staff member and want a complete, organized first-week orientation package built from your organization's basic facts.
prompts.prompt: Build a first-week orientation package for a new [ROLE] joining [ORGANIZATION NAME]. Here's our basic organizational info: [PASTE MISSION, PROGRAMS, ORG STRUCTURE, KEY POLICIES]. Generate: (1) a one-page "who we are" overview, (2) a glossary of internal terms/acronyms they'll hear in their first week, (3) a suggested first-week schedule (who to meet, what to review), and (4) a list of 10 smart questions they could ask their manager to ramp up faster. Format each section clearly.
prompts.proTip: Reuse this exact prompt for every new hire, updating only the [ROLE] and any role-specific policy notes — a consistent onboarding experience saves supervisor time and helps new staff feel oriented faster in their first week.
fields: PASTE MISSION, PROGRAMS, ORG STRUCTURE, KEY POLICIES

prompts.title: Email: Weekly Client Status Update
prompts.useWhen: You need to send a quick client update or weekly recap and don't want to start from a blank page.
prompts.prompt: You are an account manager at a marketing agency writing a weekly status email to a client. Write a short, upbeat but honest update covering: what got done this week, what's in progress, what's blocked (if anything), and what's coming next week. Keep it to 150-200 words, use plain language a busy business owner can skim in 30 seconds, and end with one clear question or ask if you need something from them. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] This week's completed items: [LIST OF TASKS] In progress: [LIST OF TASKS] Blockers or open items: [BLOCKERS, IF ANY] Next week's plan: [UPCOMING TASKS]
prompts.proTip: Paste last week's email in as a second message and ask the AI to match the tone so every update sounds consistent over time.

prompts.title: Email: Explaining a Performance Dip to a Client
prompts.useWhen: Numbers went down this month and you need to explain the drop or downturn before the client notices and panics.
prompts.prompt: You are a marketing account manager explaining a performance dip to a client in a calm, confident, non-defensive way. Write an email that: names the metric that dropped, gives the likely reason in plain English (no jargon), states what you're already doing about it, and gives a realistic timeline for improvement. Do not over-apologize or make promises you can't back up. Keep it under 175 words. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Metric that dropped: [METRIC, e.g., click-through rate] Percent change: [PERCENT CHANGE] Likely cause: [CAUSE, e.g., seasonality, platform change, budget cut] Action already taken or planned: [ACTION STEPS]
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI for a second, shorter version you can use as a Slack or text message if the client prefers quick updates over email.
fields: CAUSE, e.g., seasonality, platform change, budget cut

prompts.title: Email: Kicking Off a New Client Onboarding
prompts.useWhen: You just signed a new client or closed a new account and need to send the welcome and kickoff email.
prompts.prompt: Write a warm, professional welcome email to a new marketing client kicking off a project. Introduce the agency's process in 3-4 simple steps, list what you need from them to get started (assets, access, brand guidelines, etc.), set expectations for the first two weeks, and introduce their main point of contact on your team. Keep the tone friendly and confident, not overly formal. 200 words max. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Service or project starting: [SERVICE, e.g., paid social management] Items needed from client: [LIST OF ITEMS] Primary point of contact: [TEAM MEMBER NAME AND ROLE]
prompts.proTip: Attach your actual onboarding checklist as context so the AI references real deliverables instead of generic ones.

prompts.title: Script: Talking Points for a Monthly Client Check-In Call
prompts.useWhen: You have a recurring client call or account review coming up and want a simple agenda instead of winging it.
prompts.prompt: Create a talking-points script for a 30-minute monthly client check-in call. Structure it as: opening small talk transition (1 line), quick wins to highlight (bullet list), one challenge or open item to discuss, a question to ask the client about their business priorities, and a clear close with next steps. Write it in a conversational tone, like notes a person would actually glance at during a call, not a formal script. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] This month's wins: [WINS] Open item or challenge to raise: [CHALLENGE] Business priority to ask about: [TOPIC]
prompts.proTip: Keep this prompt saved and just swap the bracketed details each month so your calls follow a consistent, professional structure.

prompts.title: Email: Requesting Overdue Client Assets, Approvals, or Access
prompts.useWhen: A client is holding up work by not sending logos, copy sign-off, login access, or approvals, and you need a polite but firm nudge.
prompts.prompt: Write a friendly but firm follow-up email asking a client for overdue items that are blocking their project. Reference that this was requested before, state clearly what's needed and why it matters (tie it to their timeline or deadline), and make it easy for them to act by listing exactly what to send and by when. Avoid sounding passive-aggressive. Under 130 words. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Items needed: [LIST OF ITEMS, e.g., logo files, ad account access, copy approval] Deadline this is blocking: [DEADLINE OR MILESTONE] Date originally requested: [DATE]
prompts.proTip: Ask for a follow-up version that's 20% firmer in case this is the second or third reminder.

prompts.title: Response: Answering "Why Isn't This Working Yet"
prompts.useWhen: A client asks why they haven't seen results yet, whether by email, on a call, or in a message you need to reply to in writing.
prompts.prompt: A client is asking why their marketing campaign isn't producing results yet. Write a response that validates their concern without being defensive, explains realistic timelines for this type of campaign in plain terms, shares one specific data point that shows progress (even if small), and reassures them with a concrete next step or checkpoint date. Keep it honest, not falsely optimistic. 150 words max. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign type: [CAMPAIGN TYPE, e.g., SEO, paid ads, email] Time campaign has been live: [TIMEFRAME] Positive data point to share: [METRIC OR SIGNAL] Next checkpoint: [DATE OR MILESTONE]
prompts.proTip: If the concern is really about budget, use Prompt #64 instead, it's built specifically for that conversation.
fields: CAMPAIGN TYPE, e.g., SEO, paid ads, email

prompts.title: Email: Recap and Next Steps After a Client Meeting
prompts.useWhen: You just got off a client call and need to send a recap email before you forget what was decided.
prompts.prompt: Turn these rough meeting notes into a clean recap email for a marketing client. Organize it into three sections: Decisions Made, Action Items (with who owns each one and a due date), and Open Questions. Keep the tone professional and organized. Do not add anything that wasn't in the notes. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Meeting notes: [PASTE ROUGH NOTES OR BULLET POINTS] Action item owners: [NAMES]
prompts.proTip: Paste in messy, unstructured notes exactly as you typed them during the call. The AI is better at organizing than you'd expect.
fields: PASTE ROUGH NOTES OR BULLET POINTS

prompts.title: Checklist: Client Onboarding Questionnaire
prompts.useWhen: You need a discovery questionnaire to send a new client so you're not missing key info before starting work.
prompts.prompt: Create a client onboarding questionnaire for a marketing agency starting a new [SERVICE TYPE] engagement. Include 12-15 questions covering: business background, target audience, past marketing efforts and results, brand voice and guidelines, competitors, goals for this engagement, and internal approval process. Format as a numbered list a client can fill out directly, with a short one-line explanation under any question that might be unclear. Service type: [SERVICE TYPE, e.g., social media management, PPC, SEO] Client industry: [INDUSTRY]
prompts.proTip: Turn this into a reusable Google Form or Notion template once, and you'll never have to write a discovery questionnaire from scratch again.
fields: SERVICE TYPE, e.g., social media management, PPC, SEO

prompts.title: Email: Re-Engaging a Client Who Has Gone Quiet
prompts.useWhen: A client has stopped responding to emails or Slack messages and you need to reopen the conversation without sounding annoyed.
prompts.prompt: Write a friendly check-in email to a client who has gone quiet or unresponsive for a couple of weeks. Keep it light, not guilt-tripping. Reference the last thing you were working on together, offer one small piece of value or update, and ask a low-pressure question that's easy to answer in one line. End with an easy out in case they're just swamped. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Last topic discussed: [TOPIC OR PROJECT] Small update or value-add to include: [UPDATE, e.g., a quick win or resource] Number of weeks since last response: [TIMEFRAME]
prompts.proTip: Ask for two versions: one casual and one more formal, then pick based on how that client normally communicates. New Business & Pitching
fields: UPDATE, e.g., a quick win or resource

prompts.title: Proposal: Scope of Work for a New Client
prompts.useWhen: You're closing a deal or writing a contract and need a clear scope of work document, sometimes called a statement of work.
prompts.prompt: Write a scope of work section for a marketing services proposal. Include: a one-paragraph project summary, a bulleted list of specific deliverables with frequency (e.g., "4 static ads per month"), what is explicitly NOT included to prevent scope creep later, the timeline for the first phase, and payment terms. Use clear, plain-English business language, no fluff or filler phrases. Client/prospect name: [CLIENT NAME] Service being sold: [SERVICE, e.g., paid social, SEO, full-funnel marketing] Monthly deliverables: [LIST DELIVERABLES] Monthly retainer or project price: [PRICE] Contract length: [LENGTH, e.g., 3-month minimum]
prompts.proTip: The "not included" section is the most important part for preventing scope creep later. Never skip it, even for small projects.
fields: SERVICE, e.g., paid social, SEO, full-funnel marketing

prompts.title: Email: Cold Outreach to a Potential Client
prompts.useWhen: You're prospecting for new business and need a cold email that doesn't sound like every other agency pitch in their inbox.
prompts.prompt: Write a cold outreach email to a potential client from a marketing agency. Open with a specific, researched observation about their business (not a generic compliment), state one concrete way you could help tied to a result, not a service name, ask a low-commitment question instead of pushing for a call right away, and keep the whole email under 100 words. No buzzwords like "synergy" or "gamechanging." Prospect business name: [PROSPECT NAME] Specific observation about their business: [OBSERVATION, e.g., recent launch, ad they're running, review pattern] Result you could help with: [RESULT, e.g., more booked calls, lower cost per lead] Your agency's relevant proof point: [PROOF POINT, e.g., client result, years in business]
prompts.proTip: Generate 3 different opening lines and test which gets more replies before locking in one template.
fields: RESULT, e.g., more booked calls, lower cost per lead
PROOF POINT, e.g., client result, years in business

prompts.title: Script: Talking Points for a Discovery Call With a Prospect
prompts.useWhen: You have a first call booked with a potential client and want a simple guide so you ask the right questions instead of just pitching.
prompts.prompt: Create a discovery call script for a marketing agency's first call with a new prospect. Include: a 2sentence opener to build rapport, 6-8 open-ended questions covering their goals, budget range, past marketing experience, and decision timeline, and 2 questions to uncover their real pain point versus their stated one. End with a suggested transition line into next steps. Format as a scannable outline, not a paragraph. Prospect business type: [INDUSTRY/BUSINESS TYPE] Service they inquired about: [SERVICE]
prompts.proTip: Ask a follow-up question after the call: paste your notes back in and have the AI draft the recap email using Prompt #7's structure.

prompts.title: Response: Answering an RFP Question About Past Results
prompts.useWhen: You're filling out a request for proposal (RFP) and need to answer a question about case studies or past performance persuasively but honestly.
prompts.prompt: Help me write a response to an RFP question asking about our agency's past results and relevant case studies. Use the details below to write a confident, specific, results-first answer in 100-150 words. Lead with the number or outcome, then briefly explain how we achieved it, then tie it back to what this prospect is trying to achieve. Avoid vague claims like "we drive great results." RFP question: [PASTE EXACT QUESTION] Relevant past client result: [RESULT, e.g., "40% increase in qualified leads in 90 days"] How you achieved it: [BRIEF METHOD] What this prospect cares about most: [PROSPECT'S STATED GOAL]
prompts.proTip: Never let the AI invent a statistic. Always feed it your real numbers, even rounded or approximate ones.
fields: RESULT, e.g., "40% increase in qualified leads in 90 days"

prompts.title: Deck Outline: Structure for a New Business Pitch
prompts.useWhen: You need to build a pitch deck for a prospective client and want a solid slideby-slide outline before you start designing.
prompts.prompt: Create a slide-by-slide outline for a new business pitch deck for a marketing agency. Give me 10-12 slides with a title and 2-3 bullet points of suggested content for each, covering: the prospect's challenge, our understanding of their business, our proposed approach, relevant case studies, team, pricing, and next steps. Keep the flow persuasive and logical, building toward a clear call to action on the last slide. Prospect name: [PROSPECT NAME] Prospect's main challenge: [CHALLENGE] Proposed approach or service: [SERVICE/APPROACH] Relevant case study to feature: [CASE STUDY SUMMARY]
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to also write speaker notes for each slide so whoever presents doesn't have to improvise.

prompts.title: Email: Following Up After a Pitch With No Response
prompts.useWhen: You sent a proposal or pitched a prospect and haven't heard back, and need a follow-up that doesn't sound needy.
prompts.prompt: Write a follow-up email to a prospect after a pitch or proposal with no response in [NUMBER] days. Keep it short and low-pressure, assume they're just busy rather than uninterested, add one small new piece of value (an insight, a relevant article, or a quick idea specific to their business), and end with an easy yes-or-no question rather than "just checking in." Prospect name: [PROSPECT NAME] Days since proposal sent: [NUMBER] New value-add to include: [INSIGHT OR IDEA]
prompts.proTip: Ask for a 3-email follow-up sequence at once (day 3, day 10, day 21) so you're not writing these one at a time.

prompts.title: Proposal: Retainer Package Tiers (Good/Better/Best)
prompts.useWhen: You're presenting pricing options and want to structure them as tiered packages instead of one take-it-or-leave-it price.
prompts.prompt: Write three tiered retainer package descriptions (Good, Better, Best) for a marketing agency's proposal. For each tier, list the name, monthly price, included deliverables, and one sentence on who it's best for. Make the middle tier the clear best value option through what's included, not through pushy sales language. Format as a comparison a client could scan in under a minute. Service category: [SERVICE, e.g., paid media management] Entry-level price point: [PRICE] Deliverables available across tiers: [LIST OF POSSIBLE DELIVERABLES]
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to reformat the output as a markdown table so it's easy to paste directly into a proposal document or slide.

prompts.title: Email: Declining a Bad-Fit Prospect Gracefully
prompts.useWhen: A prospect isn't a good fit for your agency, whether on budget, industry, or expectations, and you need to say no without burning the bridge.
prompts.prompt: Write an email declining a prospective client because they're not the right fit for our agency right now. Be honest but tactful about the reason without being harsh, thank them for their time, and if appropriate, refer them to a different type of resource or suggest they reach back out in the future. Keep it warm and under 100 words. Prospect name: [PROSPECT NAME] Reason it's not a fit: [REASON, e.g., budget too low, outside our specialty] Alternative to suggest, if any: [ALTERNATIVE OR NONE]
prompts.proTip: A gracious no often turns into a referral later. Always leave the door open unless there's a real reason not to.
fields: REASON, e.g., budget too low, outside our specialty

prompts.title: Script: Handling "What Makes You Different From Other Agencies"
prompts.useWhen: A prospect asks how you compare to other agencies or freelancers they're considering, on a call or in writing.
prompts.prompt: Help me answer the question "what makes your agency different from others we're considering" in a confident, specific way that avoids generic claims like "we really care" or "we're more strategic." Use the real differentiators below to build a 3-part answer: our approach, our results, and our client experience. Keep it conversational, like something I'd actually say out loud, 100 words max. Real differentiator #1: [E.g., specialize in one industry] Real differentiator #2: [E.g., in-house creative team, no freelancers] Real differentiator #3: [E.g., weekly reporting, no black box]
prompts.proTip: Practice saying the answer out loud, not just reading it. Scripts that sound natural spoken often need shorter sentences than what reads well on a page. Ad Copy & Creative Production
fields: E.g., in-house creative team, no freelancers
E.g., weekly reporting, no black box

prompts.title: Headlines: 10 Google Search Ad Headlines for a Promotion
prompts.useWhen: You need a batch of Google Search ad headlines fast and don't want to write them one at a time.
prompts.prompt: Write 10 Google Search ad headlines (30 characters max each) for the offer below. Vary the angle across the set: some benefit-led, some urgency-led, some price-led, and at least one questionbased. Label each headline with its character count so I know it fits. Avoid exclamation points on more than 2 of them. Business/client name: [CLIENT NAME] Offer or promotion: [OFFER, e.g., "20% off first order"] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Deadline or urgency element, if any: [DEADLINE]
prompts.proTip: Ask for the character count on every headline. AI tools frequently miscount and go over the platform limit.

prompts.title: Ad Copy: Facebook/Instagram Ad in 3 Variations
prompts.useWhen: You're launching or testing a Meta ad and want a few different angles to A/B test instead of guessing which one will work.
prompts.prompt: Write 3 versions of a Facebook/Instagram ad for the offer below. Each version should have a hook line, 2-3 sentences of body copy, and a call to action. Make each version a genuinely different angle (for example: one pain-point led, one social-proof led, one curiosity led), not just reworded versions of the same idea. Keep each version under 125 words and write in a [TONE] voice. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Product or offer: [OFFER] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Tone: [TONE, e.g., friendly and casual, bold and direct] Call to action: [CTA, e.g., "Shop Now", "Book a Call"]
prompts.proTip: Run all 3 as a real split test before declaring a winner. The version that reads best to you is often not the one that performs best.
fields: TONE, e.g., friendly and casual, bold and direct

prompts.title: Ad Copy: LinkedIn Ad for B2B Lead Generation
prompts.useWhen: You're writing a LinkedIn ad for a B2B client and need copy that sounds credible to a professional audience, not consumer-facing.
prompts.prompt: Write a LinkedIn ad for a B2B lead generation campaign. Include a headline (under 70 characters), body copy (under 150 words) that leads with a specific business problem before the solution, and a call to action suited to a professional buyer (like "Download the Guide" or "Book a Demo," not "Shop Now"). Avoid consumer-style hype language; keep the tone credible and specific. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Target job titles or roles: [JOB TITLES] Business problem being solved: [PROBLEM] Lead magnet or offer: [OFFER, e.g., free audit, whitepaper, demo]
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version that opens with a statistic and a version that opens with a question, then see which one your audience responds to.
fields: OFFER, e.g., free audit, whitepaper, demo

prompts.title: Headlines: Landing Page Hero Section for a New Offer
prompts.useWhen: You need the top-of-page headline and subheadline for a client's landing page and the blank page is winning.
prompts.prompt: Write 5 options for a landing page hero section for the offer below. Each option should include a headline (under 10 words) and a one-sentence subheadline that clarifies the offer. Focus on the specific outcome the visitor gets, not generic phrases like "best solution" or "take your business to the next level." Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Offer or product: [OFFER] Specific outcome for the customer: [OUTCOME] Target audience: [AUDIENCE]
prompts.proTip: Read each headline out loud. If it could apply to any business in any industry, it's too generic, ask for a more specific rewrite.

prompts.title: Ad Copy: Retargeting Ad for Cart Abandoners
prompts.useWhen: You need a retargeting or remarketing ad aimed at people who visited a site or added to cart but didn't buy.
prompts.prompt: Write a retargeting ad aimed at people who viewed a product or added it to cart but didn't purchase. Address the likely hesitation directly (price, trust, or indecision), include a nudge like a limited-time incentive if one exists, and keep the tone helpful rather than pushy. Provide a headline, one line of body copy, and a call to action. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Product: [PRODUCT] Likely reason for hesitation: [REASON, e.g., price, shipping cost, comparing options] Incentive available, if any: [INCENTIVE, e.g., free shipping, 10% off, or none]
prompts.proTip: If there's no discount to offer, ask the AI to lean on trust signals (reviews, guarantees) instead of manufacturing fake urgency.
fields: REASON, e.g., price, shipping cost, comparing options
INCENTIVE, e.g., free shipping, 10% off, or none

prompts.title: Script: 15-Second Video Ad Script
prompts.useWhen: You need a short-form video ad script for TikTok, Reels, or YouTube Shorts and want a tight, scroll-stopping structure.
prompts.prompt: Write a 15-second video ad script for the product below. Structure it as: a hook in the first 3 seconds that stops the scroll, a quick problem/solution beat, and a clear call to action at the end. Write it as a simple two-column script with "VISUAL" and "VOICEOVER/TEXT" side by side so it's easy to hand to whoever is filming or editing. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Product or service: [PRODUCT] Hook angle to use: [ANGLE, e.g., relatable problem, bold claim, surprising stat] Platform: [PLATFORM, e.g., TikTok, Instagram Reels]
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 different hook lines for the same script so you can film one version and swap just the opening for quick A/B testing.
fields: ANGLE, e.g., relatable problem, bold claim, surprising stat

prompts.title: Ad Copy: Seasonal or Holiday Promotion Across 3 Platforms
prompts.useWhen: You need to adapt one seasonal promotion into ad copy for multiple platforms at once instead of writing each one separately.
prompts.prompt: Take this seasonal promotion and write platform-specific ad copy for Google Search, Facebook/ Instagram, and email subject lines. Keep the core offer identical across all three, but adjust the tone, length, and format to fit each platform's norms (short and direct for Google, more visual/emotional for Meta, curiosity-driven for the email subject line). Output as three clearly labeled sections. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Holiday or season: [HOLIDAY/SEASON] Offer: [OFFER] End date of promotion: [DATE]
prompts.proTip: Batch this at the start of the season for every major holiday your client runs promotions for, so you're never scrambling the week before.

prompts.title: Headlines: A/B Test Variations for an Underperforming Ad
prompts.useWhen: An existing ad's click-through rate has dropped or stalled and you need fresh headline variations to test against it.
prompts.prompt: Here is an ad that's underperforming. Write 5 new headline variations that keep the same core offer but change the angle: try one that leads with a number or stat, one that asks a question, one that names the specific audience, one that creates urgency, and one that leads with a customer outcome. Flag which existing element (if any) might be causing fatigue. Current headline: [PASTE CURRENT HEADLINE] Current performance note: [E.g., "CTR dropped 30% over 2 weeks"] Offer: [OFFER] Audience: [AUDIENCE]
prompts.proTip: Ad fatigue is often the real problem, not the copy. If a new angle doesn't help within a week, consider that the audience needs to grow, not the headline to change again.

prompts.title: Ad Copy: Local Service Ad for a Location-Based Business
prompts.useWhen: You're writing ad copy for a local business (a dentist, contractor, gym, restaurant) where location and trust matter more than a broad national pitch.
prompts.prompt: Write a local service ad for the business below. Lead with the neighborhood or city name to signal relevance, include a trust element (years in business, review count, or licensing/certification), and end with a low-friction call to action suited to local intent, like "Call Now" or "Get Directions." Keep it under 100 words and avoid sounding like a national chain ad. Business name: [BUSINESS NAME] City or neighborhood: [LOCATION] Service: [SERVICE] Trust element: [TRUST ELEMENT, e.g., "15 years in business," "500+ 5-star reviews"]
prompts.proTip: Always double-check that any claim about reviews, licensing, or awards is current and accurate before it goes live. Local ads get reported for false claims more than people expect. Social Media & Content Marketing

prompts.title: Post: Month of Instagram Captions From One Client Brief
prompts.useWhen: You need to fill out a content calendar fast and want a batch of captions instead of writing them one post at a time.
prompts.prompt: Using the client info below, write 12 Instagram captions for one month of posts (about 3 per week). Vary the post type across the set: include a mix of educational tips, behind-the-scenes, customer proof, and promotional posts. Each caption should be 2-4 sentences, end with a call to action or question to drive comments, and include 3-5 relevant hashtag suggestions. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Industry: [INDUSTRY] Brand voice: [VOICE, e.g., playful, professional, warm] Current promotion or focus, if any: [PROMOTION OR TOPIC]
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to label each caption by post type (educational, BTS, proof, promo) so you can quickly check the mix isn't too promotional.

prompts.title: Post: LinkedIn Thought-Leadership Post for a Client Executive
prompts.useWhen: A client's founder or executive wants to post on LinkedIn to build their personal brand but doesn't have time to write it themselves.
prompts.prompt: Write a LinkedIn post in the voice of a company executive sharing a professional opinion or lesson learned. Open with a strong first line that works even if the post gets cut off ("see more"), tell a brief, specific story or observation rather than generic advice, and end with a question that invites comments. Write in first person, 150-200 words, no corporate jargon. Executive name and title: [NAME, TITLE] Industry: [INDUSTRY] Topic or lesson to share: [TOPIC] Specific example or story detail to include: [DETAIL]
prompts.proTip: Feed the AI a few of the executive's past posts or even a voice memo transcript so the writing sounds like them, not like a generic LinkedIn influencer.

prompts.title: Plan: Content Calendar Themes for a Client's Industry
prompts.useWhen: You're planning next month's content and need theme ideas before you can fill in specific posts.
prompts.prompt: Create a monthly content theme plan for a client in the [INDUSTRY] industry. Give me 4 weekly themes that connect to their business goals, and under each theme, list 3 content angle ideas (not full posts, just ideas) that could work across social media, email, or blog. Include any relevant awareness days or seasonal moments that month worth tying content to. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Industry: [INDUSTRY] Month: [MONTH] Business goal this content should support: [GOAL, e.g., drive bookings, build trust, launch a product]
prompts.proTip: Once themes are approved, feed them back into Prompt #28 to generate the actual captions for each theme.
fields: GOAL, e.g., drive bookings, build trust, launch a product

prompts.title: Post: Turning a Client Case Study Into 5 Social Posts
prompts.useWhen: You have a great client result or testimonial and want to squeeze more content out of it instead of posting it once and moving on.
prompts.prompt: Turn this case study or client result into 5 different social media posts, each highlighting a different angle: the specific number/result, the emotional before-and-after, the process behind the result, a direct quote treatment, and a "lesson other customers can apply" angle. Keep each post platformneutral in length (under 100 words) so it can be adapted to Instagram, LinkedIn, or Facebook. Case study or result summary: [PASTE SUMMARY OR KEY DETAILS] Client/customer name (or "a client" if anonymous): [NAME OR "a client"] Specific metric or result: [METRIC]
prompts.proTip: One good case study can realistically fuel content for 2-3 weeks. Don't post it once and let it die, run this prompt every time you land a strong result.

prompts.title: Script: Short-Form Video Hook Ideas (TikTok/Reels)
prompts.useWhen: You're planning short-form video content and the hardest part is always the first line, so you need hook options before scripting the rest.
prompts.prompt: Write 10 hook lines (the first 1-2 spoken seconds) for a short-form video about the topic below. Vary the style: include a few "wait, what" curiosity hooks, a few direct-benefit hooks, a few relatableproblem hooks, and at least one that's a bold or contrarian statement. Keep each hook under 12 words so it works as on-screen text too. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Video topic: [TOPIC] Target audience: [AUDIENCE]
prompts.proTip: Test hooks by watching the first 2 seconds with the sound off. If it doesn't make sense as on-screen text alone, it's not a strong enough hook yet.

prompts.title: Post: Responding to Comments on a Client's Viral Post
prompts.useWhen: A client's post unexpectedly took off and now there are dozens of comments (good and bad) that need responses fast.
prompts.prompt: Here are comments on a client's social post that's getting more engagement than usual. Group them into categories (questions, compliments, complaints, spam/trolls) and write a suggested reply for each category that matches the brand's voice. Keep replies short, human, and specific enough that they don't look copy-pasted, even though they're templated by category. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Brand voice: [VOICE] Comments to respond to: [PASTE A SAMPLE OF COMMENTS]
prompts.proTip: Never post AI-drafted replies to sensitive complaints without reading them fully first. Use Prompt #72 instead if a comment is really a public complaint that needs careful handling.

prompts.title: Email: Newsletter for a Client's Subscriber List
prompts.useWhen: A client has a monthly or weekly email newsletter that needs writing and you're staring at last month's blank template.
prompts.prompt: Write an email newsletter for the client below. Structure it as: a short personal-feeling opener (2-3 sentences), a main content section (a tip, update, or story related to their business), a secondary section (a product highlight, promotion, or upcoming event), and a clear call to action. Write a subject line and preview text too. Keep the tone conversational, like a note from a real person, not a corporate blast. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Main topic or update this month: [TOPIC] Secondary item to include: [PROMOTION/EVENT/PRODUCT] Brand voice: [VOICE]
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 subject line options and note which type each one is (curiosity, benefit, or personal) so you can track which style gets better open rates over time.

prompts.title: Post: Repurposing a Blog Post Into a Social Carousel
prompts.useWhen: A client has a blog post or long article and you want to turn it into a multi-slide social carousel without starting from scratch.
prompts.prompt: Turn this blog post into a 6-8 slide social media carousel. Slide 1 should be a scroll-stopping title slide, the middle slides should each cover one key point in a short, punchy sentence or two (not full paragraphs), and the final slide should have a call to action. Write the text for each slide clearly labeled "Slide 1," "Slide 2," and so on. Blog post content or summary: [PASTE CONTENT OR SUMMARY] Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Call to action for final slide: [CTA]
prompts.proTip: Keep each slide's text under 20 words. If a slide feels like a paragraph, ask the AI to split it into two slides instead.

prompts.title: Plan: Community Management Response Guidelines for a Client
prompts.useWhen: You're managing a client's social accounts and want a reference guide so anyone on the team can respond to comments and DMs consistently.
prompts.prompt: Create a community management response guide for a client's social media accounts. Include: 3-4 example responses to common positive comments, 3-4 example responses to common questions (pricing, hours, availability), guidance on tone (what to do and avoid), and a clear rule for when a comment or DM should be escalated to a human on the account team instead of answered directly. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Brand voice: [VOICE] Common questions this business gets: [LIST COMMON QUESTIONS] Escalation trigger (e.g., complaints, legal, pricing disputes): [TRIGGER TYPES]
prompts.proTip: Revisit this guide every quarter. New products, promotions, and recurring complaints all change what "common" comments look like. Strategy & Campaign Planning

prompts.title: Plan: 90-Day Marketing Strategy for a New Client
prompts.useWhen: You just signed a new client and need a strategic roadmap for their first quarter, not just a task list.
prompts.prompt: Build a 90-day marketing strategy outline for a new client. Break it into three 30-day phases (Foundation, Momentum, Optimization), and under each phase list 3-4 key priorities and what success looks like at the end of that phase. Tie every priority back to the client's stated goal. Keep it strategic and high-level, this is a roadmap, not a detailed task list. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Industry: [INDUSTRY] Primary goal: [GOAL, e.g., increase leads, grow online sales, build brand awareness] Current marketing state: [CURRENT STATE, e.g., "no paid ads running, weak social presence"]
prompts.proTip: Once this is approved, feed each phase back in separately and ask for a detailed task breakdown with owners and dates.

prompts.title: Plan: Media Mix Recommendation for a Given Budget
prompts.useWhen: A client gives you a budget number and you need to recommend how to split it across channels with reasoning they'll understand.
prompts.prompt: Recommend a media mix for the monthly budget below. Suggest a percentage split across relevant channels (for example: paid search, paid social, email, content/SEO), explain in one sentence why each channel gets that allocation given the client's goal and audience, and flag any channel you'd recommend skipping entirely for now and why. Present as a simple table: Channel, % of Budget, Reason. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Monthly budget: [BUDGET] Primary goal: [GOAL] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Channels already in use, if any: [CURRENT CHANNELS]
prompts.proTip: Always sanity-check the AI's split against real benchmarks for the client's industry before presenting it, budget splits should reflect what's actually worked for similar businesses.

prompts.title: Plan: Product Launch Campaign Timeline
prompts.useWhen: A client is launching a new product or service and needs a marketing timeline built out from announcement to post-launch.
prompts.prompt: Build a marketing campaign timeline for a product launch. Break it into three phases: Pre-Launch (teaser/anticipation building), Launch Day, and Post-Launch (momentum and retargeting). For each phase, list the key activities, which channels they run on, and roughly how many days before or after launch they should happen. Format as a simple timeline table. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Product/service launching: [PRODUCT] Launch date: [DATE] Channels available: [CHANNELS, e.g., email, social, paid ads, PR]
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version that assumes half the budget, in case the client's launch budget ends up smaller than planned.
fields: CHANNELS, e.g., email, social, paid ads, PR

prompts.title: Analysis: Choosing Between Two Campaign Concepts
prompts.useWhen: Your team has two creative or strategic directions for a campaign and needs a clear-eyed comparison before presenting to the client.
prompts.prompt: Compare these two campaign concepts and help me think through which one better serves the client's goal. For each concept, list the strengths, the risks, and what type of audience or moment it would work best for. Then give a recommendation with reasoning, but note that the final call depends on factors only the team knows, like client risk tolerance or brand history. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Goal this campaign should achieve: [GOAL] Concept A: [DESCRIBE CONCEPT A] Concept B: [DESCRIBE CONCEPT B]
prompts.proTip: Use this as a thinking tool before the client meeting, not as the final answer. It's meant to sharpen your own reasoning, not replace it.

prompts.title: Plan: Audience Segmentation for a Client's Target Market
prompts.useWhen: A client says "everyone is my customer" and you need to help them (and your campaign) get more specific.
prompts.prompt: Based on the information below, break this client's broad target market into 3 distinct audience segments. For each segment, describe their key characteristics, their main motivation for buying, and one messaging angle that would resonate specifically with them. Keep descriptions grounded in the info given, don't invent demographic details that weren't provided. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Product/service: [PRODUCT] What the client currently says about their audience: [CURRENT AUDIENCE DESCRIPTION] Any customer data or notes available: [DATA OR NOTES, IF ANY]
prompts.proTip: If the client has real customer data (surveys, purchase history, reviews), always feed that in. Segments built on real signals beat segments built on assumptions every time.

prompts.title: Plan: Budget Reallocation After Mid-Campaign Results
prompts.useWhen: A campaign is halfway through and some channels or ads are clearly outperforming others, and you need to recommend shifting spend.
prompts.prompt: Based on the mid-campaign performance below, recommend how to reallocate the remaining budget. Identify which channels or ads are outperforming and underperforming, suggest a specific new percentage split for the rest of the campaign, and explain the reasoning in language a non- technical client would understand. Flag anything you'd want more data on before making a bigger shift. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Original budget split: [ORIGINAL SPLIT] Remaining budget: [AMOUNT] Performance so far by channel: [PASTE PERFORMANCE DATA]
prompts.proTip: Wait for statistically meaningful data before reallocating. A channel that's "underperforming" after 3 days of spend might just need more time.

prompts.title: Plan: Seasonal Campaign Calendar for a Retail Client
prompts.useWhen: A retail or seasonal-business client needs a full year (or quarter) of campaign moments planned out at once.
prompts.prompt: Build a seasonal campaign calendar for a retail client covering [TIMEFRAME]. List the key sales moments and seasonal opportunities relevant to their business, and for each one note: the approximate date range, a suggested campaign theme, and which channels it should run on. Prioritize moments that actually fit this specific business, not every generic retail holiday. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Industry/product category: [INDUSTRY] Timeframe: [TIMEFRAME, e.g., Q4, full year] Channels available: [CHANNELS]
prompts.proTip: Cross-check any dates the AI suggests (holidays, awareness days) against a real calendar. Date accuracy is one thing worth verifying yourself every time.

prompts.title: Analysis: Setting Realistic KPIs for a New Campaign
prompts.useWhen: A client wants specific performance targets before a campaign launches and you need numbers grounded in reality, not guesses.
prompts.prompt: Help me set realistic KPI targets for a new campaign. Based on the details below, suggest a reasonable target range (not a single exact number) for the primary metric, explain what factors could push results toward the high or low end of that range, and suggest one leading indicator we can check early to see if we're on track before the final result is in. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign type: [CAMPAIGN TYPE] Budget: [BUDGET] Primary metric to set a target for: [METRIC, e.g., cost per lead, ROAS] Any past performance data available: [PAST DATA, IF ANY]
prompts.proTip: Present KPI targets as a range, not a single number, to the client. It sets more honest expectations and protects you if results land on the lower end.
fields: METRIC, e.g., cost per lead, ROAS

prompts.title: Plan: Multi-Channel Campaign Brief for the Creative Team
prompts.useWhen: Strategy is locked and now you need to brief your internal creative or design team so they can start building assets.
prompts.prompt: Turn this campaign strategy into a creative brief for our internal design and content team. Include: campaign objective, target audience in one sentence, key message, tone/mood direction, list of deliverables needed by channel, and any mandatory elements (logo usage, legal disclaimers, brand colors). Keep it tight and actionable, this should save the creative team from having to ask clarifying questions. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign objective: [OBJECTIVE] Key message: [MESSAGE] Deliverables needed: [LIST, e.g., 3 static ads, 1 video, 2 email banners] Mandatory brand elements: [ELEMENTS]
prompts.proTip: A good brief prevents most revision rounds. Spend the extra 5 minutes filling in every field rather than leaving "TBD" for the creative team to guess at. Research & Competitive Analysis
fields: LIST, e.g., 3 static ads, 1 video, 2 email banners

prompts.title: Analysis: Competitor Ad Strategy Teardown
prompts.useWhen: You want to break down what a competitor is doing in their ads before building a client's own campaign strategy.
prompts.prompt: Analyze the competitor ads described below and give me a teardown. Identify the likely target audience for each ad, the core message or hook being used, the offer or call to action, and one thing our client's ads could do differently to stand out. Organize the output by ad, then end with a short summary of the overall pattern across all of them. Competitor name: [COMPETITOR NAME] Ads to analyze (paste copy, describe visuals, or summarize): [PASTE OR DESCRIBE ADS] Our client's business: [CLIENT NAME/BUSINESS]
prompts.proTip: Screenshot competitor ads from the Meta Ad Library or Google Ads Transparency Center and describe what you see in detail, the more specific your input, the sharper the teardown.

prompts.title: Research: Industry Trends Brief for a Client Kickoff
prompts.useWhen: You're onboarding a new client and want to show up to the first strategy meeting with a sharp view of their industry.
prompts.prompt: Based on what's publicly known and commonly discussed about the [INDUSTRY] industry, put together a brief covering: 3 current trends affecting businesses like this one, 2 common challenges businesses in this space are facing, and 2 opportunities a business could capitalize on right now. Keep it practical and specific to this business size and type, not a generic industry overview. Industry: [INDUSTRY] Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Business size or context: [SIZE/CONTEXT, e.g., "local, 2 locations, 10 employees"]
prompts.proTip: Treat this as a starting hypothesis to validate, not a finished fact sheet. Confirm anything specific with a quick web search before presenting it as current.

prompts.title: Analysis: SWOT for a Client Entering a New Market
prompts.useWhen: A client is expanding into a new market, product line, or geography and wants a strategic gut-check before committing budget.
prompts.prompt: Create a SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) for this client entering a new market. Base the strengths and weaknesses on their existing business, and base the opportunities and threats on the new market itself. Keep each section to 3-4 specific bullet points, avoid generic statements that could apply to any business entering any market. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Existing business and strengths: [CURRENT BUSINESS DETAILS] New market or segment being entered: [NEW MARKET]
prompts.proTip: Ask a follow-up question: "Given this SWOT, what are the 3 highest-priority marketing actions for the first 60 days?" to turn the analysis into next steps.

prompts.title: Research: Target Audience Persona From Client Notes
prompts.useWhen: You have scattered notes about a client's customers and need them organized into a usable persona document.
prompts.prompt: Turn these notes into a clear target audience persona for a marketing campaign. Organize it into: demographics/firmographics, goals and motivations, pain points and objections, where they spend time online, and the message that would resonate most with them. Keep it grounded strictly in the notes provided, do not invent details that weren't mentioned. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Raw notes about the audience: [PASTE NOTES, SURVEY RESULTS, OR OBSERVATIONS]
prompts.proTip: If you're inventing details because real data is thin, label them clearly as "assumption to validate" so the client knows what's confirmed versus a working guess.
fields: PASTE NOTES, SURVEY RESULTS, OR OBSERVATIONS

prompts.title: Analysis: Competitor Social Media Content Comparison
prompts.useWhen: You want to see how a client's social content compares to competitors before recommending changes to their content strategy.
prompts.prompt: Compare the social media approach of our client against the competitors listed below. For each, note their apparent posting frequency, content mix (educational, promotional, entertainment, etc.), and one thing they do well. End with 3 specific recommendations for how our client's content could differentiate or improve based on this comparison. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Client's current content approach: [DESCRIBE CURRENT APPROACH] Competitor 1: [NAME AND WHAT THEY POST] Competitor 2: [NAME AND WHAT THEY POST]
prompts.proTip: Pull actual recent post examples from competitor profiles rather than describing them from memory. Specific input produces specific, usable recommendations.

prompts.title: Research: Keyword and Messaging Angles Competitors Are Missing
prompts.useWhen: You want to find a messaging gap or content angle competitors haven't claimed, instead of copying what everyone else is already saying.
prompts.prompt: Based on the competitor messaging below, identify 5 messaging angles or topics that none of them seem to be using, but that would likely matter to their shared target audience. For each gap, briefly explain why it could work as a differentiator for our client. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Competitor messaging observed: [LIST WHAT COMPETITORS ARE SAYING/CLAIMING]
prompts.proTip: The best gaps are usually about a customer worry nobody is addressing out loud, not a clever slogan. Look for what audiences complain about in reviews that competitors never mention.

prompts.title: Analysis: Pricing Comparison Against Three Competitors
prompts.useWhen: A client wants to know how their pricing stacks up before you build messaging around value or price positioning.
prompts.prompt: Compare our client's pricing against the three competitors below. Present it as a simple table, then write 2-3 sentences on where our client sits in the market (premium, mid-market, budget) and one suggestion for how to message price in marketing based on that position, whether that's leading with value, leading with premium quality, or avoiding price mentions entirely. Client/business name and price: [CLIENT NAME AND PRICE] Competitor 1 name and price: [NAME AND PRICE] Competitor 2 name and price: [NAME AND PRICE] Competitor 3 name and price: [NAME AND PRICE]
prompts.proTip: Make sure you're comparing like-for-like offers (same tier, same included features), a pricing table that compares apples to oranges will lead to the wrong positioning advice.

prompts.title: Research: Summarizing a Client's Customer Reviews for Insights
prompts.useWhen: A client has a pile of Google, Yelp, or Amazon reviews and you want the marketing-relevant patterns pulled out, not just a sentiment score.
prompts.prompt: Read through these customer reviews and summarize the patterns. Identify: the 3 most common things customers praise, the 3 most common complaints or concerns, and any recurring phrases customers use that could be reused in marketing copy because they sound authentic. Keep quotes exact, don't paraphrase things customers actually said. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Reviews to analyze: [PASTE A SAMPLE OF REVIEWS, 10-20 IS PLENTY]
prompts.proTip: The exact phrases customers use in reviews often make the best headlines and ad copy because they sound like a real person, not a marketer.
fields: PASTE A SAMPLE OF REVIEWS, 10-20 IS PLENTY

prompts.title: Analysis: Identifying a Client's Unique Selling Proposition
prompts.useWhen: A client can't clearly articulate what makes them different, and you need a sharper unique selling proposition (USP) before you can write any effective marketing.
prompts.prompt: Based on the information below, help me identify a clear, specific unique selling proposition for this client. Give me 3 candidate USP statements, each one sentence long, and briefly explain the reasoning behind each. Avoid vague phrases like "quality service" or "customer first," push for something specific and provable. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] What they offer: [OFFER/PRODUCT] What competitors typically claim: [COMPETITOR CLAIMS] What customers specifically say they like: [CUSTOMER FEEDBACK, IF KNOWN]
prompts.proTip: Test candidate USPs by asking "could a competitor honestly claim this too?" If yes, it's not specific enough yet. Reporting & Performance Analysis

prompts.title: Report: Monthly Performance Report Summary in Plain English
prompts.useWhen: You have raw campaign numbers and need to turn them into a client-friendly summary instead of a spreadsheet dump.
prompts.prompt: Turn this month's raw performance data into a plain-English summary for a client who isn't a marketing expert. Structure it as: a one-sentence headline takeaway, 3 key metrics with what changed and why it matters, one thing that's working well, and one area to watch. Avoid jargon like "CPA" or "CTR" without explaining what it means in context. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Raw data: [PASTE METRICS, e.g., spend, clicks, conversions, cost per result] Comparison period: [E.g., "vs. last month"]
prompts.proTip: Always lead with the headline takeaway. Busy clients often only read the first line, make it count.

prompts.title: Analysis: Explaining a Drop in Ad Performance
prompts.useWhen: A specific metric tanked and you need to investigate possible causes before you can explain it to anyone.
prompts.prompt: Here's data showing a drop in [METRIC] for this campaign. Walk through the most likely explanations in order of probability (things like seasonality, audience fatigue, increased competition, budget or bid changes, tracking issues), and for each one suggest a quick way to check if that's actually the cause. End with your best guess at the top 1-2 likely reasons. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Metric that dropped: [METRIC] Data or context: [PASTE RELEVANT DATA, e.g., timeframe, recent changes made]
prompts.proTip: Always check for a tracking or pixel issue first. A surprising number of "performance drops" turn out to be a broken tracking tag, not a real decline.
fields: PASTE RELEVANT DATA, e.g., timeframe, recent changes made

prompts.title: Report: Quarterly Business Review Talking Points
prompts.useWhen: You have a quarterly business review (QBR) coming up and need to prep talking points that go beyond just reading the slides.
prompts.prompt: Create talking points for a quarterly business review with this client. For each major metric or initiative, give me a one-sentence summary of what happened, why, and what we're doing about it next quarter. Then suggest 2 strategic questions to ask the client about their business priorities for the upcoming quarter, so the meeting feels like a partnership conversation, not just a report-out. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Key metrics/initiatives this quarter: [LIST METRICS AND RESULTS] Upcoming quarter's known priorities, if any: [PRIORITIES]
prompts.proTip: Save the strategic questions for the end of the meeting. Leading with numbers first builds credibility before you ask the client to think bigger-picture.

prompts.title: Analysis: Turning Raw Campaign Data Into 3 Key Insights
prompts.useWhen: You're staring at a spreadsheet of numbers and need to find the story in the data before you can report on it.
prompts.prompt: Look at this raw campaign data and pull out the 3 most important insights, not just a restatement of the numbers. For each insight, state what the data shows, why it matters for this client's goals, and one recommended action based on it. Prioritize insights that would actually change what we do next, not just interesting trivia. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Client's primary goal: [GOAL] Raw data: [PASTE DATA]
prompts.proTip: If the AI's insights feel obvious or generic, ask it to dig one level deeper: "what's the insight behind that insight?"

prompts.title: Report: Comparing This Month to Last Month for a Client
prompts.useWhen: You need a simple month-over-month comparison for a report or update and want the framing done for you, not just a table of numbers.
prompts.prompt: Compare this month's performance to last month's using the data below. For each metric, state the percent change and whether that's a good, neutral, or concerning result given the client's goals, not just whether the number went up or down. Write it as a short narrative paragraph, not a bullet list of numbers. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] This month's data: [PASTE DATA] Last month's data: [PASTE DATA] Client's primary goal: [GOAL]
prompts.proTip: A metric going up isn't automatically good news, and going down isn't automatically bad. Always tie the interpretation back to what the client is actually trying to achieve.

prompts.title: Analysis: ROI Summary for a Client's Marketing Spend
prompts.useWhen: A client (or their boss, or their accountant) wants a clear answer on whether the marketing spend is paying off.
prompts.prompt: Using the numbers below, write a plain-language return-on-investment summary for this client's marketing spend over the period given. Show the math simply (spend, revenue attributed, and the resulting return), note any assumptions or limitations in how that revenue was attributed, and give one honest sentence on whether this is a strong, average, or weak return for a business like this. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Time period: [PERIOD] Total marketing spend: [SPEND] Revenue attributed to marketing: [REVENUE] Attribution method used, if known: [METHOD, e.g., last-click, platform-reported]
prompts.proTip: Always disclose the attribution method. Different tracking methods can make the same campaign look wildly different, transparency here builds long-term trust.

prompts.title: Report: Year-End Recap Deck Talking Points
prompts.useWhen: You're building a year-in-review presentation for a client and need the narrative arc, not just a list of monthly stats.
prompts.prompt: Create talking points for a year-end recap presentation for this client. Structure it as: the year's overall story in 2-3 sentences, the top 3 wins with their supporting numbers, one honest challenge and what was learned from it, and a forward-looking close connecting this year's results to next year's plan. Make it feel like a narrative, not a data dump. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Top results this year: [LIST TOP RESULTS/NUMBERS] A challenge faced this year: [CHALLENGE] Direction for next year: [NEXT YEAR PLAN OR FOCUS]
prompts.proTip: Including one honest challenge (framed constructively) makes the wins more believable. An all-wins recap can come across as less credible to a skeptical client.

prompts.title: Analysis: Diagnosing Why Leads Aren't Converting to Sales
prompts.useWhen: A campaign is generating leads or traffic, but the client says those leads aren't turning into paying customers, and you need to figure out where the funnel breaks.
prompts.prompt: This client is getting leads from our campaigns, but few are converting to sales. Based on the funnel details below, walk through the most likely points of breakdown (lead quality, follow-up speed, sales process, offer mismatch, pricing objections) and suggest what data or questions would help confirm which one is the real issue. Note this may not be a marketing problem at all. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Funnel stage details: [DESCRIBE FUNNEL, e.g., "ad -> landing page -> phone call -> close"] Lead volume and current conversion rate: [NUMBERS] What the client has said about the leads: [CLIENT'S FEEDBACK]
prompts.proTip: Sit in on (or ask for a recording of) a sales call with a marketing-generated lead before assuming the campaign is the problem. Often the gap is in follow-up speed or the sales pitch, not the ad.

prompts.title: Report: Dashboard Walkthrough Script for a Client Call
prompts.useWhen: You're about to screen-share a reporting dashboard on a client call and want a script so you don't just read numbers off the screen.
prompts.prompt: Write a short script for walking a client through their performance dashboard on a live call. For each key metric on the dashboard, give me one sentence explaining what it means in plain terms and one sentence on why it matters to their business specifically, not a generic definition. End with a transition line into discussing next steps. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Metrics shown on the dashboard: [LIST METRICS] Client's primary business goal: [GOAL]
prompts.proTip: Practice explaining the dashboard without looking at notes first. If you can't explain a metric simply out loud, that's often a sign it doesn't belong on this client's dashboard. Difficult Conversations & Objection Handling

prompts.title: Response: Handling a Client Who Wants to Cut the Budget
prompts.useWhen: A client tells you they want to reduce their marketing spend or budget, and you need a thoughtful response instead of just accepting it or arguing.
prompts.prompt: A client wants to cut their marketing budget by [PERCENT/AMOUNT]. Write a response that acknowledges their reasoning without being defensive, explains honestly what impact this reduction is likely to have on results, and offers 1-2 alternative options (like reallocating instead of cutting, or a phased reduction) so they don't feel boxed into an all-or-nothing decision. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Requested budget cut: [PERCENT OR AMOUNT] Likely impact of the cut: [IMPACT, e.g., "fewer leads, longer time to hit goals"] Alternative option to offer: [ALTERNATIVE, e.g., pause one channel instead of all]
prompts.proTip: Never guilt a client for wanting to cut spend, budgets change for real business reasons. Focus the conversation on trade-offs, not loyalty.
fields: IMPACT, e.g., "fewer leads, longer time to hit goals"
ALTERNATIVE, e.g., pause one channel instead of all

prompts.title: Response: Addressing Scope Creep Without Damaging the Relationship
prompts.useWhen: A client keeps asking for extra work outside the contract, sometimes called scope creep, and you need to draw a line without sounding petty.
prompts.prompt: A client keeps requesting work outside our agreed scope. Write a response that's warm but clear: acknowledge the request has value, explain that it falls outside the current scope of work, and offer a path forward, either adding it as a paid add-on or revisiting it at the next contract renewal. Avoid sounding like you're punishing them for asking. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Out-of-scope request: [REQUEST] Current scope/contract summary: [SCOPE SUMMARY] Option to offer: [OPTION, e.g., "add-on for $X" or "include in next renewal"]
prompts.proTip: Address scope creep the first time it happens, not the fifth. Each unaddressed instance makes the eventual conversation harder, not easier.
fields: OPTION, e.g., "add-on for $X" or "include in next renewal"

prompts.title: Response: Responding to "We're Thinking of Leaving the Agency"
prompts.useWhen: A client hints they're considering ending the relationship or moving to another agency, and you need to respond thoughtfully, not defensively.
prompts.prompt: A client has indicated they're considering ending our engagement or moving to another agency. Write a response that takes the concern seriously without being desperate or overly apologetic, asks a genuine, specific question to understand the real reason behind it, and offers one concrete next step (like a call to discuss, or a specific fix) rather than a vague "let's talk." Client name: [CLIENT NAME] What they said or signaled: [WHAT THEY SAID] Relationship history/context: [CONTEXT, e.g., "3 years, recent results dip"]
prompts.proTip: Resist the urge to immediately offer a discount. Understand the real reason first, price is rarely the actual issue when a client talks about leaving.
fields: CONTEXT, e.g., "3 years, recent results dip"

prompts.title: Response: Explaining Why Results Take Time to a New Client
prompts.useWhen: A newer client is getting impatient early in the engagement and needs a clear, honest explanation of realistic timelines.
prompts.prompt: A relatively new client is asking why they haven't seen bigger results yet. Write a response that sets realistic expectations for this type of campaign without sounding like an excuse. Explain what typically happens in this timeframe for campaigns like theirs, share one early positive signal if one exists, and give a specific date or milestone when they can expect a clearer picture. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign/service type: [TYPE] Time live so far: [TIMEFRAME] Early positive signal, if any: [SIGNAL OR "none yet"] Milestone/checkpoint date: [DATE]
prompts.proTip: This conversation is much easier if you set timeline expectations clearly during onboarding. Use Prompt #3 to build that expectation-setting in from day one.

prompts.title: Response: Handling a Client Comparing You to a Cheaper Competitor
prompts.useWhen: A client mentions a cheaper agency or freelancer they're considering instead, and you need to respond without trashing the competitor or sounding defensive about price.
prompts.prompt: A client mentioned a cheaper option they're considering instead of our agency. Write a response that doesn't criticize the other option, reframes the conversation around value and outcomes rather than price alone, and asks a clarifying question to understand what's driving the price concern (budget pressure, doubting ROI, or something else). Keep the tone confident, not anxious. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Our differentiator/value point: [VALUE POINT, e.g., dedicated account manager, proven results] What the client said about the cheaper option: [WHAT THEY SAID]
prompts.proTip: If price really is the core issue, it's often more effective to offer a smaller scope at a lower price than to just discount the same scope.
fields: VALUE POINT, e.g., dedicated account manager, proven results

prompts.title: Email: Delivering Bad News About a Missed Deadline
prompts.useWhen: Your team is going to miss a deadline you promised a client, and you need to tell them before they find out on their own.
prompts.prompt: Write an email to a client letting them know a deliverable will be late. Take ownership without overapologizing, give the real reason briefly and honestly, provide a new, realistic delivery date, and mention what's being done to prevent this from happening again if relevant. Keep it under 100 words, direct and professional. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Deliverable that's late: [DELIVERABLE] Original deadline: [DATE] New realistic deadline: [DATE] Reason for delay: [REASON]
prompts.proTip: Send this proactively as soon as you know about the delay. A client who hears it from you first is far more forgiving than one who has to ask where something is.

prompts.title: Response: Pushing Back on a Client's Bad Creative Idea
prompts.useWhen: A client wants to run a creative direction, headline, or campaign idea you genuinely think will hurt their results, and you need to push back professionally.
prompts.prompt: A client wants to move forward with a creative idea I have concerns about. Write a response that respects their input, states the specific concern clearly with reasoning (not just "I don't like it"), and offers an alternative or a way to test both options safely (like a small A/B test) rather than an outright refusal. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Client's proposed idea: [IDEA] Specific concern: [CONCERN, e.g., "likely to feel too salesy for this audience"] Alternative or compromise to suggest: [ALTERNATIVE, e.g., small budget test]
prompts.proTip: Whenever possible, suggest testing instead of blocking. It respects the client's instincts while still protecting them from a costly full-budget mistake.
fields: CONCERN, e.g., "likely to feel too salesy for this audience"

prompts.title: Response: Negotiating a Rate Increase With an Existing Client
prompts.useWhen: You need to raise prices on an existing client relationship and want to do it without triggering churn.
prompts.prompt: Write a message to an existing client announcing a rate increase. Give clear advance notice, explain the reason in a way that's about value delivered or rising costs rather than apologetic, state the new rate and effective date clearly, and reaffirm the value of the relationship without sounding like you're trying too hard to justify it. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Current rate: [CURRENT RATE] New rate: [NEW RATE] Effective date: [DATE] Reason for increase: [REASON, e.g., added services, market rate adjustment]
prompts.proTip: Give at least 30-60 days notice on rate increases. It reads as respectful rather than sprung-on-them, and gives the client time to plan.
fields: REASON, e.g., added services, market rate adjustment

prompts.title: Response: Responding to a Negative Public Review of the Agency
prompts.useWhen: Your agency itself gets a negative public review (Google, Clutch, social media) and needs a professional public response.
prompts.prompt: Write a public response to this negative review about our agency. Acknowledge the concern without being defensive or admitting fault we don't actually have, keep it brief and professional since other potential clients will read this too, and invite the reviewer to continue the conversation privately rather than airing details publicly. Review content: [PASTE REVIEW] Our honest take on what happened: [YOUR SIDE OF THE SITUATION] Contact method to offer: [E.g., "please email us at..."]
prompts.proTip: Never argue details point-by-point in a public reply. Keep the public response short and move the real conversation to a private channel every time. Operations, SOPs & Admin

prompts.title: SOP: Client Onboarding Process Documentation
prompts.useWhen: You want to write down your client onboarding process so it's consistent no matter who on the team runs it.
prompts.prompt: Write a standard operating procedure (SOP) for onboarding a new client at a marketing agency. Format it as a numbered, step-by-step process from contract signed to first deliverable, noting who is responsible for each step (account manager, strategist, designer, etc.) and roughly how many days each step should take. Include a short "common mistakes to avoid" section at the end. Service type: [SERVICE TYPE] Team roles involved: [ROLES, e.g., account manager, strategist, designer] Typical onboarding length: [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 2 weeks]
prompts.proTip: Turn this into a checklist in your project management tool once it's finalized, an SOP that only lives in a document tends to get skipped under deadline pressure.
fields: ROLES, e.g., account manager, strategist, designer

prompts.title: Checklist: Pre-Launch Campaign QA Checklist
prompts.useWhen: A campaign is about to go live and you want a final quality-check pass so nothing embarrassing slips through.
prompts.prompt: Create a pre-launch QA checklist for a [CAMPAIGN TYPE] campaign before it goes live. Cover: creative/copy accuracy (spelling, client name, offer details), tracking setup (pixels, UTM parameters, conversion goals), targeting settings, budget and schedule confirmation, and final client approval. Format as a checkbox list someone can go through in 10 minutes before hitting publish. Campaign type: [CAMPAIGN TYPE, e.g., paid social, email, Google Ads] Platform(s): [PLATFORMS]
prompts.proTip: Make this checklist a required step in your project management workflow before any campaign can be marked "ready to launch." Catching one broken tracking link before launch saves hours of confused reporting later.
fields: CAMPAIGN TYPE, e.g., paid social, email, Google Ads

prompts.title: Email: Internal Handoff Notes Between Account Managers
prompts.useWhen: A client account is being transferred to a new team member and you need clean handoff notes so nothing falls through the cracks.
prompts.prompt: Turn these rough notes into a clean internal handoff document for transferring a client account to a new account manager. Organize it into: client background and key contacts, current status and active projects, known sensitivities or history to be aware of, and immediate priorities for the first two weeks. Keep it factual and useful, not a narrative. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] Raw handoff notes: [PASTE NOTES] New account manager name: [NAME]
prompts.proTip: Include "known sensitivities" honestly, past complaints, pricing history, personality quirks. A handoff document that only shares the good news sets the new person up to repeat old mistakes.

prompts.title: SOP: Creative Approval Workflow for a Client
prompts.useWhen: You want to formalize how creative assets move from your team to client approval so revisions don't spiral out of control.
prompts.prompt: Write a creative approval workflow SOP for how assets move from our design team to client sign-off. Include the steps in order, who reviews at each stage internally before it goes to the client, how many rounds of client revisions are included before additional charges apply, and the format clients should use to give feedback (to avoid vague comments like "make it pop"). Client name/type: [CLIENT NAME OR TYPE] Number of included revision rounds: [NUMBER] Feedback format to request: [FORMAT, e.g., a numbered comment doc]
prompts.proTip: Explicitly stating the number of included revision rounds in writing, and repeating it at the top of every review request, prevents most scope creep arguments before they start.
fields: FORMAT, e.g., a numbered comment doc

prompts.title: Checklist: Monthly Agency Invoicing and Billing Review
prompts.useWhen: It's time to send monthly invoices and you want a checklist to make sure nothing gets billed incorrectly or missed.
prompts.prompt: Create a monthly invoicing checklist for a marketing agency to run through before sending client invoices. Cover: confirming hours or deliverables match the contract, checking for any approved scope changes or add-ons that need billing, verifying ad spend pass-throughs are accurate, and a final review step before sending. Format as a simple checkbox list. Billing structure: [E.g., flat retainer, hourly, retainer plus ad spend pass-through] Number of active clients: [NUMBER]
prompts.proTip: Run this checklist on the same day every month so it becomes a habit instead of a scramble, billing errors are one of the fastest ways to damage client trust.

prompts.title: Plan: Meeting Agenda for a Weekly Team Standup
prompts.useWhen: Your internal team meetings feel unfocused or run long, and you want a tight agenda structure.
prompts.prompt: Create a 15-minute weekly team standup agenda template for a marketing agency team. Structure it around: quick wins from the past week (2 minutes), blockers or items needing help (5 minutes), priorities for this week by person or account (5 minutes), and any announcements (3 minutes). Keep the format simple enough that anyone on the team could run the meeting from it. Team size: [NUMBER] Team roles: [ROLES, e.g., account managers, designers, media buyers]
prompts.proTip: Time-box each section out loud during the meeting. Standups drift long when "quick wins" quietly becomes a 20-minute status report.
fields: ROLES, e.g., account managers, designers, media buyers

prompts.title: SOP: New Employee Onboarding for an Account Coordinator
prompts.useWhen: You're hiring or training a new account coordinator and want a structured first-30-days plan instead of throwing them in unprepared.
prompts.prompt: Create a 30-day onboarding plan for a new account coordinator at a marketing agency. Break it into Week 1 (orientation and shadowing), Week 2 (supported tasks with review), Week 3-4 (increasing independence), listing specific activities and what "ready to move to the next stage" looks like at each point. Agency size/type: [SIZE/TYPE] Tools the coordinator will use: [TOOLS, e.g., project management software, ad platforms] Key skills to develop: [SKILLS, e.g., client communication, reporting, scheduling]
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version formatted as a checklist their manager can literally check off week by week, it turns a vague plan into an accountable one.
fields: TOOLS, e.g., project management software, ad platforms
SKILLS, e.g., client communication, reporting, scheduling
