prompts.title: Email: Vendor or Freelancer Brief for a Project
prompts.useWhen: You're bringing in a freelancer or outside vendor (a videographer, translator, specialist) and need to brief them clearly and fast.
prompts.prompt: Write a project brief email for a freelancer or vendor joining a client project. Include: the project scope and deliverables expected, the deadline, the client's brand guidelines or tone requirements, who to contact with questions, and the approval process before anything is considered final. Keep it clear enough that a stranger to the account could execute without back-and-forth. Freelancer/vendor role: [ROLE, e.g., videographer, copywriter, translator] Project scope: [SCOPE] Deadline: [DEADLINE] Point of contact: [NAME]
prompts.proTip: Always specify the approval process and who has final sign-off. Vague briefs to outside vendors are the number one cause of expensive, unusable deliverables.

prompts.title: Checklist: Client Offboarding Process
prompts.useWhen: A client relationship is ending, whether by their choice or yours, and you want to close it out professionally and completely.
prompts.prompt: Create a client offboarding checklist for when an engagement ends. Cover: transferring account access and assets back to the client (ad accounts, logins, files), a final performance summary to send, internal steps to stop billing and archive the account, and a professional closing message. Format as a checkbox list a departing account manager can follow without missing a step. Services provided: [SERVICES] Assets/access to transfer: [LIST, e.g., ad account admin, Google Analytics, design files]
prompts.proTip: Even when a client leaves on bad terms, a clean, professional offboarding is often what determines whether they refer you to someone else later. Agency-Specific & Specialized Tasks
fields: LIST, e.g., ad account admin, Google Analytics, design files

prompts.title: Brief: Creative Brief for the Design Team
prompts.useWhen: You need to hand off a project to your design team and want to make sure they have everything they need in one document.
prompts.prompt: Write a creative brief for our design team for the project below. Include: project objective, target audience in one sentence, key message, tone/style direction, specific deliverables and sizes/formats needed, deadline, and any brand guidelines or must-include elements. Keep it structured so a designer could start work immediately without needing a follow-up call. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Project: [PROJECT, e.g., "3 static ads for spring promotion"] Deadline: [DEADLINE] Brand guidelines/must-includes: [GUIDELINES]
prompts.proTip: Attach 1-2 examples of creative the client has liked in the past. Visual references communicate tone faster than written descriptions ever will.
fields: PROJECT, e.g., "3 static ads for spring promotion"

prompts.title: Brief: Media Buy Brief for Paid Media Team
prompts.useWhen: Strategy is set and you need to hand off targeting, budget, and platform details to whoever is actually building the ad campaigns.
prompts.prompt: Write a media buy brief for our paid media team to build out this campaign. Include: campaign objective, total budget and flight dates, platform(s) to use, audience targeting parameters, and the primary metric we're optimizing toward. Format it so someone could build the campaign in-platform directly from this brief without needing clarification. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Objective: [OBJECTIVE] Budget and dates: [BUDGET AND DATES] Platforms: [PLATFORMS] Target audience: [AUDIENCE]
prompts.proTip: Always specify the single primary metric to optimize toward. A media buyer optimizing for clicks builds a very different campaign than one optimizing for purchases.

prompts.title: Plan: Influencer Outreach List Criteria for a Campaign
prompts.useWhen: A client wants to try influencer marketing and you need to define what "the right influencer" actually means before searching.
prompts.prompt: Define the ideal influencer profile for this campaign. Give me criteria across: follower range, content style/niche, audience demographics that should match our target customer, and 2-3 engagement red flags to screen out (like heavy follower purchasing signs or audience mismatch). Then suggest 3 search terms or hashtags we could use to start finding candidates manually. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign goal: [GOAL, e.g., product awareness, direct sales] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Budget range per influencer: [BUDGET RANGE]
prompts.proTip: Engagement rate matters more than follower count. An influencer with 10,000 highly engaged followers in your niche usually outperforms one with 100,000 disengaged ones.
fields: GOAL, e.g., product awareness, direct sales

prompts.title: Analysis: Choosing the Right Platform Mix for a New Client's Budget
prompts.useWhen: A new client asks "where should we even advertise" and you need a clear, reasoned recommendation instead of defaulting to whatever's trendy.
prompts.prompt: Recommend which advertising platforms this client should start with given their budget and goals. Rank the top 3 platform options in priority order, and for each one explain in plain terms why it fits (or doesn't fully fit) their budget, audience, and goal. Be honest if the budget is too small to run an effective campaign on a platform, rather than recommending it anyway. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Monthly budget: [BUDGET] Goal: [GOAL] Target audience: [AUDIENCE] Platforms client is curious about, if any: [PLATFORMS MENTIONED]
prompts.proTip: If the client's budget is genuinely too small for a platform to work well (a common issue with tiny budgets on paid social), say so directly rather than taking the budget and hoping.

prompts.title: Plan: Crisis Communication Response for a Client PR Issue
prompts.useWhen: A client is facing a PR issue (a bad viral moment, a product problem, an internal scandal going public) and needs a fast, careful communication plan.
prompts.prompt: Help draft an initial crisis communication response plan for the situation below. Include: a holding statement that can go out immediately while more facts are gathered, guidance on which channels to respond on versus stay quiet on for now, and 2-3 things to explicitly avoid saying until more is known. Keep tone calm, accountable, and non-defensive. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Situation summary: [DESCRIBE SITUATION] Channels where it's being discussed: [CHANNELS, e.g., Twitter/X, local news, Reddit]
prompts.proTip: For any real crisis involving legal, safety, or major reputational risk, always loop in the client's legal counsel before anything public goes out. This prompt is a starting draft, not a substitute for that review.
fields: CHANNELS, e.g., Twitter/X, local news, Reddit

prompts.title: Brief: SEO Content Brief for a Freelance Writer
prompts.useWhen: You're outsourcing a blog post or article and want to brief a freelance writer so the content is usable without three rounds of edits.
prompts.prompt: Write a content brief for a freelance writer creating an SEO blog post. Include: target keyword and 2-3 related terms to work in naturally, target word count, the search intent behind the keyword (what the reader actually wants), a suggested outline with headers, and the client's tone of voice. Note that keyword usage should sound natural, not stuffed. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Target keyword: [KEYWORD] Target word count: [WORD COUNT] Tone of voice: [TONE]
prompts.proTip: Always tell the writer what the reader wants to accomplish by searching that term, not just the keyword itself. Content written to intent ranks and converts better than content written to a keyword alone.

prompts.title: Plan: Email Automation Flow Outline for a Client
prompts.useWhen: A client wants an automated email sequence (welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase) and you need the structure before writing individual emails.
prompts.prompt: Outline an automated email flow for the scenario below. List each email in the sequence with its send timing (e.g., "immediately," "day 3," "day 7"), the goal of that specific email, and a one-sentence summary of what it should say. Keep the sequence to 4-6 emails so it's realistic to build and maintain. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Flow type: [TYPE, e.g., welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase] Product/service: [PRODUCT] Primary goal of the flow: [GOAL]
prompts.proTip: Once the outline is approved, run each email individually through Prompt #34's structure to write the full copy for each one.
fields: TYPE, e.g., welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase

prompts.title: Analysis: Attribution Model Explanation for a Client
prompts.useWhen: A client is confused about why different platforms report different numbers for the same campaign, and you need to explain attribution simply.
prompts.prompt: Explain to a non-technical client why their Google Ads, Facebook Ads, and Google Analytics numbers don't match, even though they're tracking the same campaign. Use a simple, non-jargon analogy, then explain which number we recommend they trust most for this specific decision and why. Keep the whole explanation under 200 words. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Platforms showing different numbers: [PLATFORMS] Specific numbers in question: [NUMBERS, IF HELPFUL] Decision the client is trying to make with this data: [DECISION]
prompts.proTip: Anchor the explanation to the specific decision the client is trying to make. Abstract attribution theory is confusing; "which number should I trust to decide X" is not.

prompts.title: Plan: Agency Rebrand Messaging Workshop Outline
prompts.useWhen: Your own agency (not a client) is rethinking its positioning or messaging and you want a structured workshop instead of an unfocused brainstorm.
prompts.prompt: Design a 90-minute internal workshop agenda for reworking our agency's own positioning and messaging. Include: a warm-up exercise to surface how the team currently describes the agency to prospects, a section for identifying gaps between that and where we want to be positioned, and a closing exercise that produces 2-3 draft positioning statements to refine afterward. Current positioning (in one sentence): [CURRENT POSITIONING] Reason for revisiting it: [REASON, e.g., new services added, market has shifted] Attendees: [ROLES/NAMES]
prompts.proTip: Run this workshop with people from outside your leadership team included. Junior team members often hear how prospects actually describe you more clearly than the founders do.
fields: REASON, e.g., new services added, market has shifted

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Generate a Month of Content From One Service Description
prompts.useWhen: You have almost nothing to start with, just a description of what a client sells, and need a full month of content ideas plus captions in one pass.
prompts.prompt: You are a content strategist and copywriter for a marketing agency. Using only the service description below, do the following in order: (1) identify 4 content pillars that make sense for this business, (2) under each pillar, generate 3 post ideas (12 total), (3) write full captions for each of the 12 posts, following the brand voice given, each with a call to action, (4) organize the final output into a simple weekly calendar (Week 1-4) so it's ready to schedule. Show your work at each step, don't skip straight to the final calendar. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Service description: [DESCRIBE WHAT THEY SELL/DO] Brand voice: [VOICE] Platform: [PLATFORM, e.g., Instagram, LinkedIn]
prompts.proTip: Review and approve the content pillars (step 1) before letting the AI continue to the full captions. Fixing direction early saves you from rewriting 12 captions built on the wrong pillars.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Full 90-Day Campaign From a One-Paragraph Brief
prompts.useWhen: A client gives you a rough, one-paragraph description of what they want and you need to turn it into a real, structured campaign plan.
prompts.prompt: You are a marketing strategist at an agency. Using the client brief below, build out a complete 90-day campaign plan: (1) restate the likely goal and target audience in your own words so I can confirm you understood correctly, (2) propose a media mix with rough budget percentages, (3) outline the campaign in three 30-day phases with key activities in each, (4) suggest 3 KPIs to track and realistic target ranges for each. Present each section clearly labeled, and flag any assumptions you had to make due to missing information. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] One-paragraph brief from the client: [PASTE ROUGH BRIEF] Available budget: [BUDGET]
prompts.proTip: Pay close attention to step 1. If the AI's restatement of the goal is wrong, everything built after it will be off too, correct it before moving forward.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Turn One Case Study Into a Full Cross-Channel Promotion Kit
prompts.useWhen: You landed a great client result and want to squeeze every possible piece of content and promotion out of it across channels, not just one social post.
prompts.prompt: You are a content and promotions specialist. Using the case study details below, build a complete promotion kit: (1) a one-paragraph written case study, (2) 3 social media posts highlighting different angles of the result, (3) a short email to send to the client list announcing the win, (4) 2 sales talking points a new business team member could use when pitching similar prospects, (5) one LinkedIn post written in the founder's voice. Clearly label each section. Client/customer name (or "a client" if anonymous): [NAME OR "a client"] Result/metric achieved: [RESULT] How it was achieved: [METHOD] Founder's name and voice notes, if available: [NAME/VOICE NOTES]
prompts.proTip: Get client permission to use their name and numbers publicly before this kit goes anywhere outside internal sales conversations.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Diagnose and Fix an Underperforming Campaign Endto-End
prompts.useWhen: A campaign isn't hitting its numbers and you need a structured diagnosis plus an actual action plan, not just a list of possible reasons.
prompts.prompt: You are a senior media strategist troubleshooting an underperforming campaign. Using the data and context below: (1) list the most likely causes of underperformance in priority order with your reasoning, (2) for the top 2 causes, suggest a specific diagnostic step to confirm it's really the problem, (3) once confirmed, propose a concrete action plan with what to change and what result to expect, (4) draft a short client-facing summary explaining the issue and the plan in plain English. Keep each section clearly separated. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Campaign type and goal: [CAMPAIGN TYPE AND GOAL] Performance data: [PASTE DATA] Anything already tried: [WHAT'S BEEN TRIED, IF ANYTHING]
prompts.proTip: Don't skip step 2. Confirming the cause before acting prevents the common mistake of "fixing" the wrong thing and wasting another few weeks of budget.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Complete New Business Pitch From a Prospect's Website
prompts.useWhen: You have a pitch coming up and only basic info about the prospect's business, and need to build out a full, tailored pitch fast.
prompts.prompt: You are a new business strategist preparing a pitch. Using the information below about this prospect: (1) summarize their likely marketing challenges based on what's described, (2) propose a tailored service approach addressing those challenges, (3) outline a 10-slide pitch deck structure with content suggestions per slide, (4) write 3 discovery call questions to confirm your assumptions are correct before the pitch. Present each section clearly, and note explicitly which parts are assumptions to validate versus confirmed facts. Prospect business name: [PROSPECT NAME] Information gathered about them (industry, size, current marketing, website notes): [PASTE INFO/ NOTES] Service we're pitching: [SERVICE]
prompts.proTip: Use the discovery questions from step 4 on your actual call before the pitch meeting, not just as filler. Confirmed insight beats an assumption every time in a pitch room.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Create a Full Client Onboarding Package From a Signed Contract
prompts.useWhen: A contract just got signed and you need to produce the entire onboarding package (welcome email, questionnaire, kickoff agenda) in one go instead of piecing it together over several days.
prompts.prompt: You are an account manager preparing a full onboarding package for a newly signed client. Using the details below, produce: (1) a welcome email introducing the process and next steps, (2) a discovery questionnaire (10-12 questions) to send before the kickoff call, (3) a kickoff call agenda, and (4) a first-30-days timeline showing what the client should expect week by week. Label each section clearly so they can be used or sent separately. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Service(s) starting: [SERVICE(S)] Primary point of contact on our team: [NAME/ROLE] Contract length: [LENGTH]
prompts.proTip: Save the final output as a template for this service type. The next new client on the same service becomes a 5-minute find-and-replace instead of a rebuild.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Turn a Client Complaint Into a Recovery Plan and Follow-Up Sequence
prompts.useWhen: A client is genuinely upset about something (a mistake, a missed deadline, disappointing results) and you need to handle it thoroughly, not just send one apology email and hope it's resolved.
prompts.prompt: You are an account director handling a serious client complaint. Using the details below: (1) write an initial response email that takes ownership and proposes a concrete resolution, (2) outline an internal action plan to actually fix the underlying issue, (3) write a follow-up email to send one week later confirming the fix worked, and (4) suggest one relationship-rebuilding gesture appropriate for this situation (not necessarily a discount). Label each part clearly. Client name: [CLIENT NAME] What went wrong: [DESCRIBE THE ISSUE] Impact on the client: [IMPACT] Relationship history: [E.g., "new client, 2 months in" or "5-year client, first issue"]
prompts.proTip: Have a human review and personalize step 1 before sending, even a well-written AI draft can feel impersonal in a moment where the client needs to feel genuinely heard.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Quarterly Business Review Deck From Raw Metrics
prompts.useWhen: You have a spreadsheet of quarterly numbers and a QBR on the calendar, and need the whole presentation narrative built from scratch.
prompts.prompt: You are preparing a quarterly business review for a client. Using the raw metrics below: (1) identify the 3 most important storylines in the data (not every metric, just what matters), (2) write a oneparagraph executive summary opening the deck, (3) outline slide-by-slide content for a 10-slide QBR deck covering results, insights, challenges, and next quarter's plan, (4) draft 2 forward-looking strategic questions to ask the client at the end. Present clearly labeled sections. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Raw quarterly metrics: [PASTE DATA] Known priorities for next quarter: [PRIORITIES, IF KNOWN]
prompts.proTip: Resist the urge to include every metric on the dashboard. A QBR that highlights 3 real storylines lands better than one that recites 20 numbers.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Create a Full Social Media Content System for a New Client
prompts.useWhen: You're starting social media management for a new client from zero and need the whole system (strategy, pillars, calendar, guidelines) built at once.
prompts.prompt: You are building a complete social media content system for a new client. Using the information below: (1) define 4 content pillars tied to their business goals, (2) build a 4-week content calendar with post topics assigned to each week (not full captions yet, just topics and pillar), (3) write a onepage brand voice guide for social content, (4) create a simple community management guideline for responding to comments and DMs. Label each section clearly so it can be shared as a standalone reference. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Industry: [INDUSTRY] Business goals: [GOALS] Brand voice notes: [VOICE NOTES]
prompts.proTip: Once this system is approved, run each week's topics through Prompt #28 to generate the actual captions, this power prompt builds the skeleton, not the final copy.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Run a Competitive Repositioning Exercise for a Client Losing Market Share
prompts.useWhen: A client is losing ground to competitors and needs more than a tweak, they need a real look at whether their positioning still makes sense.
prompts.prompt: You are a brand strategist helping a client rethink their market position. Using the details below: (1) summarize how the client currently positions itself versus how competitors are positioning themselves, (2) identify where that positioning has become outdated, crowded, or unconvincing, (3) propose 2 alternative positioning directions with reasoning for each, (4) for your recommended direction, draft a new one-sentence positioning statement and 3 messaging pillars to support it. Flag every assumption clearly. Client/business name: [CLIENT NAME] Current positioning: [CURRENT POSITIONING] Competitor positioning observed: [COMPETITOR POSITIONING] Reason for losing market share, if known: [REASON]
prompts.proTip: Treat the output as a strategic starting point for a real conversation with the client's leadership, not a final answer. Repositioning decisions carry real business risk and deserve human judgment on top of this draft.

prompts.title: Email: Reservation Confirmation with a Soft Upsell
prompts.useWhen: A guest just booked online or by phone and you want to confirm the reservation while nudging them toward an add-on, like a tasting menu or wine pairing (booking confirmation).
prompts.prompt: You are the reservations manager at [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant. Write a short confirmation email for a guest who just booked a table for [PARTY SIZE] on [DATE/TIME]. Confirm the details clearly, then add one warm, low-pressure line suggesting [UPSELL ITEM, e.g., our chef's tasting menu or the patio seating]. Keep the tone [TONE, e.g., warm and casual / polished and upscale]. End with how to reach us if they need to change anything. Keep it under 120 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version with a subject line under 50 characters — short subject lines get opened more on mobile.
fields: TONE, e.g., warm and casual / polished and upscale

prompts.title: Email: Follow-Up on a Private Event or Buyout Inquiry
prompts.useWhen: Someone emailed asking about hosting a birthday dinner, rehearsal dinner, or full restaurant buyout and you need a reply that sounds organized (event inquiry, private party request).
prompts.prompt: You are the events coordinator at [RESTAURANT NAME]. A guest inquired about hosting a [EVENT TYPE, e.g., 30th birthday dinner] for approximately [GUEST COUNT] people around [DATE/TIMEFRAME]. Write a reply email that thanks them, asks 2-3 clarifying questions you'd actually need answered (budget range, seating vs. buyout, any must-haves), and briefly mentions what makes our space work well for private events. Keep the tone friendly and confident, not salesy. End with a clear next step. Under 150 words.
prompts.proTip: Paste in your actual private-dining minimums and ask the AI to fold them in naturally instead of listing them as bullet points.

prompts.title: Script: Offering a Waitlist Spot When Fully Booked
prompts.useWhen: A caller wants a reservation time you don't have available and your host needs quick, friendly talking points instead of just saying no (fully booked, no availability, waitlist script).
prompts.prompt: You are a hospitality trainer writing a phone script for hosts at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Create a short script for when a guest requests a reservation time that's fully booked. The script should acknowledge the request, offer the closest available alternative time or the waitlist, and mention [WALK-IN POLICY, e.g., we also seat walk-ins at the bar]. Write it as natural spoken dialogue, not a formal script, so it sounds human on the phone. Keep it to 4-5 lines.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version for text/online chat, since the phone tone doesn't always translate to typed messages.
fields: WALK-IN POLICY, e.g., we also seat walk-ins at the bar

prompts.title: Email: Friendly Re-Engagement After a No-Show
prompts.useWhen: A guest missed their reservation and you want to send a warm, no-guilt-trip note that gets them to book again instead of never coming back (missed reservation, didn't show up).
prompts.prompt: You are the guest relations manager at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write a short, genuinely friendly email to a guest who missed their reservation on [DATE]. Do not sound annoyed or passive-aggressive — assume something came up. Let them know we'd love to have them another time, mention [INCENTIVE IF ANY, e.g., a complimentary appetizer on their next visit], and make rebooking easy. Keep it under 100 words and end on a warm note, not a policy reminder.
prompts.proTip: If your restaurant charges no-show fees, ask for a second version that mentions the fee gently in one sentence without making the whole email about it.

prompts.title: Email: Birthday Outreach for a Regular Guest
prompts.useWhen: A loyal, repeat guest has a birthday coming up per your reservation system or loyalty list and you want a personal-feeling touch (VIP outreach, repeat customer email).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a personal birthday email from [RESTAURANT NAME] to [GUEST NAME], a regular guest who usually orders [FAVORITE DISH OR ORDER, if known]. Write a short, warm birthday message that feels personal rather than mass-sent, offers [BIRTHDAY PERK, e.g., a free dessert or 10% off], and invites them to book their celebration with us. Keep it under 90 words and avoid generic phrases like "we value your business."
prompts.proTip: Feed the AI a few details about the guest's past visits — it makes a noticeable difference in how personal the email feels.
fields: FAVORITE DISH OR ORDER, if known
BIRTHDAY PERK, e.g., a free dessert or 10% off

prompts.title: Script: Seating Large Groups on a Packed Night
prompts.useWhen: Your host needs quick talking points for moving big parties to their tables efficiently on a busy Friday or Saturday without guests feeling rushed (group seating, busy night).
prompts.prompt: You are a front-of-house trainer for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write a short script a host can use when seating a party of [GROUP SIZE] during a packed dinner rush. It should welcome the group, explain the table setup or split-check policy in one sentence if relevant, and set expectations for wait times on food without sounding rushed or scripted. Keep it conversational, under 60 words, and easy to say out loud.
prompts.proTip: Swap in your actual split-check or gratuity policy for large parties so the host isn't improvising it live.

prompts.title: Email: Catering or Large To-Go Order Confirmation
prompts.useWhen: A guest placed a catering order or a large takeout order and needs a confirmation email with pickup or delivery details (takeout confirmation, catering order receipt).
prompts.prompt: You are the catering manager at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write a confirmation email for a catering/to-go order for [ORDER DETAILS, e.g., 2 trays of lasagna, salad for 20] being picked up on [DATE/TIME]. Confirm the order contents, total price of [PRICE], pickup location and any parking notes, and payment status. Add one line reminding them to check the order at pickup. Keep the tone efficient and professional, under 110 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version with a "reheating instructions" section added at the bottom — it cuts down on follow-up calls.
fields: ORDER DETAILS, e.g., 2 trays of lasagna, salad for 20

prompts.title: Response: Answering a Dietary Restriction or Allergy Question
prompts.useWhen: A guest messages or emails asking whether you have gluten-free, vegan, or allergy-friendly options before they book (allergy inquiry, dietary accommodation question, food allergy).
prompts.prompt: You are a guest services rep at [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant. A guest asked whether we can accommodate [DIETARY NEED, e.g., a severe nut allergy or vegan diet]. Write a clear, reassuring response that confirms what we can do, mentions [SPECIFIC MENU ITEMS OR KITCHEN PRACTICE, e.g., we have a dedicated fryer], and is honest about any limitations without sounding alarming. Keep it under 100 words and end by inviting them to let their server know when they arrive.
prompts.proTip: Never let AI guess at actual allergen handling — always verify claims about crosscontamination with your kitchen before sending.
fields: DIETARY NEED, e.g., a severe nut allergy or vegan diet

prompts.title: Response: Replying to a Negative Review About Food Quality
prompts.useWhen: A guest left a public review complaining their food was cold, bland, or not what they expected and you need a reply that doesn't sound defensive (bad review, food complaint, one-star review).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] responding publicly to a [PLATFORM, e.g., Google or Yelp] review. The guest said: "[PASTE REVIEW TEXT]." Write a reply that thanks them for the feedback, acknowledges the specific issue without being defensive or making excuses, briefly notes what we're doing about it, and invites them back with [OFFER IF ANY, e.g., a complimentary dish]. Keep it under 100 words, calm and professional, and avoid sounding scripted or corporate.
prompts.proTip: Never argue with details in the review even if you think they're wrong — ask the AI for a version that stays neutral on facts you can't verify.
fields: OFFER IF ANY, e.g., a complimentary dish

prompts.title: Response: Replying to a Review About Slow or Inattentive Service
prompts.useWhen: A review calls out long wait times, a forgotten order, or a server who seemed checked out and you need a reply that shows you take it seriously (service complaint, slow service review).
prompts.prompt: You are the general manager of [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a public review about slow service on a [NIGHT/OCCASION, e.g., busy Saturday night]. The guest said: "[PASTE REVIEW TEXT]." Write a reply that apologizes sincerely without overexplaining, mentions one concrete step we're taking (more staff on weekends, better training, etc.), and invites them to reach out directly at [CONTACT METHOD] to make it right. Keep it under 90 words and human, not corporate.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a shorter 40-word version too — some platforms cut off long replies, and a tight reply often reads better anyway.

prompts.title: Response: Thanking a Guest for a Glowing Review
prompts.useWhen: Someone left a five-star review raving about their meal and you want a reply worth reposting to social media, not just a generic "thanks!" (positive review, five-star review reply).
prompts.prompt: You are responding publicly to a five-star review of [RESTAURANT NAME]. The guest wrote: "[PASTE REVIEW TEXT]." Write a warm, specific reply that references at least one detail from their review (the dish, the server, the occasion), thanks them by name, and invites them back to try [NEW ITEM OR EVENT]. Keep it under 70 words, genuine and not overly formal — this needs to sound like a person wrote it, not a template.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to also write a one-line Instagram Story caption pulling a quote from the review — great reviews make great social content.

prompts.title: Script: Handling an In-Person Complaint About a Dish
prompts.useWhen: A guest at the table flags an issue with their food mid-meal and your server needs calm, confident language on the spot (table-side complaint, sending a dish back).
prompts.prompt: You are a hospitality trainer creating a script for servers at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write short talking points for when a guest says their dish is [ISSUE, e.g., overcooked or not what they expected]. The script should acknowledge the issue immediately, offer a clear resolution (remake it, comp it, swap it) without needing manager approval for small fixes, and keep the guest's evening from being ruined. Keep it to 3-4 lines of natural spoken dialogue.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version for when the fix requires manager sign-off, so servers know exactly when to escalate.
fields: ISSUE, e.g., overcooked or not what they expected

prompts.title: Email: Responding to a Complaint Sent Directly (Not Public)
prompts.useWhen: A guest emails or DMs you privately about a bad experience instead of posting a public review, and you want to resolve it before it becomes one (private complaint, direct feedback email).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a private email complaint about [ISSUE, e.g., a long wait with no explanation]. The guest wrote: "[PASTE MESSAGE]." Write a personal reply that thanks them for telling you directly instead of posting publicly, takes ownership of the specific problem, and offers [MAKE-GOOD OFFER, e.g., a gift card or their next meal on the house]. Keep it under 130 words and make it sound like it came from a real person who cares.
prompts.proTip: Always personalize the opening line yourself before sending — a generic "Dear Guest" undoes the whole point of a private, personal reply.
fields: ISSUE, e.g., a long wait with no explanation

prompts.title: Post: Asking Happy Guests to Leave a Review
prompts.useWhen: You want a simple message (email, receipt footer, or table card) that nudges satisfied guests toward leaving a review without sounding pushy (review request, ask for feedback).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a short review-request message for [RESTAURANT NAME] to send to guests after a positive visit. Write 3 short variations: one for a post-visit email, one for a receipt footer (under 20 words), and one for a table tent card. Each should thank the guest, make it easy (mention [REVIEW LINK/PLATFORM]), and avoid sounding like a demand. Keep the tone appreciative, not transactional.
prompts.proTip: Time the email version to send a few hours after the reservation, not the next day — memory of the meal fades fast.

prompts.title: Response: Replying to a Review That Praises a Specific Staff Member
prompts.useWhen: A guest calls out a server, bartender, or host by name in a glowing review and you want a reply that celebrates them (staff shoutout, employee praise review).
prompts.prompt: You are the manager of [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a review that specifically praised [STAFF NAME/ROLE, e.g., our server Jake]. The guest wrote: "[PASTE REVIEW TEXT]." Write a reply that thanks the guest, genuinely celebrates the staff member by name, and mentions we'll be sure they see it. Keep it under 60 words and warm — this reply should make the employee feel proud, not just check a box.
prompts.proTip: Screenshot the review and the reply together and share it in your staff group chat — recognition like this is a free retention tool.
fields: STAFF NAME/ROLE, e.g., our server Jake

prompts.title: Analysis: Summarizing Recurring Themes Across Recent Reviews
prompts.useWhen: You've got a stack of reviews from the last month and want the patterns pulled out instead of re-reading them one by one (review trends, reputation summary, what guests keep saying).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant consultant analyzing guest reviews for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Here are reviews from the last [TIME PERIOD]: [PASTE REVIEW TEXT OR SUMMARIES]. Identify the 3-5 most common themes (both positive and negative), how often each comes up, and one specific, practical fix for each negative theme. Present it as a table with columns: Theme, Frequency, Positive or Negative, Suggested Fix.
prompts.proTip: Run this monthly and keep the tables — after a few months you'll have a clear before/after record of what actually improved.

prompts.title: Post: Instagram Caption for Today's Special
prompts.useWhen: You need a quick, appetizing caption for a daily or weekly special before the lunch or dinner rush (daily special post, social media caption).
prompts.prompt: You are the social media manager for [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant. Write an Instagram caption announcing today's special: [DISH NAME AND SHORT DESCRIPTION]. Make it sound craveable using sensory language (texture, aroma, flavor), keep it under 60 words, include the price of [PRICE], and end with a simple call to action like "today only" or "while it lasts." Suggest 5 relevant hashtags separately.
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 caption variations at once so you can pick the one that best matches today's photo instead of settling for the first draft.

prompts.title: Post: "Behind the Scenes" Kitchen Content Idea and Caption
prompts.useWhen: You want to post something other than food photos — a prep video, a staff moment, or a kitchen process — but you're not sure what to say about it (BTS content, kitchen video caption).
prompts.prompt: You are a social media strategist for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Suggest 3 quick "behind the scenes" content ideas we could film in under a minute during a normal shift (things like prepping [SIGNATURE INGREDIENT] or plating [SIGNATURE DISH]), then write a short caption for the strongest idea. The caption should feel personal and unpolished, not like an ad, and end with a light question to invite comments. Keep it under 50 words.
prompts.proTip: Film these on a phone in vertical video — polished footage actually performs worse for "behind the scenes" content than a raw, real clip.

prompts.title: Email: Monthly Newsletter to Our Subscriber List
prompts.useWhen: It's time to send the monthly update to your email list and you don't want to start from a blank page (email newsletter, monthly update to guests).
prompts.prompt: You are writing the monthly email newsletter for [RESTAURANT NAME]. This month's highlights are: [LIST 2-4 THINGS, e.g., new fall menu, live music Fridays, a charity night]. Write a newsletter with a short, friendly intro paragraph, a scannable section for each highlight with one sentence each, and a closing line that invites people to book a table. Keep the whole thing under 200 words and write a subject line under 45 characters.
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 subject line options and test different ones each month — open rates can swing a lot based on subject line alone.

prompts.title: Post: Announcing a New Menu Item
prompts.useWhen: You're adding a new dish or drink to the menu and need launch posts for Instagram, Facebook, and a short text blast (new menu item announcement, menu launch post).
prompts.prompt: You are announcing a new menu item at [RESTAURANT NAME]: [DISH NAME AND KEY INGREDIENTS/INSPIRATION]. Write three versions of the announcement: an Instagram caption (under 60 words, sensory and exciting), a Facebook post (slightly longer, can include the backstory of the dish), and a one-line text message blast for our SMS list. Keep the tone [TONE, e.g., playful and fun / elevated and refined] across all three.
prompts.proTip: Ask the AI to also draft a "why we made this dish" mini-story — origin stories consistently get more engagement than plain announcements.
fields: TONE, e.g., playful and fun / elevated and refined

prompts.title: Post: Seasonal or Holiday Promotion Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You're running a special for a holiday or season (Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, football season, first day of patio weather) and need to announce it (holiday promo, seasonal special post).
prompts.prompt: You are promoting a [HOLIDAY/SEASON, e.g., Valentine's Day] special at [RESTAURANT NAME]: [DETAILS OF THE OFFER, e.g., a 4-course prix fixe menu for $65 per person]. Write a social post announcing the promotion that creates gentle urgency (limited seating, reservations filling up), clearly states the price and what's included, and includes a call to action to book. Keep it under 80 words and avoid sounding like a coupon flyer.
prompts.proTip: Post this 2-3 weeks before the holiday and again 3 days before — most bookings come in that final push.

prompts.title: Plan: One Week of Content From a Single Dish
prompts.useWhen: You're low on content ideas and want to stretch one dish or ingredient into a full week of posts without repeating yourself (content calendar, week of social posts).
prompts.prompt: You are a social media strategist for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Take one dish, [DISH NAME], and turn it into 5 different pieces of content for one week — each with a different angle (the ingredients, the plating process, a guest reaction, a pairing suggestion, a "did you know" fact about the dish). For each, give a one-line content idea and a short caption. Present it as a table with columns: Day, Content Idea, Caption.
prompts.proTip: Batch-shoot the photos and videos for all 5 posts in one prep session — it's the fastest way to actually stick to the calendar.

prompts.title: Post: Reposting a Guest Photo or Review as Content
prompts.useWhen: A guest tagged you in a great photo or left a glowing comment and you want to repost it with a caption that gives them credit (user-generated content, repost guest photo).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a repost caption for [RESTAURANT NAME]. A guest, [GUEST HANDLE OR NAME], posted a photo of [WHAT'S IN THE PHOTO, e.g., our brunch spread] with the caption: "[PASTE THEIR CAPTION OR COMMENT]." Write a repost caption that thanks them by tag, adds a bit of our own voice or a light joke, and includes a call to action to visit or order the same dish. Keep it under 50 words.
prompts.proTip: Always ask the guest for permission to repost before you do, even if they tagged you — a quick DM takes ten seconds and avoids awkwardness.
fields: WHAT'S IN THE PHOTO, e.g., our brunch spread

prompts.title: Post: Tying a Post to a Local Event
prompts.useWhen: There's a local event happening nearby (a festival, game day, farmers market, concert) and you want a post that connects your restaurant to it without forcing it (local event tie-in, game day post).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a social post for [RESTAURANT NAME] tying us to [LOCAL EVENT, e.g., the town's fall festival or a home game for the local team] happening on [DATE]. Write a caption that naturally connects the event to something we're offering (a special, extended hours, a watch party) without feeling like a stretch. Keep it under 60 words and match the excitement of the event itself.
prompts.proTip: Mention the event by its actual name and hashtag if it has one — it puts your post in front of people actively searching for event info.

prompts.title: Description: Appetizing Copy for a New Menu Item
prompts.useWhen: You're adding a dish to the printed or online menu and need copy that sells it without sounding like a cookbook ingredient list (menu description, dish copy).
prompts.prompt: You are a menu copywriter for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write a menu description for [DISH NAME], made with [KEY INGREDIENTS]. The description should be 15-25 words, use one or two vivid sensory words (not five), highlight what makes it different from a version a guest could get elsewhere, and match a [TONE, e.g., upscale / homestyle / playful] voice. Avoid overused words like "delicious," "amazing," or "mouthwatering."
prompts.proTip: Ask for 3 versions at different lengths (short, medium, one-sentence) so you have options for the printed menu, the online ordering site, and social captions.

prompts.title: Analysis: Which Menu Items to Promote or Cut
prompts.useWhen: You want a clear-eyed look at which dishes are pulling their weight and which are quietly costing you money, based on cost and popularity (menu engineering, menu analysis, what to 86 permanently).
prompts.prompt: You are a menu engineering consultant. Here is data for menu items at [RESTAURANT NAME]: [PASTE A LIST WITH ITEM NAME, FOOD COST, PRICE, AND MONTHLY UNITS SOLD]. Categorize each item as a Star (high profit, high popularity), Plow Horse (low profit, high popularity), Puzzle (high profit, low popularity), or Dog (low profit, low popularity). Present as a table, then give one specific recommendation per category (reprice, reposition on menu, promote, or cut).
prompts.proTip: Re-run this every quarter with fresh sales numbers — menu engineering is only useful when it reflects what's actually selling right now, not last year.

prompts.title: Plan: Seasonal Menu Refresh Ideas
prompts.useWhen: It's time to update the menu for a new season and you want a starting point built around what's actually in season, not a random brainstorm (seasonal menu, menu refresh).
prompts.prompt: You are a chef consultant helping [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant, refresh its menu for [SEASON]. Our current menu style is [BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF STYLE]. Suggest 5 dish concepts using ingredients that are in season during [SEASON] in [REGION], noting which existing dish each could replace or complement. For each, give a one-line concept description. Present as a table with columns: Dish Concept, Key Seasonal Ingredients, Replaces/Complements.
prompts.proTip: Hand the final list to your chef for a gut-check on kitchen labor and equipment before committing — AI can suggest concepts, but it can't see your line.

prompts.title: Description: Wine or Drink Pairing Suggestions
prompts.useWhen: You want pairing suggestions to print on the menu or train servers on, without guessing off the top of your head (wine pairing, drink pairing suggestions).
prompts.prompt: You are a beverage consultant for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Suggest 3 drink pairings for [DISH NAME, WITH KEY FLAVORS/PREPARATION] from our current beverage list: [PASTE A FEW WINE/COCKTAIL/BEER OPTIONS]. For each pairing, give a onesentence explanation of why it works (acidity, weight, contrast, etc.) that a server could repeat to a guest without sounding like a sommelier script. Keep each explanation under 20 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for the same pairings written as a 5-second server soundbite — servers are far more likely to actually recommend pairings when the explanation is short enough to remember.

prompts.title: Description: Kids Menu Item Names and Descriptions
prompts.useWhen: You're building or refreshing a kids menu and want names and descriptions that appeal to both kids and the parents paying the bill (kids menu, children's menu copy).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a kids menu for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Here are the dishes: [LIST DISHES, e.g., mini cheese quesadilla, chicken tenders, mac and cheese]. Write a fun, simple name and a one-line description for each that would appeal to kids ages [AGE RANGE], while reassuring parents about portion size or ingredients where relevant. Keep descriptions under 10 words each. Present as a table with columns: Dish, Kid-Friendly Name, Description.
prompts.proTip: Read the names out loud before finalizing — the best kids menu names are fun to say, not just fun to read.

prompts.title: Plan: Limited-Time Offer Concept Ideas
prompts.useWhen: You want to run a limited-time item or promotion to create buzz but need a few solid concepts to choose from instead of picking randomly (LTO ideas, limited-time menu item).
prompts.prompt: You are a menu strategist for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We want to run a limitedtime offer during [TIMEFRAME, e.g., the next 3 weeks] to drive traffic on [SLOW DAY/SHIFT, if applicable]. Our kitchen is strong at [STRENGTHS, e.g., grilling, baking, house-made sauces]. Suggest 3 LTO concepts that use ingredients we likely already stock, explain the hook for each (what makes it shareable or urgent), and estimate relative kitchen complexity as Low, Medium, or High.
prompts.proTip: Pick the Low-complexity option for your first LTO — a smooth first run builds staff buy-in for bigger ones later.
fields: STRENGTHS, e.g., grilling, baking, house-made sauces

prompts.title: Description: Dessert Menu Copy
prompts.useWhen: You're writing or updating dessert descriptions and want language that makes people order dessert even when they're full (dessert menu, dessert descriptions).
prompts.prompt: You are a menu copywriter for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write descriptions for these desserts: [LIST DESSERTS WITH KEY COMPONENTS]. Each description should be 12-20 words, emphasize texture and temperature contrast (warm/cold, crisp/soft) where it applies, and avoid the word "decadent." Match a [TONE, e.g., playful / elegant] voice consistent with the rest of the menu.
prompts.proTip: Ask servers which dessert they find easiest to sell and hardest to sell, then have the AI punch up the description for the hard sell first.

prompts.title: Checklist: Menu Quality Check Before It Goes to Print
prompts.useWhen: You're about to send a new menu to the printer or update the online ordering platform and want one last pass to catch pricing, allergen, and consistency mistakes (menu proofread, pre-print checklist).
prompts.prompt: You are a meticulous menu editor. Create a pre-print quality checklist for [RESTAURANT NAME]'s menu covering: pricing consistency across sections, allergen and dietary labeling completeness, spelling of ingredient and dish names, consistent formatting (capitalization, punctuation, description length), and matching item names to POS system names. Present it as a checklist with 8-10 items a manager can physically check off before approving the final print.
prompts.proTip: Print the checklist out and have a second person do the actual check — a fresh set of eyes catches typos AI and the original writer both miss.

prompts.title: Ad: Facebook/Instagram Ad Copy for a Promotion
prompts.useWhen: You're running a paid social ad for a promotion and need copy built for a scroll-stopping first line, not a regular post caption (Facebook ad, Instagram ad copy).
prompts.prompt: You are a paid social copywriter for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Write Facebook/ Instagram ad copy for this promotion: [PROMOTION DETAILS, e.g., $10 off any entree, valid this week only]. Give me a hook line under 10 words designed to stop a scroll, a body of 2-3 short sentences building interest, and a clear call to action with urgency. Also suggest 2 headline variations under 40 characters for the ad's headline field.
prompts.proTip: Make sure every claim in the ad is something you can actually deliver on — "today only" only works if it's actually today only.

prompts.title: Ad: Google Search Ad Headlines and Descriptions
prompts.useWhen: You're setting up a Google Ads campaign and need multiple headline and description options to fill in the character-limited fields (Google Ads, search ad copy).
prompts.prompt: You are writing Google Search Ads for [RESTAURANT NAME], located in [NEIGHBORHOOD/CITY], known for [CUISINE TYPE OR SPECIALTY]. Write 5 headlines (30 characters max each) and 3 descriptions (90 characters max each) targeting people searching for "[SEARCH TERM, e.g., best Italian restaurant near me]." Make each headline distinct so they can be rotated and tested against each other.
prompts.proTip: Pull your actual highest-rated dish or feature into at least one headline — specific beats generic in search ads every time.
fields: SEARCH TERM, e.g., best Italian restaurant near me

prompts.title: Post: Happy Hour Promotion Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You're launching or refreshing a happy hour and need a post that clearly states the deal without burying it in fluff (happy hour ad, drink specials post).
prompts.prompt: You are promoting happy hour at [RESTAURANT NAME]. The details are: [DAYS/TIMES AND SPECIALS, e.g., Mon-Thu 4-6pm, $2 off drafts, half-price apps]. Write a social post that leads with the specific deal in the first line (not a vague teaser), lists what's included clearly, and ends with the days/times restated for anyone skimming. Keep it under 70 words.
prompts.proTip: Pin this post to the top of your Instagram and Facebook pages and refresh the wording every month so it doesn't look stale to repeat visitors.

prompts.title: Ad: Grand Opening or Re-Opening Announcement
prompts.useWhen: You're opening a new location or re-opening after a closure/renovation and need announcement copy across channels (grand opening ad, re-opening announcement).
prompts.prompt: You are announcing the [GRAND OPENING/RE-OPENING] of [RESTAURANT NAME] at [LOCATION] on [DATE]. Write three versions: a social media post building excitement with a countdown feel, a short local press release opener (2-3 sentences a local paper or blog could use), and a text blast for our subscriber list. Mention [OPENING SPECIAL/EVENT IF ANY]. Keep the tone genuinely excited, not corporate.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version of the press release opener addressed "For Immediate Release" with a placeholder for a media contact — it saves a step if you plan to pitch local outlets.

prompts.title: Post: Loyalty Program Sign-Up Promotion
prompts.useWhen: You want to grow sign-ups for your loyalty or rewards program and need copy that explains the value fast (loyalty program promo, rewards signup).
prompts.prompt: You are promoting the [LOYALTY PROGRAM NAME] at [RESTAURANT NAME]. The program works like this: [HOW IT WORKS, e.g., earn 1 point per dollar, 100 points = $10 off]. Write a short social post and a table-tent card version that explain the value in one sentence, make signing up sound effortless (mention how, e.g., scan a QR code), and give one reason to join today instead of "eventually." Keep each version under 50 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version that leads with a specific dollar example ("spend $200 over time, get $20 back") — concrete numbers convert better than "earn rewards."

prompts.title: Ad: Delivery App Promo Description
prompts.useWhen: You're setting up a promoted item or store description on DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Grubhub and want copy tuned for a delivery audience, not dine-in guests (delivery app description, DoorDash promo).
prompts.prompt: You are writing store and promo copy for [RESTAURANT NAME] on delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats. Write a short restaurant bio (2 sentences, focused on what makes us worth ordering from when there are 20 other options on the app) and a promo blurb for [SPECIFIC DEAL, e.g., free delivery on orders over $25]. Keep both tight — delivery app users skim fast and decide in seconds.
prompts.proTip: Lead with your single best-selling, most photogenic dish by name — delivery app browsers decide based on cravings, not restaurant history.
fields: SPECIFIC DEAL, e.g., free delivery on orders over $25

prompts.title: Ad: 30-Second Local Radio or Print Ad Script
prompts.useWhen: You've got local radio or print ad space and need a tight script that hits the key points in a short read (radio ad script, local print ad).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a 30-second local radio ad script for [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant in [LOCATION]. Highlight [1-2 KEY SELLING POINTS, e.g., our patio and live music] and include [CALL TO ACTION, e.g., our address and a website]. Write it to be read aloud in roughly 75-80 words at a natural conversational pace, with a warm, inviting tone — not a fast-talking hard sell.
prompts.proTip: Read the script out loud and time it yourself before recording — AI word counts don't always match real speaking pace.
fields: 1-2 KEY SELLING POINTS, e.g., our patio and live music
CALL TO ACTION, e.g., our address and a website

prompts.title: Ad: Win-Back Offer for Guests Who Haven't Returned
prompts.useWhen: You want to re-engage guests who used to visit regularly but haven't been back in a while, via email or a retargeting ad (win-back campaign, lapsed customer offer).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a win-back message for [RESTAURANT NAME] targeting guests who haven't visited in [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 90 days]. Write an email and a short retargeting ad version that acknowledges it's been a while without guilt-tripping, reminds them what they're missing (a specific dish or experience), and offers [INCENTIVE, e.g., 15% off their next visit]. Keep the email under 100 words and the ad under 30 words.
prompts.proTip: Set an actual expiration date on the incentive — an open-ended offer creates zero urgency to act now.
fields: INCENTIVE, e.g., 15% off their next visit

prompts.title: SOP: Opening or Closing Checklist
prompts.useWhen: You want a clear, written step-by-step checklist for opening or closing shifts so nothing gets skipped when a new or rushed employee is running it (opening checklist, closing procedures, side work list).
prompts.prompt: You are an operations manager writing a [OPENING/CLOSING] checklist for the [FRONT OF HOUSE/BACK OF HOUSE] at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Include tasks in the order they should be done, covering [KEY AREAS, e.g., line setup, POS system, cleaning, cash drawer]. Write it as a numbered checklist of 10-15 items, each specific enough that a new employee could follow it without asking questions. Note which items require manager sign-off.
prompts.proTip: Laminate the final checklist and post it at the relevant station — a checklist that lives only in a binder in the office never gets used.

prompts.title: Job Posting: Hiring Ad for an Open Role
prompts.useWhen: You need to post a job opening and want it to actually stand out from generic "now hiring" listings (hiring ad, job posting, help wanted ad).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a job posting for a [ROLE, e.g., line cook, server, bartender] at [RESTAURANT NAME], a [CUISINE TYPE] restaurant in [LOCATION]. Include what makes working here different (culture, growth opportunity, tips, schedule flexibility — whatever is actually true), the core responsibilities in plain language, and what we're looking for in a candidate. Keep it under 180 words, friendly and specific, and end with how to apply.
prompts.proTip: Mention the actual pay range or tip average if you're comfortable sharing it — job posts with pay transparency consistently get more qualified applicants.
fields: ROLE, e.g., line cook, server, bartender

prompts.title: Script: Welcome Message for a New Hire
prompts.useWhen: Someone just accepted a job offer and you want a warm welcome message before their first day that sets the tone (new hire welcome, first day message).
prompts.prompt: You are the manager at [RESTAURANT NAME] writing a welcome message for [NEW HIRE NAME], who just accepted the [ROLE] position. Write a short, genuinely warm message confirming their start date of [DATE], what to bring/wear on day one, who to ask for when they arrive, and one sentence about what excites you about them joining the team. Keep it under 100 words and personal, not like a corporate HR template.
prompts.proTip: Send this the same day they accept the offer — the sooner a new hire feels welcomed, the less likely they are to ghost before day one.

prompts.title: Training: New Server Menu Knowledge Outline
prompts.useWhen: You're training a new server and want a structured way to teach the menu instead of just handing them a copy and saying "memorize it" (server training, menu knowledge training).
prompts.prompt: You are a training manager at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Our menu includes these sections: [LIST MENU SECTIONS, e.g., starters, entrees, desserts, bar]. Create a 3day training outline for a new server to learn the menu, with each day focused on a specific goal (day 1: sections and top sellers, day 2: allergens and modifications, day 3: pairing and upselling). For each day, list 3-4 specific things they should be able to do by the end.
prompts.proTip: Turn each day into a short quiz you give verbally at the end of the shift — active recall sticks far better than passive reading.
fields: LIST MENU SECTIONS, e.g., starters, entrees, desserts, bar

prompts.title: Response: Shift Swap Request Policy Explanation
prompts.useWhen: A staff member asks to swap a shift last-minute and you want a consistent, fair way to respond that you can reuse every time (shift swap, schedule change request).
prompts.prompt: You are a shift manager at [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a staff member's request to swap their shift on [DATE]. Our policy is: [PASTE YOUR ACTUAL POLICY, e.g., swaps need a same-role replacement approved 24 hours in advance]. Write a short, friendly text or message response that explains what they need to do next, without sounding like a rulebook. Keep it under 50 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a second version for when the request breaks policy (too last-minute, no replacement) so you have a firm-but-kind way to say no ready to go.

prompts.title: Script: Giving Constructive Feedback to an Underperforming Team Member
prompts.useWhen: You need to have a one-on-one conversation about performance (missed side work, attitude, speed) and want to prep talking points that are direct but not harsh (performance conversation, coaching a staff member).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant manager preparing for a one-on-one conversation with a team member about [SPECIFIC ISSUE, e.g., consistently missing closing side work]. Write 4-5 talking points that open with something genuine and positive about them, state the specific issue factually without generalizing ("always" or "never"), explain the impact on the team, and end with a clear, achievable expectation going forward. Keep the tone direct but respectful.
prompts.proTip: Practice saying the talking points out loud once before the conversation — reading feedback and delivering it calmly in person are two different skills.
fields: SPECIFIC ISSUE, e.g., consistently missing closing side work

prompts.title: Announcement: Pre-Shift Meeting Talking Points
prompts.useWhen: You run quick pre-shift meetings ("family meal" or "lineup") and want a fast way to organize what needs covering before service starts (pre-shift meeting, lineup notes, staff huddle).
prompts.prompt: You are a manager prepping for today's pre-shift meeting at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Today's key points are: [LIST 3-5 THINGS, e.g., 86'd items, a VIP reservation, a new special, a reminder about upselling dessert]. Turn this into a tight 90-second talking script a manager could read almost verbatim, ordered from most to least urgent, ending on an energizing note before service.
prompts.proTip: Keep a running doc of these and reuse the format daily — writing it fresh from scratch each time is the part that eats up managers' mornings.

prompts.title: Policy: Staff Handbook Section
prompts.useWhen: You're building or updating your staff handbook and need a clearly written policy section on a specific topic (handbook policy, staff rules section).
prompts.prompt: You are writing a section of the staff handbook for [RESTAURANT NAME] covering our policy on [TOPIC, e.g., dress code, tardiness, cell phone use during shifts]. Our actual policy is: [DESCRIBE YOUR POLICY IN PLAIN LANGUAGE]. Turn this into a clearly written handbook section with a short intro sentence, the specific rules as a bulleted list, and the consequence for not following it. Keep the tone firm but respectful, not punitive.
prompts.proTip: Have a labor attorney or HR advisor review any handbook language involving discipline or termination before you finalize it — AI drafts wording, it doesn't know your local labor law.
fields: DESCRIBE YOUR POLICY IN PLAIN LANGUAGE

prompts.title: Email: Negotiating Better Pricing with a Food Vendor
prompts.useWhen: Your food costs are creeping up and you want to approach a supplier about pricing without burning the relationship (vendor negotiation, supplier pricing email).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] writing to [VENDOR NAME], our supplier for [PRODUCT CATEGORY, e.g., produce or proteins]. We've been ordering [ORDER VOLUME/FREQUENCY] for [LENGTH OF RELATIONSHIP], and recent pricing on [SPECIFIC ITEM(S)] has increased. Write an email that acknowledges the relationship, asks directly about options (volume discount, locking in a rate, alternative products), and stays collaborative rather than confrontational. Keep it under 130 words.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a version that mentions a competing quote you've received — even referencing it generally often opens up flexibility a vendor wouldn't offer otherwise.
fields: PRODUCT CATEGORY, e.g., produce or proteins

prompts.title: Email: Following Up on a Late or Incorrect Delivery
prompts.useWhen: A vendor delivery showed up late, short, or with the wrong items and you need a clear, professional email documenting it (delivery issue, wrong order from supplier, late shipment).
prompts.prompt: You are writing to [VENDOR NAME] about a delivery issue on [DATE]. The order was supposed to include [WHAT WAS ORDERED] but instead [WHAT WENT WRONG, e.g., arrived 3 hours late / was missing 2 cases]. Write a firm but professional email that states the facts clearly, explains the operational impact (a specific example, like having to 86 a dish), and asks for a specific resolution (credit, redelivery, or both) by [TIMEFRAME].
prompts.proTip: Attach a photo of the short or incorrect delivery if you have one — vendors resolve documented issues faster than verbal-only complaints.

prompts.title: Checklist: Setting Up an Inventory Count Sheet
prompts.useWhen: You're building or cleaning up your par-level and inventory count process and want a structured starting sheet (inventory sheet, par level list, stock count template).
prompts.prompt: You are a back-of-house operations consultant. Help [RESTAURANT NAME] build an inventory count sheet for [CATEGORY, e.g., dry goods, walk-in cooler, bar]. List the item categories we should be tracking based on a typical [CUISINE TYPE] kitchen, and for each, note the unit of measure to count in (case, lb, bottle) and a placeholder column for par level. Present it as a table with columns: Item Category, Unit of Measure, Par Level (fill in), Current Count (fill in).
prompts.proTip: Fill in your real par levels once, save the sheet as a template, and reuse it weekly — the AI's job is building the structure, not guessing your actual numbers.
fields: CATEGORY, e.g., dry goods, walk-in cooler, bar

prompts.title: Email: Requesting Quotes From a New Potential Supplier
prompts.useWhen: You're shopping around for a new vendor (produce, linens, cleaning supplies) and need a clear request-for-quote email (RFQ email, new vendor inquiry).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] reaching out to [POTENTIAL VENDOR NAME] for the first time about [PRODUCT/SERVICE CATEGORY]. Write an email introducing our restaurant briefly, stating our approximate order volume or frequency of [FREQUENCY], and asking for pricing, minimum order requirements, and delivery schedule. Keep it under 120 words and professional — this is a first impression email.
prompts.proTip: Ask 2-3 vendors the exact same questions using this template so the quotes actually come back in a format you can compare apples to apples.

prompts.title: SOP: Handling an Equipment Breakdown Emergency
prompts.useWhen: A walk-in cooler, fryer, or other critical piece of equipment goes down midshift and staff need clear steps instead of scrambling (equipment failure, walk-in breakdown, emergency SOP).
prompts.prompt: You are an operations manager writing an emergency SOP for [RESTAURANT NAME] covering what to do if [EQUIPMENT, e.g., the walk-in cooler] breaks down during service. Include the immediate first steps (who to notify, what to do with food safety), who to call for repair ([REPAIR CONTACT INFO PLACEHOLDER]), and how to communicate the impact to the kitchen and front of house. Write it as a numbered step-by-step list of no more than 8 steps.
prompts.proTip: Print this and tape it inside the office door or near the equipment itself — in an actual emergency, nobody is searching a shared drive for the right document.

prompts.title: Plan: Weekly Staff Scheduling Approach
prompts.useWhen: You're building next week's schedule and want a structured way to think through coverage instead of just filling slots from memory (staff schedule, weekly scheduling plan).
prompts.prompt: You are a scheduling consultant for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Our typical weekly volume pattern is: [DESCRIBE, e.g., slow Mon-Tue, moderate Wed-Thu, packed Fri-Sun]. We have [NUMBER] staff across [ROLES, e.g., servers, cooks, hosts]. Give me a framework for how to allocate more staff to peak shifts without overstaffing slow ones, including how many people per role I'd realistically need on a slow night versus a peak night. Present it as a simple table by day and role.
prompts.proTip: Feed in last month's actual sales-per-hour data if you have it — the more real numbers you give the AI, the less generic the staffing suggestions will be.

prompts.title: Email: Notifying Guests of a Temporary Closure
prompts.useWhen: You need to let guests know about a closure for renovation, weather, a private buyout, or a holiday, and want to avoid a wall of cancellations (temporary closure notice, closed for renovation announcement).
prompts.prompt: You are writing an announcement for [RESTAURANT NAME] about being closed [DATES] due to [REASON, e.g., kitchen renovation, a private event, severe weather]. Write a short email and matching social post that clearly states the closure dates, briefly explains why in a positive light if appropriate, and tells guests what to do if they have an existing reservation. Keep both under 90 words and reassuring, not alarming.
prompts.proTip: Post the social version to your Google Business Profile too, not just Instagram — that's often the first place people check before showing up.

prompts.title: Checklist: Health Inspection Prep
prompts.useWhen: You know a health inspection is coming (or want to always be ready for a surprise one) and want a walkthrough checklist covering the areas inspectors actually check (health inspection prep, food safety walkthrough).
prompts.prompt: You are a food safety consultant preparing [RESTAURANT NAME] for a routine health inspection. Create a pre-inspection walkthrough checklist covering the major areas inspectors typically review: food storage temperatures, handwashing stations, date labeling, pest control signs, cleanliness of prep surfaces, and employee food safety practices. Present it as a checklist of 12-15 specific, actionable items a manager could walk through in 30 minutes.
prompts.proTip: Treat this as a weekly self-check, not a once-a-year scramble — restaurants that pass easily are usually the ones that never let it slide in between visits.

prompts.title: Analysis: Calculating Food Cost % and Setting a Menu Price
prompts.useWhen: You're pricing a new dish and want to make sure the price actually hits your target food cost percentage instead of guessing (food cost calculation, menu pricing).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant cost accountant. Help me price [DISH NAME]. The ingredients and costs per portion are: [LIST INGREDIENTS WITH COSTS]. Our target food cost percentage is [TARGET %, e.g., 28%]. Calculate the total plate cost, then show me the menu price needed to hit that target percentage, plus what the actual food cost percentage would be at two nearby price points (one slightly lower, one slightly higher) so I can see the tradeoff. Present it as a simple table.
prompts.proTip: Round the final price to match your menu's existing pricing pattern (like always ending in .95 or .00) — a technically correct price that looks out of place hurts more than it helps.

prompts.title: Report: Weekly Sales Summary for Owner or Investors
prompts.useWhen: You need to turn raw weekly sales numbers into a short, readable summary for an owner, partner, or investor instead of just forwarding a spreadsheet (weekly sales report, owner update).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant financial analyst. Here is this week's sales data for [RESTAURANT NAME]: [PASTE NUMBERS: total sales, comparison to last week or last year, top-selling items, any notable events]. Write a short summary covering total sales performance, the standout positive, one area of concern if the data shows one, and a onesentence outlook for next week. Keep it under 150 words and written for someone who doesn't want to dig through the numbers themselves.
prompts.proTip: Keep these summaries in one running document — after a few months, you'll be able to ask the AI to compare trends across the whole stretch instead of just week to week.

prompts.title: Analysis: Checking Labor Cost Percentage Against Target
prompts.useWhen: You want to see whether your labor spend is in a healthy range compared to sales, and get specific ideas if it's running hot (labor cost percentage, overstaffing analysis).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant operations consultant. Our total labor cost last [PERIOD, e.g., week or month] was [LABOR COST $] against total sales of [SALES $]. Our target labor cost percentage is [TARGET %, e.g., 30%]. Calculate our actual labor cost percentage, tell me how far off target we are in dollars, and suggest 3 specific, realistic ways to close the gap without cutting service quality (schedule adjustments, cross-training, shift length changes).
prompts.proTip: Break this out by shift (lunch vs. dinner, weekday vs. weekend) if you have the data — restaurant labor problems are almost always concentrated in a few specific shifts, not spread evenly.

prompts.title: Email/Post: Explaining a Price Increase to Staff or Guests
prompts.useWhen: You need to raise menu prices and want to communicate it honestly to your team or your regulars without it feeling like an apology or a confession (price increase announcement, explaining higher prices).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] communicating a menu price increase of [AMOUNT/PERCENTAGE] effective [DATE], driven by [REASON, e.g., rising ingredient and labor costs]. Write two versions: a short, honest note to staff so they can speak confidently if guests ask, and a brief, low-key social post for guests that doesn't overapologize or dwell on it. Keep both under 90 words and confident in tone, not defensive.
prompts.proTip: Brief your servers on this before it goes public — nothing undermines a confident price-increase message like a server who seems caught off guard when a guest mentions it.
fields: REASON, e.g., rising ingredient and labor costs

prompts.title: Analysis: Break-Even Analysis for a New Item or Expansion
prompts.useWhen: You're considering adding a new piece of equipment, a patio expansion, or a new service (like brunch) and want to know roughly how much extra revenue it needs to pay for itself (break-even analysis, ROI on new equipment or service).
prompts.prompt: You are a small business financial analyst. We are considering [INVESTMENT, e.g., adding a patio with 20 seats, or launching a weekend brunch service]. The estimated upfront and ongoing costs are: [LIST COSTS]. The expected additional revenue per [DAY/ WEEK/MONTH] is roughly [ESTIMATE]. Calculate approximately how long it would take to break even, and note 2 assumptions in this estimate that are worth double-checking before committing.
prompts.proTip: Run this with a conservative revenue estimate and an optimistic one side by side — knowing your break-even range under both scenarios is far more useful than one single number.

prompts.title: Report: Monthly P&L Summary in Plain Language
prompts.useWhen: You have a profit and loss statement from your bookkeeper or POS system and want it translated into plain language you can actually explain to a partner or lender (P&L summary, monthly financial recap).
prompts.prompt: You are a financial translator for small business owners. Here is our profit and loss summary for [MONTH]: [PASTE KEY NUMBERS: revenue, COGS, labor, rent, other expenses, net profit/loss]. Explain in plain English how the month went, which expense category grew the most compared to typical restaurant benchmarks, and one question I should ask my bookkeeper based on this data. Keep it under 150 words and avoid accounting jargon.
prompts.proTip: Always verify any benchmark percentages the AI references against your specific market and restaurant type — a fine-dining benchmark and a fast-casual benchmark can look very different.

prompts.title: Plan: Budgeting for a Slow Season
prompts.useWhen: You know a slow season is coming (post-holiday January, a summer lull, a slow month for your specific concept) and want to plan for it instead of reacting to it (slow season budget, seasonal cash flow planning).
prompts.prompt: You are a small business financial planner. [RESTAURANT NAME] historically sees a [PERCENTAGE, e.g., 20%] drop in sales during [SLOW PERIOD, e.g., January and February]. Our typical monthly expenses are: [LIST KEY EXPENSE CATEGORIES AND AMOUNTS]. Suggest a practical budgeting approach for this slow period, including which costs are safest to trim temporarily and which should stay fixed to protect quality and staff retention. Present it as a table: Expense Category, Recommendation, Why.
prompts.proTip: Start this planning process at least 6-8 weeks before the slow season hits — reactive cost-cutting during the slump itself almost always damages guest experience.
fields: SLOW PERIOD, e.g., January and February
LIST KEY EXPENSE CATEGORIES AND AMOUNTS

prompts.title: Analysis: Preparing to Negotiate a Lease Renewal
prompts.useWhen: Your lease is coming up for renewal and you want to walk into the conversation with the landlord prepared instead of just accepting the new number (lease renewal, rent negotiation prep).
prompts.prompt: You are a small business advisor helping [RESTAURANT NAME] prepare to negotiate a lease renewal. Our current rent is [CURRENT RENT], the landlord has proposed [PROPOSED NEW RENT], and our lease is up on [DATE]. Our sales have [TRENDED UP/ DOWN/STAYED FLAT] over the lease term. Help me build 3 talking points for the negotiation (using our track record, market comparisons, or a longer lease term as leverage), and one fallback ask if they won't move on the rent itself (build-out credit, longer free-rent period, etc.).
prompts.proTip: Research 2-3 comparable local lease rates before this conversation if you can — landlords respond much better to specific numbers than general pushback.

prompts.title: Response: A Guest Is Demanding a Refund You Don't Think Is Warranted
prompts.useWhen: A guest is pushing for a full refund over something minor and you want to hold a fair line without escalating the situation (refund dispute, unreasonable refund request).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant manager responding to a guest who is requesting a full refund for [SITUATION, e.g., a dish they ate most of before complaining]. Write a response that acknowledges their frustration genuinely, explains what we're able to offer instead (partial refund, credit, remake) and why, and stays firm without sounding dismissive or accusatory. Keep it under 100 words and calm throughout.
prompts.proTip: Always offer something, even if it's smaller than what they asked for — a guest who feels heard and gets a partial gesture is far less likely to escalate than one who gets a flat no.
fields: SITUATION, e.g., a dish they ate most of before complaining

prompts.title: Script: De-Escalating an Angry Guest In Person
prompts.useWhen: A guest is visibly upset at the table or host stand and a manager needs calm, in-the-moment language to defuse it before it disrupts the room (angry customer, deescalation script).
prompts.prompt: You are a hospitality trainer writing de-escalation talking points for managers at [RESTAURANT NAME].
