Create a short script for approaching an upset guest whose complaint is about [GENERAL SITUATION, e.g., a long wait or a mistake with their order]. The script should open by lowering the temperature (not defending first), ask one clarifying question, and offer a concrete next step. Keep it to 4 lines of natural spoken language, not corporate phrasing.
prompts.proTip: Have the manager physically step slightly to the side or crouch to table height when delivering this — body language does as much de-escalating as the words.

prompts.title: Email: Responding to a Reported Health or Cleanliness Concern
prompts.useWhen: A guest raises a serious concern about cleanliness or food handling (not a routine complaint) and you need a careful, honest written response (health concern complaint, cleanliness allegation).
prompts.prompt: You are the owner of [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a guest who raised a concern about [SPECIFIC CONCERN, e.g., something they saw in the kitchen or dining room]. Write a serious, respectful response that thanks them for flagging it, confirms we're looking into it directly (without admitting fault or making promises about outcomes), and asks for any additional detail that would help us address it. Keep it under 110 words and avoid sounding defensive.
prompts.proTip: For anything involving a real health or safety allegation, loop in ownership and, if it's serious, your insurance provider before sending a final response — get the specifics right before you put anything in writing.

prompts.title: Response: A Guest Says They Got Sick After Eating With You
prompts.useWhen: A guest reports getting sick after a visit and you need a careful, empathetic first response while the situation is still being looked into (foodborne illness claim, guest got sick complaint).
prompts.prompt: You are responding to a guest who reported feeling sick after visiting [RESTAURANT NAME] on [DATE]. Write an empathetic first-response message that takes their report seriously, asks for helpful details (what they ordered, when symptoms started, whether others in their party were affected) to help us investigate, and avoids admitting cause or fault since that hasn't been determined. Keep it under 100 words and sincerely concerned in tone.
prompts.proTip: Treat any illness report as something to escalate to ownership and your insurance/ legal contact immediately — this prompt is for your first considerate response, not for handling the situation on your own from here.

prompts.title: Script: Addressing a Conflict Between Two Staff Members
prompts.useWhen: Tension between two employees is affecting the shift and you need to prepare for a conversation that resolves it instead of picking a side (staff conflict, coworker dispute).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant manager preparing to mediate a conflict between two staff members over [GENERAL ISSUE, e.g., a disagreement about side work or a personality clash]. Write 4-5 talking points for a joint conversation that stays neutral, focuses on the specific behaviors affecting the team rather than character judgments, and ends with both people agreeing to one concrete change. Keep the tone fair and calm, not like a lecture.
prompts.proTip: Meet with each person separately first to hear their side before the joint conversation — walking in with context prevents the meeting from turning into two people just repeating themselves at each other.

prompts.title: Response: Suspecting a Negative Review Isn't Genuine
prompts.useWhen: A review seems suspicious — from a competitor, someone who never actually visited, or wildly inconsistent with your records — and you need a measured public response while you look into it (fake review, suspicious review, competitor review).
prompts.prompt: You are responding publicly to a review of [RESTAURANT NAME] that raises questions because [REASON FOR SUSPICION, e.g., we have no record of a reservation or order matching the details]. Write a calm, professional reply that doesn't accuse the reviewer outright, politely notes we couldn't locate a matching visit in our system, and invites them to reach out directly with more details. Keep it under 80 words and avoid sounding defensive or paranoid.
prompts.proTip: If you genuinely believe a review is fake, report it directly to the platform (Google, Yelp) using their official process — a calm public reply and a formal report are two separate, both-necessary steps.

prompts.title: Response: Handling an Overcharge or Billing Dispute
prompts.useWhen: A guest contacts you saying they were charged incorrectly (double-charged, wrong total, unauthorized tip amount) and you need a clear, reassuring response (billing dispute, overcharge complaint, wrong charge).
prompts.prompt: You are a manager at [RESTAURANT NAME] responding to a guest who says they were [SPECIFIC BILLING ISSUE, e.g., charged twice for their meal on DATE]. Write a response that apologizes for the inconvenience, confirms the specific next step you're taking to verify and fix it (checking the POS, processing a refund, timeline), and gives a realistic timeframe for resolution. Keep it under 90 words and reassuring.
prompts.proTip: Always verify the actual transaction in your POS or payment processor before promising a refund amount — commit to the fix in the message, but confirm the number before you send it.

prompts.title: Script: Talking Points for Letting an Employee Go
prompts.useWhen: You need to have a termination conversation and want clear, respectful talking points prepared in advance instead of improvising in the moment (firing an employee, termination conversation).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant manager preparing talking points for letting go of an employee due to [GENERAL REASON, e.g., repeated policy violations after prior warnings]. Write 4-5 talking points that state the decision clearly and early in the conversation (don't bury it), reference the specific documented issues without being harsh, explain next steps (final pay, any paperwork), and end respectfully. Keep the tone direct, calm, and dignified.
prompts.proTip: Review your state's requirements for final paycheck timing and any required termination paperwork with an HR advisor or employment attorney before the conversation — the talking points here cover what to say, not the legal requirements around how you say goodbye.

prompts.title: Plan: Themed Event Night Concept
prompts.useWhen: You want to fill a slow night with a themed event (trivia, wine dinner, live music) and need a full concept, not just a vague idea (themed event night, restaurant event planning).
prompts.prompt: You are an events planner for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We want to launch a [EVENT TYPE, e.g., trivia night or wine pairing dinner] on our slowest night, [DAY OF WEEK]. Build a concept including a suggested format/schedule for the evening, a simple pricing structure, what we'd need to prep or promote in advance, and one idea to make it feel like a signature event rather than a one-off. Present it as a short outline with headers, not a wall of text.
prompts.proTip: Run it as a 4-week trial before committing to it as a permanent weekly fixture — give it time to build word of mouth before judging attendance.
fields: EVENT TYPE, e.g., trivia night or wine pairing dinner

prompts.title: Proposal: Catering Quote for a Corporate Client
prompts.useWhen: A local business or organization wants a catering quote for an office event and you need a professional proposal fast (corporate catering proposal, catering quote).
prompts.prompt: You are the catering manager at [RESTAURANT NAME] preparing a proposal for [CLIENT/COMPANY NAME] for an event of [GUEST COUNT] people on [DATE]. They're interested in [EVENT TYPE, e.g., a lunch buffet]. Build a proposal with 2-3 package options at different price points using items we regularly cater ([LIST A FEW MENU ITEMS]), what's included (setup, disposable ware, delivery), and a note on how far in advance we need final headcount. Present the packages as a table.
prompts.proTip: Ask for a shorter "quick quote" version too — many corporate clients just want a single number by email before they'll even look at a full proposal.
fields: EVENT TYPE, e.g., a lunch buffet

prompts.title: Plan: Annual Slow-Season vs. Peak-Season Strategy
prompts.useWhen: You want to map out the whole year at a glance so you're not caught off guard by predictable slow and busy stretches (annual planning calendar, seasonal strategy).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant strategy consultant. [RESTAURANT NAME]'s historical pattern is: peak months are [LIST], slow months are [LIST]. Build a simple month-by-month strategic focus for the year — for peak months, note the priority (staffing up, reservation management); for slow months, note the priority (promotions, staff training, maintenance projects). Present it as a 12-row table: Month, Expected Volume, Strategic Focus.
prompts.proTip: Revisit and adjust this table every quarter with actual results — the first version is a hypothesis, not a fixed plan.

prompts.title: Plan: Feasibility Considerations for a Second Location
prompts.useWhen: You're seriously considering expanding to a second location and want a structured list of what to evaluate before committing (second location, restaurant expansion planning).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant expansion consultant. [RESTAURANT NAME] is considering opening a second location in [POTENTIAL NEW AREA/NEIGHBORHOOD]. Our current location does [APPROXIMATE ANNUAL REVENUE] with [SEATING CAPACITY] seats. Build a checklist of the key factors to evaluate before committing — covering market/ demographics, cost, operational capacity (can current management actually run two), and financing — with 2-3 specific questions under each factor.
prompts.proTip: Be honest with the AI about your current management bandwidth, not just the market opportunity — most second-location struggles come from operational strain, not a bad market pick.

prompts.title: Plan: Cross-Promotion Ideas with Local Businesses
prompts.useWhen: You want to partner with nearby businesses (a brewery, a theater, a gym) for mutual promotion but need concrete ideas instead of a vague "let's collab" (local business partnership, cross-promotion).
prompts.prompt: You are a local marketing strategist for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We want to build a cross-promotion partnership with [TYPE OF BUSINESS, e.g., a nearby brewery or boutique fitness studio]. Suggest 3 concrete cross-promotion ideas (a joint discount, a bundled event, a referral perk) that would benefit both businesses roughly equally, and a short outreach message I could send to propose the partnership. Keep the outreach message under 100 words.
prompts.proTip: Propose partnerships with businesses that share your ideal customer but aren't direct competitors — a yoga studio and a healthy-focused restaurant works; two restaurants on the same block competing for the same table usually doesn't.

prompts.title: Plan: Holiday Rush Prep Timeline
prompts.useWhen: A major holiday season (Thanksgiving, Christmas, Valentine's Day) is coming and you want a countdown timeline so nothing gets missed in the crunch (holiday prep timeline, Thanksgiving rush planning).
prompts.prompt: You are an operations manager building a prep timeline for [RESTAURANT NAME] ahead of [HOLIDAY/BUSY PERIOD], which is [NUMBER] weeks away. Cover the key workstreams: staffing/scheduling, inventory ordering, marketing/reservations, and any special menu prep. Build a week-by-week countdown from now until the holiday, with 2-3 specific action items per week. Present it as a table: Week, Focus Area, Action Items.
prompts.proTip: Assign a specific person's name to each row once you finalize it — a timeline with no owner attached to each task tends to quietly slip.

prompts.title: Plan: Local Sourcing or Sustainability Initiative
prompts.useWhen: You want to start sourcing more locally or reduce waste and need both a practical plan and messaging to tell guests about it honestly (local sourcing initiative, sustainability messaging).
prompts.prompt: You are a sustainability consultant for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We want to start [INITIATIVE, e.g., sourcing produce from local farms or reducing single-use packaging]. Suggest 3 realistic first steps to start this without disrupting current operations, and draft one short, honest paragraph we could use on our menu or website describing the initiative — factual and specific, not vague "eco-friendly" language we can't back up.
prompts.proTip: Only claim what you can specifically point to (a named local farm, an actual percentage reduction) — vague sustainability claims invite more scrutiny than they're worth.

prompts.title: Plan: Annual Strengths/Weaknesses Planning Session Prep
prompts.useWhen: You're heading into a year-end or quarterly planning session with your management team and want a structured discussion guide instead of an unfocused conversation (annual planning meeting, SWOT-style review, management strategy session).
prompts.prompt: You are a facilitator helping [RESTAURANT NAME] prep for a management planning session. Build a discussion guide with 4 sections: what worked well this year, what didn't work and why, the 2-3 biggest opportunities for next year, and the 2-3 biggest risks to watch. For each section, write 2-3 open-ended discussion questions to prompt real conversation rather than yes/no answers.
prompts.proTip: Send the discussion guide to your managers a few days ahead of the meeting — people give sharper, more honest answers when they've had time to think instead of being put on the spot.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Turn One Seasonal Ingredient Into a Month of Content
prompts.useWhen: You have one great seasonal ingredient or dish and want an entire month of social content built around it in one go instead of brainstorming post by post (monthly content calendar, seasonal ingredient content plan).
prompts.prompt: You are a social media strategist for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We're featuring [SEASONAL INGREDIENT OR DISH] throughout [MONTH]. Do this in steps: (1) suggest 4 different dishes or drink specials we could build around it across the month, (2) for each, write a short Instagram caption, (3) organize all 4 into a posting calendar noting which week to post each one and why that timing makes sense (building anticipation, mid-month reminder, lastchance urgency), and (4) suggest one piece of "behind the scenes" content to post between the dish announcements. Present the final calendar as a table.
prompts.proTip: Batch your photography for all 4 dishes in one session at the start of the month — this prompt gives you the words, but you'll still need the visuals ready to match the calendar.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Complete New-Hire Onboarding Packet
prompts.useWhen: You've just hired someone and want the whole onboarding experience — welcome message, first-week plan, and handbook excerpt — built together so it's consistent, not assembled from scattered documents (new hire packet, onboarding bundle).
prompts.prompt: You are building a complete onboarding packet for a new [ROLE] at [RESTAURANT NAME]. Do this in steps: (1) write a warm welcome message confirming their start date of [DATE] and what to bring, (2) build a simple day-by-day plan for their first week covering what they should learn or shadow each day, (3) write a short "who's who" section introducing key people they'll work with by role, and (4) list 3 questions they should feel free to ask during week one so they don't feel awkward asking. Format it as one clean document with headers for each section.
prompts.proTip: Reuse this exact prompt for every new hire in the same role — swap only the name and date, and you'll have a consistent onboarding experience without rebuilding it each time.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Launch a Limited-Time Offer Across Every Channel
prompts.useWhen: You've decided on a new limited-time dish or promotion and need everything needed to launch it — description, social posts, email, and staff talking points — built together so the messaging matches everywhere (LTO campaign, full promotion rollout).
prompts.prompt: You are launching a limited-time offer at [RESTAURANT NAME]: [DISH/ PROMOTION DETAILS], available [DATE RANGE]. Do this in steps: (1) write a menu description (15-25 words), (2) write an Instagram caption and a Facebook post announcing it, (3) write a one-line staff talking point servers can use to recommend it at the table, and (4) write a short "last chance" follow-up post to run in the final few days of the promotion. Keep the tone consistent across all four and label each piece clearly.
prompts.proTip: Schedule the "last chance" post before you get busy — it's the piece that gets forgotten most often, and it's usually the highest-converting one.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Full Negative-Review Recovery Plan
prompts.useWhen: A bad review points to a real, recurring problem and you want to handle the public response, the internal fix, and the guest follow-up all at once instead of just replying and moving on (review recovery system, fixing the root cause of a complaint).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant reputation and operations consultant for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Here's a recent negative review: "[PASTE REVIEW TEXT]." Do this in steps: (1) write a public reply following our usual tone of [TONE], (2) identify the likely root operational cause behind the complaint (not just the symptom), (3) suggest one concrete, low-cost fix we could implement this week, and (4) draft a short private follow-up message we could send the guest once the fix is in place, inviting them back. Label each of the four parts clearly.
prompts.proTip: Actually follow through on step 3 before you send step 4 — inviting a guest back to see "we fixed it" only works if something really changed.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Plan and Announce a Menu Price Increase End-to-End
prompts.useWhen: You've decided prices need to go up and want the pricing math, the staff briefing, and the guest-facing message all handled consistently in one pass (price increase rollout, raising menu prices).
prompts.prompt: You are helping [RESTAURANT NAME] roll out a menu price increase. Our food and labor costs have risen by [PERCENTAGE/AMOUNT], and we're increasing prices on [ITEMS OR "across the board"] by [AMOUNT/PERCENTAGE], effective [DATE]. Do this in steps: (1) suggest how to round the new prices so they feel intentional, not arbitrary, (2) write a short internal note to staff explaining the change so they can speak to it confidently, (3) write a brief, confident social post for guests, and (4) write one talking point servers can use if a regular guest comments on the new price. Label each part clearly.
prompts.proTip: Time the staff note to go out at least 3 days before the guest-facing post — your team should never learn about a price change from a customer before they hear it from you.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Two-Week Grand Opening Campaign
prompts.useWhen: You're opening a new restaurant or location and need a full two-week campaign — press outreach, social calendar, and email — built together instead of piecing it together channel by channel (grand opening campaign, opening week marketing plan).
prompts.prompt: You are building a two-week grand opening campaign for [RESTAURANT NAME], opening [DATE] at [LOCATION]. Our concept is [BRIEF CONCEPT DESCRIPTION]. Do this in steps: (1) write a short local press release opener pitching the opening to local media, (2) build a 2-week social content calendar with one post idea and caption per key day (announcement, countdown, opening day, first-week highlight), (3) write a launch email for our list offering [OPENING OFFER IF ANY], and (4) suggest 2 local businesses or influencers worth personally inviting to opening week. Present the social calendar as a table.
prompts.proTip: Send the press release at least 2 weeks before opening — local media and bloggers need lead time to plan a feature, not a same-week pitch.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Full Holiday Catering Sales Push
prompts.useWhen: Holiday catering season is approaching and you want the outreach email, social promotion, and follow-up sequence built together to actually convert inquiries into booked orders (holiday catering campaign, catering sales push).
prompts.prompt: You are building a holiday catering sales campaign for [RESTAURANT NAME] ahead of [HOLIDAY, e.g., Thanksgiving]. Our catering menu includes [LIST 2-3 POPULAR CATERING ITEMS]. Do this in steps: (1) write an email to past catering customers announcing holiday catering availability with an order-by deadline of [DATE], (2) write a social post promoting the same, (3) write a short reply template for when someone inquires, asking the key details you need (headcount, date, dietary needs), and (4) write a one-line reminder message to send to anyone who inquired but hasn't confirmed, one week before the order deadline. Label each part clearly.
prompts.proTip: Set your order-by deadline earlier than you think you need to — holiday week always brings a wave of last-minute requests you can't fulfill if your kitchen is already maxed out.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Staff Culture and Retention Action Plan
prompts.useWhen: Turnover has been high and you want a real plan — not just a vague "improve culture" goal — built from a quick pulse-check through to a concrete action plan (staff retention plan, improving team culture).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant culture consultant for [RESTAURANT NAME]. We've had higher-than-normal turnover recently, particularly among [ROLE/SHIFT IF KNOWN]. Do this in steps: (1) write 5 short, anonymous pulse-check questions we could ask staff to understand what's driving it, (2) suggest 3 likely root causes based on common reasons restaurant staff leave, (3) for each likely cause, suggest one realistic, low-cost action we could take, and (4) write a short message to the team introducing the pulse-check so it doesn't feel like a trap. Label each part clearly.
prompts.proTip: Actually share a summary of what you heard and what you're changing back with the team afterward — a survey that visibly goes nowhere does more damage to trust than not asking at all.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Complete Private Event Sales Funnel
prompts.useWhen: You want every touchpoint of a private event inquiry — first reply, proposal, follow-up, and post-event thank you — written together so nothing falls through the cracks between steps (private event funnel, full event booking sequence).
prompts.prompt: You are building the full private event communication sequence for [RESTAURANT NAME]. Do this in steps: (1) write a first-reply email to a new private event inquiry that asks the key qualifying questions (date, headcount, budget, occasion), (2) write a short proposal template with 2 package tiers based on our typical private event minimums of [MINIMUM SPEND/GUEST COUNT], (3) write a gentle follow-up email for if they go quiet for a week after receiving the proposal, and (4) write a post-event thank-you email that also asks for a review. Label each part clearly and keep the tone warm and professional throughout.
prompts.proTip: Set a calendar reminder to actually send step 3 exactly one week after every proposal — most lost private events aren't lost to a "no," they're lost to nobody following up.

prompts.title: Power Prompt: Build a Competitor Positioning and Marketing Angle
prompts.useWhen: You want to understand how you stack up against nearby competitors and turn that into a clear marketing angle, not just a list of what other restaurants offer (competitive analysis, finding your restaurant's marketing angle).
prompts.prompt: You are a restaurant positioning strategist. [RESTAURANT NAME] competes with [LIST 2-3 NEARBY COMPETITORS AND WHAT THEY'RE KNOWN FOR]. Our strengths are [YOUR STRENGTHS, e.g., made-from-scratch everything, a specific chef background, a unique setting]. Do this in steps: (1) build a simple comparison table of price point, cuisine style, and standout feature for us versus each competitor, (2) identify one gap none of them are filling that we credibly could, (3) turn that gap into a one-sentence positioning statement for us, and (4) suggest 2 marketing angles (a tagline direction and a content theme) built on that positioning.
prompts.proTip: Be honest about competitor strengths instead of only listing their weaknesses — a positioning strategy built on wishful thinking about the competition falls apart the first time a guest compares you directly.
fields: LIST 2-3 NEARBY COMPETITORS AND WHAT THEY'RE KNOWN FOR
